Bring the Suns Place to the Meridian above the Horizon, for his Noon - Altitude which will shew the Degrees of it, counted from the Horizon. For his Midnight - Deprejfion below the North Point of the Horizon, you must bring the opposite Point to the Sun ’ s present Place, as before to the Meridian and the Degrees there intercepted between thatPoint and the Horizon, are his Midnight - Depression.

plotson.c: PLOTS ON, br Flotsam, is a Word proper to the Sea, signifying any Goods loft by Shipwreck, and lie floating and swimming upon the Top of the Water; which, with Jetfon, and Lagon, and others, are given to the Lord Admiral by his Letters Pa - tent. Jetfon, is a thing cast out of the Ship, being in danger of Wreck, and beaten to the Shore by the Waters, or cast on the Shore by the Mariners. Lagon, or Lagan, or Ligan, is that which lieth in the Bottom of the Sea. Shares, are ‘ Goods duetomoreby Proportion. ’

palatumthepalate.c: PALATUM, the Palate, is the upper part of the Mouth, which because it resembles the Roof of an House, is thence called the Roof of the Mouth

palatios.c: PALATI Os, is a small One almost square, it makes the posterior part of the Roof of the Mouth: It is joined to that part of the Os Ma - xi Hare, which makes the fore - part of the Palate; it is also joined to its fellow, and the PrCceffus Ptetigoidceus., It has a small Hole, thro ’ which a Branch of the fifth pair of Nerves goes to the Membrane of the Palate.

palindrome.c: PALINDROME, is a Disease into which one Blanchard.

pale.c: PALE, one of the Eight Ho - nourable Ordinaries in Heral - dry, containing the third part of the Escutcheon, thus. He beared ! Gules, a Pale Or,

palltheheralds.c: PALL, the Heralds have a kind of Cross, which they call by this Name and they describe it thus. , He beareth Gules a Cross Pall Argent

pallet.c: PALLET, is the Moiety, or half of the Pale l and trust never be charged with any thing either Quick or Dead; neither can it be divided into two equal parts, but it may into four, for one fourth part of the Pallet, or ? part of the Pale, is called an Endorse. If the Pale be upon any Beast, they lay the Beast is Debrufed with the Pale: But if the Beast be upon the Pale, they fay he is Supported of the Pale. Pallets alio is a Term which belongs to the Balance of a Watch, or Movement. See Balance.

PALLET is a Room within the Hold of a Ship, closely parted from it, in Which by laying some Pigs of Lead, c. a Ship may be fuffici - entry Balafted, without losing room in the Hold which therefore will serve for Stowing the more Goods.

palliation.c: PALLIATION of a Disease, or a Palliative Cure, is a Method which helps ( as much as is possible incurable Diseases by the Application of present Remedies.

pallieralanding.c: PALLIER, a Landing - place in a Stair - Case of a Step, which being ifiuch broader than the others, serves to reft upon. P ALLIS ADOES, Or Pall [ fades in Fortification are strong Wooden harp - pointed Stakes, fix or f even. Inches square, eight Foot long, of which three Foot is in the Ground, fet up half a Foot sometimes one above another, With a cross piece of Timber that binds them together. Some of these are also sometimes arm ’ d with two or three Iron Spikes. These Pallifadoes are usually sited in the void Spaces Without the Glacis, near the Bastions and Curtains and in the Avenues of all such Polls as are liable to be surprize by the Enemy, of carried by A fault. Sometimes they are driven downright in the Ground, and sometimes Hand at an Acute Angle towards the Enemy, that if they Ihould throw Cords about them to pull them up, they may flip of again. Pallifadoes are always ' planted on the Berrhe of Bastions, and at the Gorges of Half - Moons and o - ther Out - works: They also Pallifade usually the Bottom of the Ditch; and to be sure, the Para - pet of the Covert way Z And tho ’ sometimes they have placed thele Pallifadoes three Foot from the said Parapet outwards towards the Campaign, yet of late they have been planted in the very mid - dle of the Covert Way: All Pallifadoes fiiould Hand so close, as to admit between them only the Muzzle of a Mufquet, or a Pike.

palmarislongus.c: PALMARIS Longus, is a Musele of the Palm of the Hand, which has an Acute beginning from the Internal Extuberance of the Or Humeri / yard soon becoming a Plelfey Belly / and contra - Sing it felt again to a long, flat, lender Tendon, inarches Obliquely with the Tendon of the Flexor Carpi Superior - and palling over the Ligamentum Annulare, where it expands it self, and cleaves firmly to the Skin of the Palm, is inferred to the Roots of the Fingers laterally; it being there di - vided. to transmit the Tendons that bend them. Columbus observes the long beginning of this Muscle, ' from the Extuberance of the Os - Humeri, is sometimes wanting, which Observation is alio Confirmed by our Experience ( faith ME Cowper: ) It assists, in firmly grasping any Tadile Body, and defends the subjacent Tendons from External Injuries.

paemarisbrevis.c: PAEMARIS Brevis, is a Muscle of the Palm of the Hand, by Spigelim, called, Caro Muftulofa Quadrata. Anatomists ( faith Cowper ) have been extreamly deceived in their Idea ’ s of this Muscle; it not arising from the Membrana Carnosa, as Co - lumbus pretends, or from the eighth Bone of the Carpus, as Fallopius writes; but it springeth with a broad Membrane - like Tendon from the Enter - nal part of the Os Metacarpi Minimi Digiti, and one of the Bones of the Carpus whence amend - ing over the AbduRor Minimi Digiti, it becomes a thin disgregate Fleshy Muscle, marching under the Tendinous expansion of the former in the Palm; and is inserted by a short, strong Tendon, to the eighth Boite of the Carpus. This a ( fling draws tlte Mans Luna; towards the Os Metacarpi Minimi Digiti, whereby the Palm becomes hol - low contrary to the Opinion of Spigelim, who pretends it extends the Hand when we open it; which is not done by any proper Muscle, but by the Common Extenders of the Fingers.

palmus.c: PALMUS, is a Shivering, or Palpitation of the Heart, caused by a Convulfioiij or Irritation of the Nerves. Blanchard.

palpebr.c: PALPEBR E are the Eye - Lids, or Coverings of the Eyes; they consist outwardly of a very thin Skin; inwardly they are lined with the Peri - cranium, which is here molt thin and smooth; and between these two, is the Membrana Carnosa, which is also very thin. Stem observed several P anil a Lachrymalia in the Inner Membrane, which run on each side in - to one Dud ( which he calls Collide ) whereby the superfluous Moisture of the Eye - Lids is con - vered into the Nostrils. At their Edges they have little soft Cartilages called Cilia, which serve to strengthen them, and to make them meet and close the more exactly. Their Corners are called Canthi, the outer and letter of which hath a Gland in it called Innominata, which might well be called Lachrymal is, because it supplies most of the Mat - ter of the Tears.

palpitation.c: PALPITATION of the Heart when Natural, Is in the Systole thereof; whilst the Cone and the Sides are press ’ d together, the Basis and the Roots of the Vessels being blown up with J the Blood that gathers there, grows big and swoln. But it oft alio proceeds from an extraordinary Contra - ction of the Heart, or a Thick and irritating Mat - ter which sticks in the Heart; and this is a Dis - ease and preternatural. Blanchard.

paly.c: PALY, when an Escutcheon is divided into,, or to Even Divisions P ale - wife tis al - ways Blazon ’ d, Paly of,, or io, cc. Pieces but if the Number be odd, then the Field is firfh earned, and the Number of the Pales specified. The like is to be understood also of Barry and Bendy.

palybendy.c: PALY Bendy, is when a Coas: is divided both Pale and Bend - wife, as here. The Field Paly Bendy Lopa and Diamond. Guilliih, p.,.

panacea.c: PANACEA, was anciently a Name given by Galen to some Medicines which he had a great Opinion of: After, bf the Chymifts, it was the Term for their Boafted Universal Medicine, which they pretended would Cure all Diseases in all Cir cumftances, Ages, and Cohftitutiohs. There are several Panacea's whose Preparation you will find in Books of Chymistry and Pharmacy; as that of Mercury, of Antimony, &c. which perhaps may be good Medicines in many Cafes, but do all fall short of the Character of being Universal Me - - dicines, and indeed it seems impossible there can be any such thing. The Word Panacea comes from the Greek,, erav and rio / zs, omnia sand. There is ' also a Plant of this Name.

panaritium.c: PANARITIUM. Vid. Paronychias PANCHYMAGOGUES are Universal Pur - native Medicines that expel ail kinds of Humours; according to the ancient Way of expression.

pancreasthesweet.c: PANCREAS, the Sweet - bread, Pancratitm / Pancreon, Callicreas, Callicrcon, and LaRes, are all Synonymous. It is a conglomerated Glandule in the Abdomen, compared out of many Globe - les, or knots of Glands included in a common Membrane Which it hath from the Peritoneum; these Globules are joined to ' oneanother, partly by Membranes, and partly by Vessels. It is pla - ced behind the Ventricle, and fattened to the Gut Duodenum, and readies from the Cavity of the Liver cross the Abdomen, to the lower end of the Spleen: By its Dud at is annexed to the Duode - num, and sometimes to the Porus Bilarim, to the Rami Splenici, the Caul, the upper part of the. Mesentery, and the upper Nervous Plexus of the Abdomen; the Use and Office thereof, is to con - very a Volatile, Insipid, and Lymphatick Juice, or as others will have it ( for it is a disputable Point ) a something acid Juice, by its own DuRm to the Gut Duodenum, in order to a farther Fer - tentation and Volatilization of the Chyle, and to attemperate and allay the Qualities of the Gall: It is the biggest Glandule in the whole Body, but bigger in d Dog than a Man. Its Vessels are of five Kinds; for it hath Veins from the Ramus Splenicus; Arteries from the Left Branch of the Cceliaca, and sometimes from the Splenica. Nerves it receives from the Intercostal Pair, especially from the Upper Plexus of the Abdomen. It hath also many Lymphatick, Vessels, which pass as the reft do, to the common Recep - table of the Chyle. Besides which it hath a pro - per Dud of its own, which is sometimes called DuRus Wirtfnngianus, because found out by one iVirt fungus at Padua, about Years ago, but we usually call it the Pancrcatick, Dull: This Vessel hath usually but one Trunk, whose Orifice opens into the lower end of the Duodenum, or beginning of the Jejunum, and sometimes is joined to the DuRus Bilarius, with which it makes but one Mouth into the Insetting; within the Pancreas ( faith What ? J Wharton ) it is divided into two Branches which lend forth abundance of little Twigs into all the Globules, of which the Substance of the P ancreas is composed, where they imbibe the Humour that is separated by them from the Arteries, and by their Trunk transmit it to the Guts. The Pan - creatick Juice is never found in this Dud: any more than Urine is found in the Vreters by reason of the swiftness of its Motion, and the steepness of the way.

pandalea.c: PANDALEA, as the Modern Physicians call it, is the fame with a Solid Eleduary, but that it remains intire, for the Sugar being rightly boil - ed, is let grow hard; the Patient takes a piece of it like a Lambitive; it only differs from Rolls and Morfels, as to its shape. Blanchard.

pandemius.c: PANDEMIUS, ( fc. Morbus ) is a Disease which is universally rife in any place.

pandiculation.c: PANDICULATION, is the Reftleflhefs, Stretching, and EJneafinefs that usually accompt - nies the cold Fit of an Intermitting Fever ’ Tis supposed to be occasioned by a Convulsive Dila - tation of the Muscles, by which Nature'endea - vors to thro ’ off something that is disagreeable to them.

panicula.c: PANICULA, is a Term in Botany, for a kind of soft Woolly Beard or String, on which the eeds of sore Plants do hang Pendulous, as in Speeds, Millet, &c. it signifies the fame with Juba, and is opposed to Spica.

panniculuscarnosus.c: PANNICULUS Carnosus, is a fiat fort of Membrane in some part thick and Musculous; in other parts thin, with many Dublus ’ s of Fat in it: It covers the whole Body.

panis.c: PANIS fortis & durus. See Paine fort & dure.

panus.c: PANUS, is a Sort of Botch or Sore under the Arm - pits, Jaws, Ears, and Groins; to wit in the Glandulous Parts. It is also taken for Phy - gethus.

paper.c: PAPER - ce. All the Ads of the Council - board, occasional Proclamations, Difpatches, and Inftrudions for Foreign Ministers, Letters of In - telligence, and many other Publick Papers com - tunicated to the King ’ s Council, or the two Se - cretaries of State, are afterwards transmitted to the Paper - Office, wherein they are all disposed in a place of good Security and Convenience within the King ’ s Royal Palace. Also an Office so called, belonging to the Kings - Bench.

papilionaceousflower.c: PAPILIONACEOUS Flower of a Plants is by the Botanists accounted such an one as rere - lents something of the Figure of a Butter - fiy with its Wings displayed: And here the Pet ala, or Flower Leaves are always of a very Difform Fi - gure. They are four in Number, but joined to - gether at the Extremities, wherefore they are rather Monopetalous, than truly Tetrapetalous. One of these four Leaves is usually larger than the reft, and is ereded in the middle of the Flower, and by some called Vexillum. and Clypeus., The Plants that have this Flower, are of the Leguminous kind, as Pease, Vetches, &c.

papilla.c: PAPILLA, or the Nipple, is a red Excrefcency in the middle of each Brealb in the Pores whereof are received all theMilkyTubesor Pipes proceeding from the Glandules of the Breast It is of a Spongy Substance and covered with a very thin Skin: it is of Exquisite Sense, that both the Infants Mouth in Sucking, and the Trickling of the Milk thro ’ it, may afted the Nurse with Pleafnre in Suckiin the Child.

papillaeintejlinorum.c: PAPILLAE Intejlinorum, are little Glandules wherewith the innermost Tunick of the Intestines or Guts is full: They soak in th e percolated Chyle, and dispense it to the La deal Veins. Pecquet calls this Lining of the Guts a Spungy Pe - riftoma; and Biljius, a Woolly Moss. ’ Tis proba - ble also that these Papillae hinder the Excoriation of the Intestines. Willis takes them for a distend Coat, and calls it Glandulofa and Villofa Tunica Intejlinorum.

papillarumprccejjus.c: PAPILLARUM Prccejjus, or the Procejfus Ma - mi ares are the Extremities of the Olfadory Nerves, which convey the slimy viscous Humours by the Fibres, which perforate the Os cribriforms to the Nostrils and Palate.

pappusinbotany.c: PAPPUS in Botany, is that soft light Down ) which grows out of the Seeds of some Plants, such as Thi files, Dandelion, Hawkypccd, ec. and which buoys them up so in the Air, that they can be blown any where by the Wind. And therefore this distinguishes one kind of Plants which is called Pappofa or Pappi flora.

papulae.c: PAPULAE, the fame with PuJluLe also a kind of Small - Pox. See Exanthemata.

paracentesis.c: PARACENTESIS, or PunSlio, is a Perforation of the Chest, or Abdomen It is made in the Breast, when that is fluffed with purified Mat - ter, or Water, and then the Perforation is made in the Side between the fifth and sixth Vertebra. It is made in the Abdomen, when that is swelled by a Dropsie, and near the Line a Alba, in the Muscles that either ascend right or oblique In which last Case, if a Man be strong, and has taken a Purge, and also his Lungs, and. the reft of his Entrails be uncorrupted, when you see the Navel doth Protuberate, there you must make the Incision; don ’ t let Purulency and Water come out both together, for that were to kill the Pa - tient, but one after the other: As in seven Days about a Pound, or a Pound and a half, as the Pa - tient can endure it: After the Operation is finish - ed,. ' draw the Wound up with an Astringent Plain - ster. Blanchard.

parade.c: PARADE, is a Military Word, signifying the Place where Troops usually draw together, in order to mount the Guards, or for any other Service.

parallax.c: PARALLAX is that Arch of a great Circle, paTing thro ’ the Zenith and true Place of the Sun Or Stars, and intercepted between the true and apparent Place. Let B D be divided into three equal parts then AD: S H:: B D: B H, by the fe cond Property of the Parabola ) that is, as to and A D: T I:: B D: B I:: ’ Wherefore ’ tis plain. That the Squares on S H, T I and A D, ( as also on S h, T i, and A C ) and the Circles answering to them, Will be in Arith - metical Progression, or as,,; and thus it will be ad Infinitum, if the three Divisions be bis - fe & ed, and those again biffeded, &c. But a Rank of Numbers in simple Arithmetick Pro - greflion, will be to a Rank of as many equal to the greatest as to, and consequently, the Pa - in this Figure, ’ A, denotes the Centre of the Earth B, the Place on the Superficies of the Earth ’ from whence the Star is seen. ? d O l, the Stars or Planets Places in their Orbs. A cf C, A E, A ) G, the Lines of their true Places, B d Dz B c ? D, B O F, B C, the Lines of their ap - parent Places. Here the Angle made by the Intersection of the said two Lines thro ’ the Body of the Planet, is the Angle of Parallax. That is,. In Mars, the Angle A d B Angle C d D, ( by e. i. ) In the Sun, the Angle of Parallax, is the Angle A G B Angle E F. In the Moon, it is the Angle A B Angle G ( H. Here ’ tis manifest, that the nearer the Star is to the Horizon and Center of the Earth, the greater is the Parallax: Whence it is, That the ! Orbit of the Moon being nearest to the Earth, her Parallax is greatest and most perceptible: For the Semi - diameter of the Earth bears a greater Pro - portion to the Semi - diameter of the Moons Or - bit, than to any of the reft., The Horizontal Parallax of the Moon is the Difference between her Real and Apparent Place when Ihe is either Riling or Serting. As suppose her Setting, then the Angle of the Horizontal Pa - rallax will be B ( A O A R. The know - ledge of the Quantity of which, is of the greatest use in Astronomy; because from thence the Di - stance of the Moon, Sun, ( or any other Planet ) from the Earth may most easily be had; for in the Triangle B A C; A B the Semi - diameter of the Earth, B the Right Angle, and C the Angle of the Parallax being known, ’ tis easie to find any Side or Angle fought, and consequently A C, the Distance of the Moon from the Earth. This came first to be discovered by the Ancient Astronomers, thus. They observed, That the Apparent Semi - Di - urinal Motion of the Moon was but Degrees, whereas in reality and truth, it was Degrees: Wherefore they concluded, That the Moon ’ s Place was put forward in her Riling one Degree, and as much put backwards in her Setting; which must needs cause her visible Motion above the Earth in Hours, to be observed nearly a De - grees less, than the half of Degrees, her app - rent Motion in Hours. Wherefore from hence they concluded the Horizontal Parallax to be just Degree: Which ha - ving found, ’ twas easie to discover that A C, must be near times A B, or Semi - diame - ters of the Earth, ( /. e. at Miles to a Degree, and Miles the Earths Radius ) Miles Englijh. Mr. Auzout, gives you a Method to find the Moon ’ s Parallax, thus on a Day token Jhe is in her Perigee, or Apogee, and in the moss Boreal Signs, Take her Diameter towards the Horizon, and then towards - the South, with her Altitude above the Horizon; the Difference of which Diameters will ( hew the Proportion of her Distance with the Semi - diameter of the Earth; but this is belt of all done in those Places where fire passes thro the Zenith.,,, If the Moons Horizontal Parallax could be truly and exactly found, it would be of prod - gious Advantage; for by it the Longitudes of Places on Land ( and tolerably well at Sea ) might be discovered. Captain Halley faith, ( at the end of his Objerva - tions and Catalogue of the Southern Stars “ That “ ’ tis the want of a true knowledge of Geometry, “ which, hath occasioned the Defeds and Mistakes “ of Astronomers as to this Point. He there gives three ways to find the Moons Parallax, which are nearly Geometrical, of Which the first seems the best; and is thus. Let two times of Observation be taken When the Sun is ( nearly ) equally distant from each Node of the Moon and when the Moon also is to be Northerly in one Node, and Southerly in the other: In these things there needs no great Exadnefs, because the Differences of Latitude may be sufficiently supplied from the Tables. At these Times of Observation let the visible Places of the Moon, both in Longitude and La - titude be taken, together with her visible Alti - tudes and Diameters, which let be reduced to the Horizontal; then from the Times and Vifi - ble Places, let in each Observation, the Vertical Angle be computed, which is made with the Circle of Latitude at the Moons Centre; and then the Difference by which the Southern Lati - tude exceeds the Northern ( in our Northern part of the World ) is the Sum of the Parallaxes of Latitude, which must be divided into two parts; which to do, put into one Sum the Logarithms of the Sine of the Horizontal Semi - diameter of the visible Distance of the Moon from the Ver - tex, and of the Complement of the Angle of the Vertical Circle, with the Circle of Latitude, in each Observation. Then out of the greater Sum take the lesser, - and to the Difference add Radius, the Sum stall be the Logarithm of the Tangent of an Ark, from whence take Degrees; then will it be as Radius to the Tangent of the Remaining Ark: So is the Tangent of the half Sum of the Parallax, to the Tangent of half their Difference: But the half Sum and half Difference together, is the greater Parallax of Latitude, and the Difference between them is the Lesser. Take this Parallax of Latitude otft of the visible Southern Latitude; or add it to the Northern, and it will shew the Inclination. And then lastly, it will be as the Rectangle un - der the Sines of the Distance seen from the Ze - with, and of the Complement of the Angle of the Verticle Circle with the Circle of Latitude, is to the Square of the Radius:: So is the Sine of the Parallax of Latitude, to the Sine of the Horizontal Parallax. And there is between the Sine of the Horizon - tal Semi - diameter of the Moon, and the Hori - ontal Parallax, so constant a Proportion, that if it can be but once known, the Moons Parallax at any time will be had from the Observation of her Diameter. All the Difficulty of this Process, is in owler - ! ving the visible Latitudes of the Moon, and which indeed cannot be had without the help of the Fix ’ d Stars, whose Latitudes are in no Catalogue yet extant, cored to a Minute: Therefore the Accurate Solution of this Problem must depend on some better Tables than are yet publiffied. And thole I hope we may ex red from the most Accurate . rs “ Accurate Astronomer, Mr. Flamftced, when he hath, finish ’ d his Catalogue of the Fix ’ d Stars, which he is now about. In the Ingenious Dr. Gregorys Ajlronomia Phy - sic and Geometrica, you have a great and very useful variety of Propositions for the finding the Parallax, Vide Lib.. Semi.. Tho ’ there be no Parallax of the Fix ’ d Stars, in respect of the Eartfis em i - diameter, the whole Body of the Earth bfcing But a Point in reference to the Distance between us and the Fix ’ d Stars: Yet in respect of the Annual Orbit of the Earth, it hath justly been expected by Astronomers, that some Parallax should be found: And this would be a Discovery of great Moment, if it could be made because it would be an undoubted De - monftration for the Annual Motion of the Earth round the Sun, if any such Parallax could be dis - covered. This the Ingenious Dr. Hool f attempted to find by observing the various Distance of a Fix ’ d Star from the Zenith: ( See a Dissertation of his de - feignedly written on this Subject:. ) And our Ex - cellent Astronomer Mr. Flamfteed, actually did ob - serve it by the Access and Recess of a Fix ’ d Star to and from the Pole of the Equator at different Tynes of the Year. And he allures us, in his Letter to Dr. Wallis, written Decemb.., and Published in the ] Latin Edition of Dr. Wallis's Works: “ That he u found the Distance of a Fix ’ d Star near the “ Pole of the World to be Seconds, or Se - “ conds nearer to it at the Winter Solstice than at “ the Summer one; And this he observed for Years together with great Accuracy. So that he judges the Objection of Ricciolus a - gainst the Earths Motion to be entirely removed, and its Revolution round the Sun proved. Dr. Gregory seems not satisfied with this Proof, ( tho ’ he believes the Doctrine from other Princi - ples ) but inclines rather to the Opinion of Co - pernicus, That the Diameter of the Earths Annu - al Orbit is insensible, in refpedfc of the Distance of the Fix ’ d Stars. But others may judge whe - ther he brings Reasons sufficient to overthrow Observations so carefully, and so often made, as those produced by Mr. Flanjieed. See his Ajlron. p.,.

parallaxoflatitude.c: PARALLAX of Latitude, is an Arch of a great Circle palling by the Poles of the Zodiack to the apparent Place of the Star, and intercepted between two Circles of the Ecliptick equally di - stant, whereof the one passeth by the true Place of the Star, and the other by the Apparent Place.

parallaxoflongitude.c: PARALLAX of Longitude, is an Arch of the E - ecliptick ( or Parallel thereto ) intercepted between two great Circles, whereof the one passeth from the Poles of the Ecliptick, and the true Place j. the other from the laid Poles by the apparent Place: So that the Parallax of Longitude is only the Dis - ference of the true and apparent Place according to the Longitude of the Ecliptick.

parallelsphere.c: PARALLEL Sphere, is where the Poles are in the Zenith and Nadir, and the Equator in the Horizon, which is the Case of such ( if any such there be ) who live directly under the North and South Pole. The Consequences of this Position are. That the Parallels of the Sun ’ s Declination will also be Parallels of his Altitude. The Inhabitants can fee only such Stars as are on their side the Equinoctial - and they muff have fix Months Day, and fix Months continual Night every Year j and the Sun can never be higher with them than Degrees Minutes, which is not so high as lie is with us in February,

parallelruler.c: PARALLEL Ruler, is an Instrument made of Brass, Steel, or Wood, to draws Lines Parallel to each other; of great use in Fortification, Architecture and many other parts of the Mathematicks.

parallelsofaltitudesoralmacanters.c: PARALLELS of Altitudes or Almacanters, are Circles Parallel to the Horizon, imagined to pass thro ’ every Degree and Minute of the Meridian, between the Horizon and Zenith, having their Poles in the Zenith. And on the Globes these are described by the Divisions on the Quadrant of Al - titude, in its Motion about the Body of the Globe, when ’ tis screw ’ d to the Zenith of any Place.

parallelsofdeclination.c: PARALLELS of Declination, are Circles Parallel to the Equinoctial, imagined t pass thro every Degree aad Minute of the Meridians, be - tween the Equinoctial and each Pole of the World.

parallelrays.c: PARALLEL Rays, in Opticks, are those that keep an equal Distance from the visible Object to the Eye, which is supposed to be infinitely re - mote from the Object.

parallelplanes.c: PARALLEL Planes, are those Planes which have all the Perpendiculars drawn betwixt them equal to each other: That is, when they are e - very where equally distant.

parallelcircles.c: PARALLEL Circles, on the Globes, the fame with the Lesser Circles.

parallels.c: PARALLELS also on the Terrestrial Globe, are Circles drawn thro ’ the middle of every Cli - mate, dividing them into two halves, which are called Parallels.

parallelism.c: PARALLELISM of the Earth ’ s Axis, is the Earth ’ s keeping its Axis in its Annual Revoluti - on round the Sun, in a Position always Parallel to its self, which it doth nearly but not exactly j for tho ’ the Difference be insensible in one Year, Dr. Gregory in his Astronomy faith, It becomes sensible enough in many Years. This Parallelism he shews to be the necessary result of the two Motions of the Earth, that is round its Axis, and its Annual one, and that there needs no third Motion be feigned to explain ir, or account for it: For as the Earth moves An - nually round the Sun ( without the Diurnal Mo - tion ) it moves only according to its Centre of Gra - city; and each Point and Line in it keeps always the fame Position. Let its Axis be one of those Lines; the Diurnal Revolution of the Earth round this ( which as to that Motion is supposed immo - veable ) able ) cannot change the Position of it j and therefore it will be always the lame, / e. always Parallel to it fell.

paramesus.c: PARAMESUS, is the next Finger to the Mid - dle one, called the Ring - finger.

parameter.c: PARAMETER, by some, as My dor gi us and Others, called the Latus peclum. of a Parabola, is a Third Proportional to the Abscissa and any Ordinate: So that the Square of the Ordinate is always equal to the Rectangle under the Para - meter and Abscissa. See the Demonstration under Parabola, This This W ord Parameter, or Latus BpBum, is also tiled as to the Ellipse arid Hyperbola; blit in those it hath another Proportion, as you will find under those Words.

paramount.c: PARAMOUNT, in our Law, lignifies the Su - pream Lord of the Fee: Sot there friday be a Te - nant to a Lord, that holdeth himself another Lord; the former of which is called Lord Mesne, and the second Lord Paramount. And a Lord Paramount consisteth only in Comparison, as one Man may be great, being compared to a left; and little, being compared with a greater. So that none lim - ply seemeth to be Lord Paramount but only the King, who is Patron Paramount to all the Benefi - ces in England.

parapetinfortification.c: PARAPET, in Fortification, is an Elevation of Earth and Stone upon the Rampart, behind which the Soldiers Hand secure from the Enemies Great and Small Shot, and where the Cannot is planted for the Defence of the Town of Fortress. Every Parapet having its Embrasures and Merlons, is about Six Foot high on the Side of the Place; and from Four to Five on that toward the Country. So that this Difference of Heights forms a kind of Glacis above, from whence the Musketeers mounting the Banquet of the Parapet, may easily fire into the Moats, or at least upon the Counterscarp. It ought also to be from to Foot thick if made of Earth; and from to if of Stone. The Earth is much better than Stone, because Stone will fly to pieces when battered, and do mischief This Word Parapet is also given to any Line that covers Men from the Enemies Fire: So there are Parapets of Barrels, of Gabions, of Bags fil - led with Earth, ( c.

paraphanalia.c: PARAPHANALIA, or, according to the Civil Law, Paraphamalia, are those Goods which a Wife, besides her Dower or Jointure, is after her Husband ’ s Death allowed to have; as Furniture for her Chamber, Wearing Apparel, ( " and Jewels, if she be of Quality ) which are not to be put into her Husband ’ s Inventory, especially in the Pro - since of York.

paraphimosis.c: PARAPHIMOSIS, is a Fault of the Yard, when the Praputiums too short; also a Narrowness and Contra sition of the Womb.

paraplegia.c: PARAPLEGIA, is a Palfie which feizeth all the Parts of the Body below the Head, thro ’ an Ob - ftrutftion of the Spinal Marrow. Blanchard.

paraphrenitis.c: PARAPHRENITIS, is Madness, accompanied with a continual Fever through the Inflammation of the Diaphragm, with Difficulty of Breathing, at the Ancients dream ’ d. But Dotffor Willis has confuted this Opinion of it, and says the Matter of it lies in the Cerebellum, whereby the Animal Spirits cannot flow, and thence the Midriff and Lungs are troubled. Blanchard.

paraphrosyne.c: PARAPHROSYNE, is a flight lort of Do - ting in the Imagination and Judgment. Blan - chard.

paraseleneamock.c: PARASELENE, a Mock - Moon, is occasion ’ d by the fame Means as the Parhelia are about the Sun tho ’ not so frequent.

parasiticalplants.c: PARASITICAL Plants, are those which some call Epidendra, because they grow not on the Ground, but on the Arms or Limbs of Trees, as our Vifcum or Mijletoe doth. PARASTATAL See Epididymis.

parasynanche.c: PARASYNANCHE, is an Inflammation of the Muscles of the Upper part of the Oefophagw, with a continued Fever. par P ARA V AILE, in Common Law signifies the lowest Tenant, or him that is Tenant to one who holdeth his Fee fiver of another; and is called Tenant Paravaile, because it is presumed he hath Profit and Avayle by the Land.

parceners.c: PARCENERS, is a Word taken either ac - cording to the Course sis the Common Law, or according to Custom. Parceners, according to the Course of the Common Law, are. Where one seized of an Estate of Inheritance, hath I slue only Daughters, and dies, and the Lands descend to the Daughters, then they are called Parceners, and are but as one Heir. The fame Law is, If he have not any Issue, but that his Sifters be his Heirs. Parceners, according to Custom, are, Where a Man is seized of Lands in Gavel - kind, as iri Kent, and other Places Frarichifed, arid Hath If - sue divers Sons, and dies, then the Sons are Par - centers by the Custom.

parcenaryinlaw.c: PARCENARY, in Law, signifies a holding or occupying of Land pro indiviso, by Joint - Tenants, or otherwise called Co - parceners: For if they refuse to divide their common Inheritance, and choose rather to hold it jointly, they are laid to hold iri Parcenary.

parc.c: PARC FraElo, is a Writ that lies against him that violently breaketh a Pound, arid taketh out Beasts thence, which for some Trespass done upon another Man ’ s Ground, are lawfully im - pounded.

parcelling.c: PARCELLING of a Ship, is laying of Pieces sis Canvafe of about a Hand ’ s breadth, over the Seams, when file is riewly Calked.
PARCELLING, of the Seam of a Ship, is af - ter it is caulked, to lay over it a narrow piece of Canvas, and then pouring on it hot Pitch and Tar.

pkkcel.c: PKKCEL - Makers, are two Officers in the Ex - chequer that make the Parcels of the Efcheators Ac - counts, wherein they charge them with every thing they have levied for the King ’ s Use within the Time of their Office, and deliver the fame to one of the Auditors of the Court to make an Ac - count with the Escheator thereof.

parencephalos.c: PARENCEPHALOS, the fame as the Cere - bellum.

parenchymousparts.c: PARENCHYMOUS Parts of the Body, by the Old Anatomists, are reckoned such Fleftiy Partp of it as fill up the Interstices between the Vessels, and not consisting of Vessels themselves. But by the Help of the Microscope, and more accurate Observations, it hath flee been discovered, that there is no Part of an Animal Body but what is a kind of Net - work of an innumerable Quantity of small Capillary Vessels.

parenchymata.c: PARENCHYMATA, are the Intrails thro ’ which the Blood passes for its better Fermentation and Perfetftion, as the Lungs, Liver, Heart, and Spleen, ( c. Sometimes the Word Parenchyma is taken in a large Sense for all the Intrails. Blanchard.

parietalbones.c: PARIETAL Bones, or the Bones of the SyncL put, are the thinnest Bones of the Cranium, in Form almost square, somewhat long; they are joined to the Os Front is by the Sutura Coronal is, to one another in the Crown of the Head by the Sutura Sagittalis, to the Os Occipitis by the Lambdoidalis, and to the Ossa Temporum by the Sutura Squamofa. They are smooth and. equal O on on their Out - side, but on their In - side they have several Furrows made for the Passage of the Veins of the Dura mater. They have each a small Hole near the Sutura Sagittalis, through which there pass some Veins which carry the Blood from the Teguments to the Sinus Longitudinalis.

paristmiaoramygdala.c: PARISTMIA, or Amygdala, are two Glan - rules of the Mouth tied together by a broad slender Production they have one common Ca - city large and oval, opening into the Mouth. The Uie they serve for is, to transmit a certain slimy or pituitous Matter into the Jaws and Mouth. They are called also T onfilla, which fee. Blanchard.

park.c: PARK of the Artillery, is a certain Place in a Camp without Cannon - lhot of the Place beside - ged, where the Cannon, Artificial Fires, Powder, and other Warlike Ammunition are kept, and guarded only by Pike - men, to avoid Cafualties which may happen by Fire. Every Attack at a Siege hath its Parity of Artillery.

parkofprovisions.c: PARK of Provisions, is another Place in the Camp, on the Rear of every Regiment, which is taken up by the Sutlers, who follow the Ar - my with all forts of Provisions, and fell them to the Soldiers.

paronychiaawhitlow.c: PARONYCHIA, a Whitlow, is a preternatu - ral Swelling in the Fingers, and very troublesome: It arises from a sharp malign Humour, which fometim'es gnaws the Tendons, Nerves, the Mem - brane about the Bone, and the. very Bone it self. Blanchard.

parotides.c: PAROTIDES, are Glandules behind the Ears; also a preternatural Swelling of those Glandules.

paroxysmafit.c: PAROXYSM, a Fit, is Part of the Period of Diseases, whereby they encrease and grow worse. It is either Regular, which returns at certain Times, as in a Tertian or Quartan Ague; or Ir - regular, that has no certain Times, but comes sometimes one Day, sometimes another, as the Erratick Ague. Blanchard.

parrels.c: PARRELS, in a Ship, are Frames made of Trucks, and Ribs, and Ropes, which having both their Ends fattened to the Yards, are so contrived as to go round about the Matts, that the Yards by their means may go up and down upon the Matts. These also, with the Breast - Ropes, do fatten the Yards to the Matts.

parricide.c: PARRICIDE, signifies properly him that kills his Father, and may be applied to him that mr - dcrs his Mother.

parsonpersona.c: PARSON, Persona, is the Law Term for the Redlor of a Church; because for his Time he re - presents his Church, and fuftaineth the Person thereof, as well in filing, as in being sued in any Adrion Touching the fame. Formerly he who had a Church by Institution and Induction only for his own Life, was called Parson Mortal. But any Collegiate or Conventual Body, to whom the Church was for ever appropriated, was called Parson Immortal. In the New book of Entries, Verb. Aid in An - unity, are these Words: Et Pradiclus A. dict ciuod isc eft Persona PradiSa Ecclefue de S. Imper - sonata in eadem ad Prtfentationem F. Patroniffa. By which it seems that Persona or Parson anciently was the Patron, and Persona Imperfonata the Refer to whom the Benefice was given by the Patron s Right; which also Dyer fiieweth, sol. lit. So that in I aw, the Parson Imperfona is he that hath the Possession of a Benefice or Redory, be it ap - propriate, or otherwise, by the Ad of another.

parsonageofrettory.c: PARSONAGE, of Rettory, is a Spiritual Li - ving composed of Glebe - Land, Tythe, and other Oblations of the People, separate or dedicate to God in any Congregation, for the Service of his Church there, and for the Maintenance of the Minister to whose Charge the fame is conv mitted.

partesfinis.c: PARTES Finis nihil habuerunt f cc. in the Common Law, is an Exception taken against a Fine levied.

partiesinlaw.c: PARTIES, in Law, are those which are na - med in a Deed, or Fine, as Parties to it; as those that levy the Fine, and to whom the Fine is levied: So those that make any Deed,. and they to whom it is made, are called Parties in the Deed.

partitionefacienda.c: PARTITIONE Facienda, is a Writ that lies for those that hold Lands or Tenements pro indi - vis, and would fever to every one his Parr, against him or them that refuse to join in Partition as Copartners, cc.

partition.c: PARTITION, is a dividing of Land defend - ed by the Common Law, or by Custom, among Co - heirs or Parceners, where there are two at least; and this Partition is made Four ways, whereof Three are by Agreement, the Fourth by Compui - sion. The First Partition by Agreement is. When they divide the Land equally themselves into so many Parts as they are Coparceners, and each to choose one Share or Part, according to Order. The Second is. When they choose some of their Friends to make the Division for them. The Third is by drawing Lots, thus: Having first di - vided the Land into as many Parts as there are Parceners, they write every part severally in a diftindl Scroll, and wrapping it up, throw each of them into a Hat, Bason, or such like thing, out of which each Parcener draws one, according to their Superiority; and so the Land is severally allotted. The Fourth Partition, which is by Com - pulsion, is, When one or more of the Parceners, by reason of the Refusal of some other, lues out a Writ of Partitione facienda by Force whereof they shall be compelled to part. In Kent, where Land is of Gavel - kind Nature, they call their Partition, Shifting. Partition also may be made by Joint - Tenants, or Tenants in Common, by Afent, by Deed, or by Writ.

partners.c: PARTNERS, in a Ship, are strong pieces of Timber bolted to the Beams incur cling the Matts, to keep them steady in their Steps, and also keep them from rowling ( that is falling ) over the Ship ’ s Sides. There are also of these Partners at the Second Deck, to the fame End; only the MiiTen - mast hath only one pair of Partners in which that Matt is wedged so firm, as that it can by no means budge. Some Ships fail not well, unless their Matts are Loose, and have leave to play in the Partners: But in a Storm this is dangerous, left the Partners should be wronged, ( as they fay ) i. e. forced out of their places; for then there is no Help, but to cut the Matt by the Board.

partnershiparuleinarithmetick.c: PARTNERSHIP, a Rule in Arithmetick; the fame with the Rule of Fellowjhip, which lee. PART Proportional, is a Part or Number agreeable and analogus to some other Part or Number; or a Medium to find out some Number or Part unknown by. Proportion and Equality of Reason. P A T

parvagum.c: PAR Vagum, a pair of Nerves arising below the Auditory ones, from the Sides of the Medulla Oblongata, behind the Prccejfus Annularis, by fe - veral Threads which join together, and go out by the fame Hole that the Sinus Later ales discharge themselves into th e Jugular cs. It is joined by a Branch of the Ifervus Spinalis, or Accejforius WH - lifii, and by a small Branch of the Portio Dura: Immediately after it comes out of the Scull, it gives a small Branch to the Larynx as it goes down the Neck, above the Intereoftal Nerve, by the Side of the Internal Carotide. At the Axillary Artery it calls back the Recurrent Nerves, of which the Right embraces the Axillary Artery, and the Left the Aorta. These two Branches ascend on each side of the Trachea, or Aspera Arteria, to the Larynx, where they are spent on the Muscles of the Larynx and Membranes of the Trachea. This Pair, after it has entred the Cavity of the Thorax,. fends out several Branches to the Pericardium, Heart, Lungs, and Concave side of the Liver. This Pair of Nerves was formerly accounted the Sixth, but is now usually reckoned the Eighth. There is a notable Fibre, or rather Nerve, co - king from the Spinal Marrow, about the Sixth or Seventh Vertebra of the Neck, which is so joined to this Par Vagum, as if they grew into one Nerve; being covered with it, with the fame Coat, from the Dura mater, but appears distinct when that is taken off. This Nerve they call the Accessory Nerve, which runs to the Muscles of the Neck and Shoulder - Blade. Out of the Trunks of this Eighth Pair spring two Nerves that they call the Recurring Nerves the Right of which rises higher, and winds about the Axillary Artery the Left springs lower, and willing about the Trunk of the defending Aorta, recurrs or returns back from thence. Dr. Willis thinks this Recurrent Nerve to be re - ally a diltindl one from the very Original, to be no Branch of the Par Vagum, but only is included in the fame Coat or Cover with it, for Safety and Convenience of PalTage. About the first, or second Rib this Pair hath a kind of Plexus or Knot, which is called Plexus Cardiacus, because it fends out Twigs which go to the Heart and its Appendages.

pavonocumento.c: PAVO Nocumento, is a Writ of Nusance which fee.

parvum.c: PARVUM & Crajfutn, is the Fourth Pair of Muscles of the Head so called, because it is but a little one, yet pretty thick. It lieth under the Complexum Trigeminum or Third Pair, and ri - les Nervous from the Tr'anfverfe Processes of the Six uppermost Vcrtebrxof the Neck, and is inserted into the hinder Root of the Mamillary Process.

parylis.c: PARYLIS, is an Inflammation, Rottenness, or Excrefcency among the Gums. Blanchard.

pascha.c: PASCHA ClauJum, signifies the OSiaves of E after, or Low - Sunday, which closes or concludes that Solemnity. Die ( tali ) poi pnfeha clausum, is a Date in some of our Old Deeds. And the first Statute of Weftminjlcr, Anno Ed.. is said to have been made lendes mend de la. close de Pas - che, that is, the Monday after Eajler - Wccl.

paschalrents.c: PASCHAL Rents, are Rents or Annual Du - ties paid by the Inferior Clergy to the Bishop, or Archdeacon, at their Eafler Vijitatkns. They are also called Syncdals which lee.

pas.c: PAS ae Souris, a French Term in Fortification: the lame with Berme which fee.

passant.c: PASSANT. The Term in Heraldry for a Lion born in any Escutcheon in a walking Posture. But this in moil other Beales, they call Tripping,

passagio.c: PASS AGIO, is a Writ dire & ed to the Keepers of the Ports, to permit a Man topafs overSea that hath the Kings Ijicenle.

passarado.c: PASSARADO, is a Rope in a Ship, whereby all the Sheet - Blocxs of the Main and Forefails are haled down after the Clevo of the Mainfail to the Cubbrige - head of the Main - mall, and the Clew of the Fore - ail to the Cat - head. This is to be done when the Ship goes larger and they are also ' kept firm down, and kindred from flying up, by: this Pajfar ado - Rope. t

passport.c: PASSPORT, signifies a Licence made by any one that hath Authority, for the safe Passage of any Man from one Place to another.

passiveprinciples.c: PASSIVE Principles. So the Chymills call Water and Earth, because either their Parts are at reft, or else at least not so rapidly moved as those of Spirit, Oil, and Salt, and so do serve to Hop and hinder the quick Motion of the Active Principles. Besides, if these Principles could be drawn pure, they would have nothing in them but bare Bulk, Figure, Colour, and Weight the one in a Fluid, the other in a Solid Form and would be without either Smell, Tast, &c. or any Adive Operation.

pastills.c: PASTILLS, are Odoriferous Tablets, or Trod chishj made up of Perfumes or Odorous Bodies, with Mucilage or Gum Tragacanth.

pateinfortification.c: PATE, in Fortification, is a kind of Platform like what they call an Horseshoe, not always regular, but generally oval, encompassed only with a Parapet, and having nothing to flank it. It is usually ereded in Marfliy Grounds to cover a Gate of a Town.

pateeaterm.c: PATEE, a Term in He raff dry for a Cross of this Figure. The Field is Sable a Cross Patee Argent, by the Name of Cross. This Form of a Cross is called also Eormee.

patella.c: PATELLA. See Mola genu, the Knee Pan.

patents.c: PATENTS. See Letters Patent. Note, That Patents differ from Writs, and a Coroner is made by Writ, and not by Patent. P ATEN EE, is he to whom the King grants his Letters Patent.

patheticknerves.c: PATHETICK Nerves, are the Fourth pair arising from the Top of the Medulla Oblongata, ( and so is different from all others, which arise either from its Base or Sides ) behind the round Protuberances, called by Anatomists the To and Testes of the Brain; whence bending forwards by the Sides of the Medulla Oblongata, they presently hide themselves under the Dura Mater under which proceeding a while, they pass out of the Skull, each in a single Trunk, at the fame Hole with the Optick Nerves, ( and they communicate with no other in their whole Passage ) and are be - allowed entirely as Willis faith, on that Muscle of the Eye which they call Trochlearis, because it serves to rowl the Eye round about which be - ing a Motion that is usually consequential upon some Passion of the Mind, such as Love, c. these Nerves i nr P A U Nerves are therefore very properly called Oculorum motores pathetick.

path.c: PATH of the Vertex, a, Term frequently used sey Mr. Flamfleed in his Doctrine of the Sphere, and signifies a Circle described by any Point of the Earth ’ s Surface, as the Earth turns round its Axis. This Point is considered as Vertical to the Earth ’ s Centre, and is the fame with what is cal - led the Vertex or the Zenith in the Ptolemaic k. Projection. The Semi - diatneter of this Path of the Vertex is always equal to the Complement of the La - titude of the Point or Place that describes it; that is, to that Places Distance from the Pole of the World

pathognomonickaterm.c: PATHOGNOMONICK, a Term in the Arc of Medicine, is a proper inseparate Sign which a - grees only to such a thing, and to all of that kind, and tells the EfTence of its SubjeCt, and also lasts from the Beginning to the End; as in a true Plurifie there ’ s always a continual Fever, hard Breathing, and Stiches, with a Cough. Blan - chard.

pathology.c: PATHOLOGY, is a part of Physick that teach - eth us the preternatural Constitution of a Man ’ s Body, so as thereby to discover the Nature and Causes of Diseases.

patonce.c: PATONCE. The Heralds Term for one of their Crosses of this Figure Gules, A Cross Pdtonce, Ardent, by the Name of Latirher,

patrimony.c: PATRIMONY, is afi Hereditary Estate, or Right, defcefided from Ancestors. The Legal En - dowment of a Church, or Religious House, was called Ecclefiajlical Patrimony.

patron.c: PATRON, is used in the Civil Law for him that hath manumitted a Servant, and thereby is both justly accounted his great BenefaCtor, and challengeth certain Reverence and Duty of him during his Life. In the Canon and Civil Law it signifies him that hath the Gift of a Benefice; and the Rea - fon is, Because the Gift of Churches and Benefices belonging unto such good Men as either built, or else endowed them with some great part of their Revenue.

patrouilleorpatroul.c: PATROUILLE, or Patroul, as we generally pronounce it, is a Round of Soldiers, to the Num - ber of Five or Six, with a Serjeant to command them: These fet out from the Corps de Gards, and walk round the Streets of, a Garrison, to prevent Quarrels, Mischief, &c. and to keep all in Order, Peace, ana Quietness.

pauseorbest.c: PAUSE or Best, in Musick, is a Silence or Ar - tisical Intermission of the Voice or Sound, proper - tioned to a certain Measure of Time, by the Mo - tion of the Hand or Foot. These Paufes or Bpfls are always equal to the Length or Quantity of the Notes whereto they are annex ’ d, and are therefore called by the fame Names as a Long - reft, Breve - reft, Semi - breve - reft, &c. Odd Befls are those which take up only some part of a Semi - breve ' s Time or Measure, and have always reference to some Odd Note for by those two Odds the Measure is made even,

paunchofpunch.c: PAUNCH, of Punch, is those Matts made " of Sinnet, which in a Ship are made fait to the Main and Fore - yards, to keep them from galling againfir the Mails.

pawle.c: PAWLE, in a Ship, is a fir, all piece of Iron bolted to one End of the Beams of the Deck, close to the Capstan, but yet so easily as that it can turn about. Its Use is to Hop the Capstan from turning back, by being made to catch hold of the Whelps: Therefore they fay, Heave a Pawls ! That is, Heave a little more for the Pawle to get hold of the Whelps: And this they call Pawling the Capstan.

paying.c: PAYING. The Seamen call laying over the Seams of a Ship a Coat of hot Pitch, paying her; which, when ’ tis done with Canvass, is called Parcelling. Also, when after she is Graved, and her Soil burned off, a new Coat of Tallow and Soap, or one of Train - Oil, Rofinand Brimstone, boiled together, is put on upon her, that is cal - led Paying ef a Ship. They fay also sometimes, when in tacking about, a Ship ’ s Sails being back - stay ’ d, fall all flat against the Masts and Shrouds, Jhe is payed.

peaninheraldry.c: PEAN, in Heraldry, is when the Field of a Coat of Arms is Sable, and the Powdering are Or.

pectenarboris.c: PECTEN Arboris, is the Grain of the Wood of any Tree. PECTINEtJS, is a Muscle of the Thigh; so cased from its Beginning at the Os Pubis or Pe - tfinis. It has a thick, broad, and. fleshy Origi - nation from the External part of the said Bone, be - tween the Psoas Magnus and the Iliacu Internus, and second Head of the Triceps and descending obliquely backwards, it becomes a flat strong ' Tendon near its Implantation to the Asperity on the Posterior part of the Os Femoris, immediately below the lesser Trochanter, at the Insertion of the Psoas Magnus and Iliacus Internus. This adding together with the Psoas Magnus and Iliacus Internus, doth not only draw the Os Femoris upwards, but direCt it outwards, by its Curve Descent from its Origination to its Infer - tion at the Posterior part of the Os Femoris; which is a Provident Contrivance of Nature in walk - ing, since the Thigh - Bones by their oblique Po - sition do thereby render the Toes liable to turn inwards.

pectinisorpubisos.c: PECTINIS, or Pubis Os, the Share - Bone, is the lower arid inner, or fore - part of the Os Into - minatum; and even before, is joined to its Sel - low by a Cartilage, called Synchondrosis y which is much thicker, but looser and softer in Women than in Men; for in Women, one Bone can a little re - cede stom the other in Travail, to make way for the Foetus. It has a very large Foramen between the Sinus of the Coxendix, and that part whereby it is joined to its Fellow, making room for two Muf - cles of the Thigh j and above this Foramen is a Sinus, by which the Crural Veins and Arteries pass to the Thighs. The Upper part of this Bone is called its Spine, into which the Muscles of the Abdomen are inserted.

pectorals.c: PECTORALS, or PeEloral Medicines, are such as are used in Diseases of the Bread ' by attenua - ting, or thickening, or allaying the Heat thereof, and render the Matter which causes coughing, fit to be expectorated or spit out. Blanchard.

pectoralisamuscle.c: PECTORALIS, a Muscle of the Arm, so cal - led from its Situation. This hath a broad semi circular k circular fie fay beginning above, from near half the Inferior part of the Clavicula: Below, from the Os PeElorale, and all the Cartilaginous End - ings of th Six iiipcrior Ribs, and from the Bony part of the Seventh, it hath a distinct Fasciculus of fleshy Fibres, ( which sometimes is confounded with the Obliquus Defcendens Abdominis. ) From this large Origin it marcheth transversely, and be - cometh narrower but thicker, and lessens it self as it passeth over the upper part of the Biceps Cubiti, and is infer ted by a short, but broad, strong Tendon, to the Superior part of the Os Hu - mer, above the Termination of the Deltcides. The Fibres of this Muscle decussate each other, near their Implantation to the Os Humeri those of the Superior part running downwards, and those; of the Inferior marching up, interbed: the former in Acute Angles. When it ads, it moves the Arm either obliquely upwards, or directly forwards, or obliquely downwards, according to the various Direction of its Series of Fibres.

peculiar.c: PECULIAR, signifies a particular Parifli or Church that hath Jurifdidicn within its self, for Probat of Wills, c. exempt from the Ordinary, and the Bishops Courts. The King ’ s Chapel is a Royal Peculiar, ex - empty from all Spiritual Jurisdiction, and refer - ved to the Visitation and immediate Govern - ment of the King Jiimfelf, who is Supreme Or - finary. ft is an Ancient Privilege of the See of Can - terbury, That wheresoever any Mannors or Ad - vowfons do belong to it, they forthwith become exempt from the Ordinary, and are reputed Pe - culiars.

pedestalinarchitecture.c: PEDESTAL, in Architecture, is that part which supports a Pillar or Column, having its pro - per Base and Cornice different, according to the fe - deal Orders of Architecture. The Tuscan Pedeflal, being the mot simple of all, hath only a Plinth for its Base, and an Aftra - gal crown ’ d for its Cornice. The Derich Pedeflal, ( according to Palladio ) borrowing the At tick. Base, ought to have for its Height z j Diameters of the Column taken below. But no Pedefials to this Order are seen among the Ancient Buildings. The lonish Pedeflal is Two Diameters and about Two thirds high. The Corinthian Pedeflal hath the Fourth part of the Column for its Height, being divided into Eight parts; whereof one must be allowed for the Cymatium, two others for the Base, and the reft for the Dye or Square. The Compoflt Pedeflal ought to have the Third part of the Pillar for its Height. PEDXCULARlS Morbus. See Phthiriafls.

pediculusinbotany.c: PEDICULUS, in Botany, is the Foot - stalk of any Leaf, Flower, or Fruit.

pedimentaterminarchitecture.c: PEDIMENT, a Term in Architecture the fame with Fronton, which fee. PEDXUM. See Tarflus.

pederero.c: PEDERERO, or, as it is usually called by the Seamen, Petterero, is a Small piece of Ordnance, molt used on board of Ships to fire Stones, Nails, broken Iron, or Partridge - shot, on the Enemy, when he attempts to broad you. Most ofthefe are open at the Breech, and have the Chamber to take out, and to be loaded that way, and not - at the Muzzle.

peekasea.c: PEEK, a Sea - word, used in these Senses; An ' Anchor is said to be a - pee, when a Ship being about to weigh, comes so over her Anchor, that the Cable is perpendicular between the Hawse and the Anchor; and to bring the Ship thus, is called Heaving a - peek. They fay alio, Peek, the Mijflen; that is, Put the Missen - yard right up and down by the Mafc A Ship is said to side a - peek., where she lies with her Main and Fore - yards hoised up j and then having one end of the Yards brought down to the Shrouds, the other is raised up an end: And this is done to contrary Sides j ( i. e. ) the Star - board Yard - arm of the Main - yard comes down to the Starboard side, and so doth the Larboard end of the Fore - yard j so that the Yards appear across each other like St. Andrews Cross. The: Way to do this, is, To let go the Starboard Top - fail - sheets from the Main - yard, and then top - king up the Larboard - lifts: And so quite contra - ry for the Fore - yard. To side a - broad peek is much after the fame manner, only the Yards are raised up but half lo high. The Reason why they thus peep up their Yards is, left lying in a River ( and they hardly ever use it but then with their Yards across, another Ship should be foul upon them, and break their Yards. There is alio a Room in the Hold of a Ship, that is called the Peek.: ’ Tis from the Bitts for - wards to the Stem. Here Men of War keep their Powder; and Merchant - men, Outward - bound, place their Victuals here.

pegasusaconstellation.c: PEGASUS, a Constellation in the Northern ' Hemisphere, containing Stars.

peirced.c: PEIRCED. When any Ordinary or Charge, in Heraldry, hath an Hole in it, so that the Field appears through, they fay that Ordinary or Charge is pierced.

pelage.c: PELAGE, is a Term used by the Writers of Natural History, to express such Sea Shell - fifties, as never or very rarely are found near the Shores, but always reside in the Deep, in those parts of the Bottom of the Sea which are most remote ' from Land.

pelicoides.c: PELICOIDES, is the Name given by some to the Figure B G D A, contained under the two inverted / x r D E inverted Quad ran tal Arks A B and A D, and the Semi - circle BCD, whose Area is to the Square A C, and that to the Rectangle E B. ’ Tis equal to the Square A C, because it wants of the Square on the Left Hand the two Seg - ments A B and A D, which are equal to the two Segments B C and D, by which it exceeds it on the Right Hand.

peldnus.c: PEL DNUS, is a Black - and - blue Colour in the Facej frequent in MelancholiCk Men.

pelletsabearinginheraldry.c: PELLETS, a Bearing in Heraldry. See Balls. PEL LIC AN, is the Chymifts Term for a kind of Double Vessel, used in Circulations. See Dou - ble Vessels.

pellicle.c: PELLICLE, a little Skin. When any Solu - tion in Chymistry is in a gentle Heat evaporated so long till a thin Skin or Film arise on the top of the Liquor, ’ tis call ’ d an Evaporation to a Pellicle; and then there is very little more Li - quor left than what will just serve to keep the Salts in Fusion.

pelvis.c: PELVIS, is the Place at the Bottom of the Belly, wherein the Bladder and Womb are con - tained.

pelvisbynum.c: PELVIS Bynum, is a Membranous Vessel or Re - ceptacle in either Kidney, which receives the U - rine, and pours it into the Bladder.

pemphigodesfebris.c: PEMPHIGODES Febris, is a Spotted Fever; feme lay a Windy, or a Flatulent Fever.

pencilofraysinoptichj.c: PENCIL of Rays in Optichj, is a double Cone of Rays joined together at the Base; one of which hath its Vertex in some one Point of the Object, and the Glass G L S for its Base; and the other hath its Bale on the fame Glass, but its Vertex in the Point of Convergence, as at C. Thus: B G S C is a Pencil of Rays, and the Line B L C, is called the Axis of that Pencil.

peninsulaingeography.c: PENINSULA, in Geography, is a Portion of Land, which being alirfoft surrounded with Wa - ter, and is joined to the Continent only by an IJlh muss or narrow Neck of Land; as Africa, the greatest Peninsula in the World, is joined to Ajia; that of More to Greece, cc.

penetrationofdimensions.c: PENETRATION of Dimensions, is a Philofo - phical way of expressing, That two Bodies are in the lame Place, so that the Parts of one do every where penetrate into, and adequately fill up the Dimensions or Places of the Parts of the other; which is manifestly impossible, and contra di & o - ry to Reason.

penumbrainastronomy.c: PENUMBRA, in Astronomy, is a faint kind of Shadow, or the utmost edge of the perfect Shadow which happens at the Eclipse of the Moon; so that it is very difficult to determine where the Shadow begins, and where the Light ends.

pendants.c: PENDANTS of a Ship, are of two kinds. i. Those long Colours, or Streamers, cut point - ing out towards the end, and there divided into two parts, and which are hung out at the Heads of the Mails, or at the Yard - Arm ends, are called Pendants; and are used for shew, and sometimes for Deftindtion of Squadrons. i. That sliort Rope is called a Pendant, Which at one end is fattened to the Head of the Mast, or to the Yard, or to the Clew of the Sail, and at the other end hath a Block and Shiver, to reeve some running Rope into. Thus the Pendant of the Tackje is made fall to the Head of the Matts; and the Pendants to the Bac Stays are fattened to, and hang down on the Inside of the Sbrowds. Also all the Yard - Arms, except the Missen, have of these Pendants, into which the Braces are reeved.

The Velocities of Pendulums in their lowest: Points are as the Chords of the Arks they fail from or describe. PROBLEM XV. According to these Principles and Experiments on Pendulums, it will not he difficult to estimate nearly the Depth of a deep Well, by the fall cf a Stone into the Water from the Mouth i Or the Di - fiance that any Ship at Sea, or that any Fort is off, by the Time between seeing the Fla / h of the Powder, and hearing the Report of the Gun: Or the Dfance that any Thunder Cloud is off, & C. For Sir Isaac Newton hath found that a Sound moves Feel in a Second of Time. ’ Tis asserted also by Mr. Hugens, and now ge - nerally agreed to, That a heavy Body descends in the first Second of Time after its beginning to salr very near Feet. An Example to find the Depth of a Well, may serve for all Suppose you hang Up a short Pendulum, that will Vibrate Quarter Seconds, ( the way to find its ' Length hath already been shewn, ) and letting gd the Stone and the Pendulum together, you find the Pendulum hath made single Vibrations before you hear the noise of the Stones fall into the Wa - ter. Then since Quarters of a Second, are e -. qual to Seconds, if you account the Accelerati - on of the Descent of heavy Bodies to be either as the Squares of the Times, or as the encrease of ' the odd Numbers, either way wi ] l give you the Number for the Depth of the Well. For since, as it is elsewhere Ihewn, a Body de - seeds Feet in the first. Second of Time, in the fourth Second it will descend times Feet j for the Times being i and, the Descent will be as their Squares; that is, as r to: Wherefore Multiplying by, you have, the Depth of the Well. Or, if according to GaliUus ’ s way, you ac - count Feet for the first Second, and then times for the next Second, times for the third Second, and times for the fourth Se - cond; all these Numbers added together, will make, the Depth as before. Indeed some Abatement must be allowed for the Time the Noise of the Stones fall into the Water takes to reach the Ear. Wherefore since a Sound moves Feet in a Second, and is a little more than of that Number, a little more than P E N than f of Foot must be taken out of the for - mer found Depth. So that the Depth of the Well may roundly be accounted Feet. But in the other Eftimations of the Distance of a Cloud, Ship, or Fort, there needs no such Al - lowance; and the bare Multiplication of, by the Number of Seconds between the Slash and the Report, will give the Distance of the Cloud or Ship from the Observer. That Night, vi. April. ) on which our late Mighty Monarch King William was Buried, we counted oftentimes very Accurately, That the Distance between seeing the Slash, and hearing the Report of the Tower Gulls, ( which were then fired very so'emnly and distinctly ) was always Seconds of Time. Multiplying then by, it produces, which is to be accounted the Distance between Amen - Corner, and the Tower of London, which is one Mile and Feet, or something more than a Mile and a Quarter.

perambulation.c: PERAMBULATION of the Forest, is the Sur - vexing or Walking about the Forest, or the Li - inks of it, by Justices, or other Officers thereto appointed to fee down the Metes and Bounds thereof, and what is within the Forest, and what without.

perambulatione.c: PERAMBULATIONE facienda, is a Writ that is sued out by two or more Lords of Man - ners lying near one another, and confenting to have their Bounds severally known. It is dire - cted to the Sheriff, command ng him to make Perambulation, and fet down their certain Limits.

perambulatororwalking.c: PERAMBULATOR, or Walking - wheel, is an Engine made of Wood or Iron, commonly half a Pole in Circumference, with a Movement and a Face divided, like a Clock with a long Rod of Iron, or Steel that goes from the Centre of the Wheel to the Work: There are also two Hands, which ( as you drive the Wheel before vou ) count the Revolution, and from the Compontion of the Movement, and by the Division on the Face, shew how many Yards, Poles, Furlongs and Miles you go. The use of this Instrument is to measure Roads, Rivers, and all Level Lands, with great Expedition.

perception.c: PERCEPTION, is the clear and diftimft ap - j & rehenfiori of any Objecft offered to us, without forming any Judgment concerning them.

perchameasure.c: PERCH, a Measure by our Statute Law of - Foot and a half in Length. See Pole.

perdonatio.c: PERDONATIO utlagaria, is a Pardon for him who for Contempts in not coming to the King ’ s Court, is Out - Law ’ d, and afterwards of his own accord, yieldeth himself to Prison.

peremptoryinlaw.c: PEREMPTORY, in Law, signifies a final and determinate Ad, without hope of renewing or altering.
