perfectnumbers.c: PERFECT Numbers, are such whose Aliquot or even parts join ’ d - together, will exactly return the whole Number, as,, &c. for of fix, the half is three, the third part two, and the sixth part one, which added together, make fix; and it hath no more aliquot parts in whole Numbers: So twenty eight, which has these parts, vi.,,, a, and, exactly return; which there - fore is a Versed Number, whereof there is but ten between one and one Million of Millions.

perforans.c: PERFORANS, is a Muscle of the Fingers, so called because its Tendons run thro ’ those of the Perforatus, it ’ s also called Profundus from its fitu - ation, and Tertii Into no did Digitorum Flexor, from Its life. It ariseth fleshy from near two Thirds of the Superior, and forepart of the Vena, as also from the Ligament, between the last named Bone j and the Radius; and becoming a large thick - bel - lied Muscle, grows outwardly Tendinous, before j it passes over the Pronator Radii Quadratus, and is i divided into four round Tendons, which march under those of the Perforated Muscle, beneath the JLigamentum Tranfverfale; from eachof these Ten - dons the Mufculi Lumbricalcs are said to arise ) after; which they pass thro ’ the Fissures of those of the Perforated Muscles, and proceeding oyer their I Extremities, terminate in the superior and fore - part of the third Bone of each Finger. .. The Tendons of this Muscle running thro ’ those of the Perforated, is a no less ulefui then stupendous Artifice in Nature. For to the End the Fingers ( like so faany Leavers J should be bended with great force, it is absolutely necessary the strongest Muscle ihould be inserted nearest their Extremities, and farthest from their Fulcimenta the Off a Metacarpi: But in regard every Internode ihould be attended with a particular Muscle, the better to accommodate them to various Employ - ments, and the origination of the Superior or Perforatus, is confined to the Apex of the Internal Extuberance of the Os Humeri, and upper part of the Radius only; wherefore. could not be a fit Instrument for lo strenuous an Addon, and that not only in regard ' to. its Magnitude, but by the Approach of its two Extreams when the Cubit or Carpus are bended; both which would be no final ! Impediments in divers Adions it ’ s therefore ne - pessary it ihould be employed in, the Motions of the second Internodes: But since these Superior Tendons would be hereby liable to interrupt the Inferiorin their right progress to the Extremities of the Fingers j it seems an Argument of great Counsel in transmitting the latter thro ’ the Sis - fures of each of the former, whereby the Adions of both are not only diftindly performed, and the Extremities of the Fingers attended with the largest Muscle, ( whose Origin is below the Os Humeri, wherefore its Extreams cannot ap - roach in the Flexion of the Cubit ) but their Motions are preferred, tho ’ the Superior Muscle is totally divided; which indeed is a Provident - Contrivance of the Author of Nature, and is in it self sufficient to excite our Admiration.

perforansamuscle.c: PERFORANS, a Muscle of the lesser Toes; so called, because its Tendons run thro ’ the Sis - fures in the Tendons of the Muf cuius Perforatus Pedis: It is also called, Flexor tertii Internodii Di - gitorum Pedis, from it use. It hath an Acute Fleshy Origination from the Back - part of the Tibia, im - mediately under the Musculus Subpoplitaus, having a double order of Fibres united in a middle Ten - don like the Flexor Pollias Longus, but ceafeth to be Fleshy as it passeth behind the Malleolus Inters nus, and running in a Channel over the Internal part of the Os Calebs, under ir, Imbanding Liga - ments in half its progress thro ’ the Sole of the Foot; it is divided into four Tendons, which march thro ’ the Perforations of the Tendons of the Perforatus Pedis, and are Inserted to the third Bone of every lesser Toe.

personaus.c: PERSONA US, is a Muscle belonging to the Fingers, and so called, because its Tendons are Perforated to admit those of the Perforating Muf - cles to pass thro ’ them to their Insertions: It is also called Sublimis from its Situation, being above the Perforating Muscles; and Flexor secundi In - ternodii Digitorum, from its use: It ariseth Tendi - nous from the Internal Extuberance of the Os Hu - mer, between the Flexores Carpi: It also has a disgregate Fleshy Origination from the forepart of the Radius, between the Pronator Radii Teres, and Flexor Pollicis Magnus, composing a Fleshy Belly, lessens it self in less than half its Progress, where it ’ s divided into four Fleshy Portions, each of which soon becomes so many roundish Ten - dons, which are included in their proper Mucila - ginous Membrane as they pals under the Ligament - turn P E R turn Trans erf ale Carpi thro ’ the Palm; near the first Internode of the Fingers each Tendon is divi - ded to admit those of the Perforating Muscle fro ’ them; then joining, and subdividing again, immediately before they are Inferred to the fupe - rior part of the second Bone of each Finger.

perforatuspedis.c: PERFORATUS Pedis, is a Muscle of the lei - fer Toes, so called, because its Tendons are Per - sorted like those of the Fingers. It is also cal - led Flexor secundi Internodii Digitorum Pedis, from its U'fe, and Sublimis from its Situation. It springeth from the Inferior and Internal part of the Os Calcis, between the Mufculi Abduct ores of the Greater and Teller Toes, dilating it self to a Fleshy Belly; after it hath palled the middle of the P Un - to, Pedis, it is divided into four Fleshy Portions, which becoming so many Tendons, are divided near their Terminations, to admit the Tendons of the P erf or an s, to pass thro ’ them to their Inferti - ons: These being united again, pass underneath them to their Implantations at the upper part of the second Bone of each Lesser Toe.

perforated.c: PERFORATED, i. r. bored thro ’. The Armorifts use it to express the palling or penetra - ting of one Ordinary ( in part ) thro ’ another; as thus. He bearer Or, a bend Errhirie Perforated thro ’ a Chevron Gules. But when there is only a Hole made thro ’ the Ordinary, and nothing in it to fill it up, they call it Piercing.

periamma.c: PERIAMMA, called also Periapt a, is a Medicine, which being tied about the Neck, is believed to expel Diseases, especially the Plague. See Appensa. PERIAPTUM. Pid. Periamma.

pericarpium.c: PERICARPIUM is a Medicine applied to the Wrifts, to cure an Ague, ( c,

pericardium.c: PERICARDIUM, is a double Membrane, Which surrounds the whole Substance of the Heart, and contains a Liquor to Moisten, Lubricate, and, as some fay, to Refrigerate the Heart; it hath five Holes, according to the number of Vessels which go out of the Heart; it adheres to the Mediafinum at the Balis, and at the Mucro to the Centre, " or Nervous part of the Diaphragma.

PERICARDIUM. Dr. Keil in An. Secretion, p.,. Ihews, that the Liquor in the Pericardi - um is the most fluid of any that is separated from the Blood because the Particles of it unite fir ft and are secreted first: and those Particles which unite first will have the greatest attrap & ive force and such must have their Corpuscles of a most Spherical Figure and must be most solid so that their Contadt will be the least that can be.

pericranium.c: PERICRANIUM, is a Membrane which in - folds the Skull, seated next to the Perioftium, co - vering the whole Skull, except just where the Temporal Muscles lie: It is of exquisite Sense; and causes intolerable Pain When the Temporal Muscle is wounded.

perleci.c: PERLECI, are those Inhabitants of the Earth Who live under the fame Parallels, but under op - posited Semi - circles of the Meridian, whence they have the fame Seasons of the Year, vi. Spring, Summer, Autumn, and Winter, at the very fame time, as also the fame Length of Days and Nights; for tis in the fame Climate, and at an equal Distance from the Equator: But the Chan - ges of Noon and Midnight, are alternate one to the other. PERIGiEON, or Perigmm, is a Point in the heavens, wherein a Planet is said to be in its nea - reft Distance possibly from the Earth. . PERIHELION, is that Point of a Planets Or - bit wherein it is nearest to the Sun.

perimeter.c: PERIMETER, is the Compass or Sum of all the Sides which bound any Figure, whether Bpfti - lineal, or Mm.

perinde.c: PERINDE V tlere, a Term belonging to the Ecclesiastical Law, signifying a Dispensation grant - ed to a Clerk, that being defective in his Capa - city to a Benefice, or other Ecclesiastical Function, is die vasto, admitted to it; and it hath the Appel - lation from the Words, which make the Faculty as effectual to the Party dispensed with, as if he had been actually capable of the thing for which he is dispensed with at the time of his AdmiiTiom It is called a Writ. PERINiEUM, is the Ligamentous Seam be - twixt the Scrotum and the Fundament.

period.c: PERIOD, is a full Stop at the end of any Sen - tence. A Period in Numbers, is a Diftindion made by a Point, or Comma after every fixrfi Place or Figure; and is used in Numeration, for the reader distinguishing and naming the several Fi - gures or Places: Which how to do, fee under Nu - aeration -

periodinchronology.c: PERIOD, in Chronology, signifies a Revolu - tion of a certain Number of Years; as the Me - tonief Period, the Julian Period, and the Calip - pick. Period; which see in their proper Places.

periodical.c: PERIODICAL, is the Term for whatever per - forms its Motion, Course, or Revolution reg - larly, so as to return again, and to dispatch it al - ways in the fame Period pr Space of Time. Thus the Periodical Motion of the Moon, is that where - by slie finishes her Course round about the Earth in a Month; and this is in Days, Hours, Minutes; and is called, The Moon ’ s

periodicalmonth.c: PERIODICAL Month; which is the space of Time that the Moon finishes her Revolution in.

periodussanguinis.c: PERIODUS Sanguinis, is a continued Circu - lation of the Blood thro ’ the Body, which is thus made: The Blood is carried out of the Arteries by Fibres, either of the Flesh or of the Entrails, pr the Membranous Parts, faith Blanchard p bur tis Certain it is by Capillary Arteries continued with the like final ! Veins, into the Mouths of the greater Veins, and implanted in them, as we fee many other little Channels in the Veins; so the Blood, palling thro these out of the Arteries, is presently sent to the Veins, that it may be carry - ed back again to the right Ventricle of the Heart; and thence by the Arterioas Vein to the Lungs; in which, after the Bipod has been accended by some Nitrous Particles, breathed in thither by the Air, it goes into the Venous Artery, thence into the left Ventricle of the Heart; which again empties it self into the Aorta, or Great Artery; so that the Body may be nourished and enlivened, it goes into every part of it. This is Blanchard ’ s Account of the Matter - See more in the Word Circulation of the Blood

periostium.c: PERIOSTIUM, is a Thin Membrane that inclosed immediately almost all the Bones in the Body, except the Teeth, Bones of the Ear, ( c. It hath a most Exquisite Sense, and probably is an Expansion of the Nervous and Tendinous Fi - bres of the Muscles. Its use is. to cover the Bones, and to fuftairi the Vessels which enter into them to nourish them. Dr. Havers in. his Excellent Book, called, Ofleologia Nova; faith, That this Mem - brane consists of two forts of Fibres, of which those that lie next the Bone, are derived from the Dura Mater, and the others from the Tendons of the Muscle ?, : PERIPATETICK Philosophy, is named from those, who from their Adion of Walking while j, they Studied ot Taught were galled

peripateticks.c: PERIPATET ICKS. The Chief of these was Ariflotle then his Successors; among whom you may reckon Theophrafius, Cratippus, Boethius, and all his very Numerous Interpreters. But about Years ago, there arose a new Set of Famous Arifiotelians, which Were called also Peripate - till s from them came the three chief Sets of the Peripatetic ! Philosophy. The T homifis from Thomas Aquinas, who flourished AD.. The Scotifis from Johannes Dim Scotus, A. D.. And the Ncminalijis from Ocham, who Was Born about A. D. ie. And now adays by the Pe - ripatetick Philosophy we understand that which was founded on the Principles of Aristotle and his Commentators and Followers; and which there - fore is as frequently called, The Arifiotelidn Phi - lofophy.

peripheryingeometry.c: PERIPHERY, in Geometry, is the Circumfe - rence of a Circle, or of any other Regular Curve - lineal Figure.

periphrasis.c: PERIPHRASIS, is a Circumlocution used to avoid certain Words, whose Idea ’ s are unpleasing; and to prevent the speaking of something that Would produce ill Effects.

periptereinarchitecture.c: PERIPTERE, in Architecture, is a Place en - compassed round with Columns, and with a kind of Wings about it; here the Pillars stand with - out, whereas in the Perifiyle they Aland within.

perscii.c: PER SCII, are the Inhabitants of the two Frozen sines, or these that live within the com - pass'of the ArBic / and Antarctic ! i Circles; for ' as the Sun never goes down to them after he is once up, but always round about, fq do their Shadows, Whence the Name, '

perissology.c: PERISSOLOGY, is a Difeonrfe fill ’ d up with unnecessary and superfluous Words.

peristaltickmotion.c: PERISTALTICK Motion, is a Vermicular or WortnlVay Motion of the Intestines, whereby the Excrements are voided. Also the Motions of the Vessels whereby Humours as Water, Chyle, the Blood, &c. ascend and descend, is fbmerimes so called.

peristiphalinus.c: PERISTIPHALINUS, internus t externus, are Muscles of the Vvula, the one pulling ir for - wards, and the other backwards.

peristyleinarchitecture.c: PERISTYLE, in Architecture, is a Place or Building encompass ’ d with Pillars, Standing round about within the Court: But this Word Perifiyle is sometimes taken for a row or rank, of Columns s well Without as within any Edifice; as in Cloyfters and Galleries: Sometimes this was call ’ d Antiprofiyle.

peritonaeum.c: PERITONAEUM, is a Membrane ( of an Oval Figure ) Which clothes the whole Abdomen on the inside, and its Entrails on the outside: It con lifts of two Tunicks, and adheres above to the Diaphragma, below to the Os Ilium - before to the Transverse Muscles, but chiefly to their Ten - dons about the Linea Alba; behind it grows to the Fleshy Heads of these Muscles. PERlTROCHlUM, in Mechanicks is a kind of Wheel, or Circular Frame of Wood, placed sore where upon an Axis, or Cylinder, round which a Rope is wound, in order to raise a Weight; and the Use of this Peritrochium, is to make the Cylinder or Axis be turned the more easily by the jpeans of Staves or Levers, which are fist ’ d in its Circumference, See ' Axis in Per trcchio.

PERITONAEUM: The External Surface of this soft thin Membrane is unequal where it adheres to the transverse Muscles the Internal is very smooth. It hath a number of small Glands which separate a Liquor, which supplies the Intestines and facile - tates their Motion: and when these ' Glands are obftrudled the Peritonceum grows thick, as in see - ral Dropfies. The Peritonceum is a double Mem - brane, containing in its Duplicature the Umbili - cal Vessels, the Bladder, Ureters, Kidneys, and Spermatick Vessels, to all which it gives a Mem - brane, as also to the Liver, Spleen, Stomach, In - testiness and Womb. Its External Lamina hath two Productions, like to two Sheaths, which pass thro ’ the Rings of the oblique and transverse Muscles in the Groin, for the passage of the Spermatick Vessels in Men and for the round Ligaments of the Womb in Women. These Productions being come to the T testicles in Men, dilate and form the Tunica Vaginalis. The Internal Lamina, which is very thin here, having accompanied the External Productions a little way, cleaves close to the Spermatick Vessels and round Ligaments of the Womb. The Peritonceum hath Veins and Arteries from the Phrenicce, the Mam - milliary, the Epigastrick, and often from the Per - maticks. Its Nerves are of those which are di - ftributed in the Muscles of the Abdomen it hath likewise a few Lymphaticks which discharge them - selves into the Iliac Glands. By the Elasticity of its Fibres it easily dilates and contracts in Refpira - tion, and in Conceptions. If it breaks it causes a Rupture either in the Navel or Groin. Its use is to contain the Bowels of the Abdomen, and to give to each of them an outer Coat.

perjury.c: PERJURY, is a Crime committed, when a lawful Oath is ministered, by any that hath Am thority, to any Persons in any Judicial Proceed - ings; who Swear absolutely and saltly in a Mat - ter material to the Issue or Cause in Question, either of their own accord, or by the Subordina - tion of others. Note, If a Man Call me Perjured Man, I may have my A & ion upon the Case; but for calling me a Forfvoorn Man, no Action lies. And Perjury is excepted out of the Ad of General Pardon.

permeating.c: PERMEATING, is penetrating into, and paR ling thro ’ the Pores of any Body. Mr. Boyle had a Smoaking Liquor, which he called, The Per erne - ating Menfiruum, and its Operations, The Pene - trant, or Permeating Fumes, It was made of equal Parts of Flos Sulphuris, Sal Armoniack, and good Quick Lime, all powdered, and well min - gled together, and then Distilled by Degrees of Fire in a Retort, till the Sand which contains the Retort, become almost red hot; for then will come over a Liquor which will be continual - ly Smoaking, and consequently must be kept well top ’ d: With this Fuming Liquor be made see - ral Experiments to evince the Pofofity of Bodies by discovering that tho ’ Coins, &c. were wrap ’ d up close in Leather, &c. yet the Fumes of this Permeating Menfiruum would get thro ’ them; and discolor the Metal. permitationearchidiaconatus.c: PERMIT ATIONE Archidiaconatus & Ec elefice eidem annexed cum Ecclefia & pr ebenda, is a Writ to an Ordinary, commanding him to admit a Clerk to a Benefice, upon exchange made with another.

per.c: PER any & per tout, in Law, a Joynt - Tenant is said to be feiled of the Lands that he holds jointly Per my Q per tout; that is, he is seised by every Parcel, and by the whole.

PER qua. Servitia, is a Writ Judicial, Issuing from the Note of a Fine, and lieth for Cognisee of a Mannor, Seigniory, chief Rent, or other Services, to compel him that his Tenant of the Land at the time of the Note of the Fine levied, to Attorn unto him.

PER j Qu e Sdrvitia, in Law, is a Writ Judicial i sling from the Note of a Fine, and lieth for Cognisee of a Mannor, Seigniory, Chief Rent or other Services to compel him that is a Tenant of, the Land at the time of the Note of the Fine levi - ed, to attorn unto him.

pernio.c: PERNIO, is a Preternatural Swelling caused by the Winter Cold, especially in the Hands and Feet, which at last breaks out.

perona.c: PERONA, is also called Fibula, because it joins the Muscles of the teg; whence the first and second Muscle in the Leg is called Peronaus. It is the lels and lender Bone, which is fattened outwardly to the greater Bone of the Leg, called Tibia.

perpendiculumchronometrum.c: PERPENDICULUM Chronometrum, the fame with the Pendulum.

perquisite.c: PERQUISITE, is any thing gotten by a Man ’ s own Industry, or purchased with his own Money, different from that which descends to him from his Father or Ancestors.
PERQUISITE, in the Law Sense, is any thing gotten by a Person ’ s own Industry, or purchased With his own Money, different from that which descends to him from his Father or Ancestors,

perquisitesofcourt.c: PERQUISITES of Court, in Law, signifies those Profits that grow to a Lord of a Mannor, by vertue of his Court Baron, over and above the certain Yearly Profits of his Land, as Fines of Copy - holds, Hariots, Amerciaments, Waifes, Strays,

PERQUISITES of Court, are such Profits as grow to a Lord of a Mannor by virtue of his Court - Baron, over and above the yearly certain Profits of his Land as Fines of Copy - hold, Harriots, Amer - ciaments, FVaifes, Strays, cc.

persickorder.c: PERSICK Order of ArchiteBure, is where the " Bodies of Men serve instead of Columns to sup - port the EntablatHre, or rather the Columns are in that form. The v, THe Rile of it was this; Paufanias having de - seated the Perfidis, the Lacedemonians, as a Mark bf their Vidory, ereded Trophies of the Arms df their Enemies, and then - represented the Perfinru under the Figures of Slaves fiipporting their Porches:, Arches, or Houjes.

perminima.c: PER MINIMA, a Termufedin Chymistry and Physick, expreding the versed Mixture of any two or more Bodies: v. gr. If Silver and Lead be melted together, they will mingle and be united with one another per minima: That is, all the smallest Particles bf one Metal, will be mingled and united with those of the other.

pernicityaword.c: PERNICITY, a Word used by some Philofo - thick Writers of Celerity, or extraordinary swift - help of Motion.

peronalus.c: PERONALUS primus, a Muscle of the Tarsus; by some it is called Longus, it being the first that offers it self to view; and the longest Muscle feat - ed on the Fibula or Os Peronce. ] It arises Externally Tendinous, and Fleshy In - ternally from above half the Superior part of the said Bone, and marching some what backwards, becomes a strong, flat Tendon, four Fingers breadth in length above the Inferior Appendage of the said Fibula, called Malleolus Externus; palling be - hind which in a Channel, like a Rope in a Put - Jey; and from thence being inflexed forwards, together with the Tendon of the following Muf - cle, they pass under an imbanking Ligament as they run over the Os Calcis, but this Tendon de - clining from its Companion, marches over the Os Cuboides, under the Musculus Abductor Minimi Di - it !, and over the Off a Cuneiformid, in the Bottom of the Foot, and under the Tendons and Muf - cles bending the Toes, and is Inferred to the Su - period and Hindmost part of the Os Metatarsi of the Great Toe. The Tendon this Muscle being conveyed over the Hmdmoft part of the Malleolus Externus, as on a Pulley, is an Elegant Contri - vance in Nature, whereby the Ball of the Great Toe ( as that part is commonly called to which it is Inferred ) is directed towards a Perpendicular bearing of the Weight of the Body on the Leg, in Standing on Tip - toe, by pulling the Foot and Toes somewhat outwards. PERONAiUS Jecundus, a Muscle of the Tarsus, by ' some called Semi - fibulans: It has an Acute Fleshy beginning above the middle of the Enter - nal part of the Fibula, under the Fleshy Belly of the Peroneus primus it also continues its Fleshy beginning from the Posterior sharp edge of the said Fibula, and becoming a Fleshy Belly, grows Ten - dinous as it runs under the Malleolus Externus, together with the Tendon of the Peroneut primus, and is Inserted to the Superior and External part efthe Os Metatarsi of the Little Toe. The pro - per Adion of this Muscle, is to pull the Foot and Toes outwards.

PERPENDICULAR, to a Parabola, is a Right Line cutting the Parabola in the Point in which any other Right Line touches it, and which is al - so its self Perpendicular to that Tangent.

perpendicularoreightplane.c: PERPENDICULAR, or Eight Plane, is where a Plane, ( like a well made Wall ) inclines and leans on one side no more than it doth on the o ther.

perpetuityaterm.c: PERPETUITY, a Term used in Law, ' where an Estate is so designed to be settled in Tail, c. that it cannot be undone or made void.

perse.c: PER SE, a Term of Art often used; as in Lo - gick, we fay a Thing is considered Per fe, when ’ tis taken in the Abftradt, and without Connexion with other things, which would confound the No - tion, and hinder its being clear. In Chymistry a Thing is said to be Distilled Per fe, when ’ tis without the usual Additaments of other things with it. We fay also a Man performs any AdHon, or Executes any Office per fe, when he doth it himself in P erf on, and not by a Deputy or Substitute.

perseusaconstellation.c: PERSEUS, a Constellation in the Northern He - mifphere, consisting of Stars.

personalverb.c: PERSONAL Verb, in Grammar, is one that is Declined, or Conjugated with all the Three Persons, and in both Numbers; whereas an Im - personal Verb in only used in the Third Person Singular.

personableinlaw.c: PERSONABLE, in Law, signifies as much as enabled to maintain Plea in a Court, thus: The Defendant was adjudged Perfonably to maintain this Adhon. Also the Tenant pleaded, that the Wife was an Alien Born in Portugal, without the Allegiance of the King; and Judgment was de - mended, Whether she should be answered: The Plaintiff faith, She was made P & sanable by Par - Lament z ? sf vT P E S liamerit; that is, as the Civilians would speak it. Habere perfinam stand in judicio. P erf enable is - also as much as to be of Capacity to take any thing granted or given.

personalinlaw.c: PERSONAL, in Law, when ’ tis join ’ d faith the Substances, Things, Goods of Chattels j as Things Personal, Goods Personal, Chattels Perfi - nal signifies any moveable thing belonging to a Man, be it Quick or Dead: Thus, they fay, Theft is an Unlawful Felonious taking away another Man ’ s Moveable Personal Goods.

personaltythes.c: PERSONAL Tythes, are Tythes paid of such Profits as come by the Labour of a Man ’ s Person, as by Buying and Selling, Gains of Merchandice and Handicrafts, c. See Tythes.

personality.c: PERSONALITY, is an Abftradt of Personal: ' the Action is in the Per signality, vis. It is brought against the right Person, or the Person against whom in Law it lies.

persons.c: PERSONS ne Prebendaries ne front charge as quinfirh, cc. is a Writ that lies for Prebendaries, or other Spiritual Persons, being distrained by the Sheriff of Collectors of Fifteens, for the Sis - tenths of their Goods, or to be contributary to

perspective.c: PERSPECTIVE, is that part of the Mathe - maticks which gives Rules for the representing of Objects on a plain Superficies, after the fame manner as they would appear to our fight, if seen thro ’ that Plain, it being supposed as transparent as Glass. PerfpeBive is either Speculative or Practical. Speculative PerfpeBive, is the Knowledge of the Keafons of the different Appearance of certain Ob - jedts, according to the several Positions of the Eye that beholds them. Practical PerfpeBive, is the Method of Deli - neating that which is apparent to our Eyes, or that which our Understanding conceives in the forms that we fee Objects. See Vol. II.

And thus proceed - ing with the Angular Points of any Figure, whe - ther regular or irregular, you may draw any thing truly in Perspective; only in practice, several compendious Methods will arise, which every one will discover on frequent Trials. And if the Scenographick Appearance of any Solid were to be represented, as suppose of a Tri - angular Prism whole Base is the Triangle M NO in the Second Figure j you need only find the up - per Surface of it after the lame w ay as you found, the Lower or the Base, and then joining the cor - desponding Points by Right Lines you will have ehetrue Representation of the Solid in Perspective. So that the Work is the fame as before, only you take a new Fundamental Line, as much higher than the former, as is the Altitude of that Solid whose Scenographick Representation you would delineate. But there is yet a more commodious way of doing this, as follows Having found, as above, the Base or Ichnogr aphis Plane no Let Perpendiculars be ereded to the Fundamental Line, from the three Angular Points, which will express the Altitudes of those Points. But because thele Altitudes, tho: equal to one another in the Body or Solid it self, will appear unequal in the Scenographick view, for those that are further off will appear less, and the nearer, larger. Their true proportionable Heights may be thus determined: Any where in the Fundamental Line let A B be ereded perpendicularly equal to the true Altitude ( or if the Figure hath different Altitudes, let them all be transferred into the Perpendicular A B ) and from the Points A and B ( and from all the Points of intermediate Altitude, if there be any luch ) draw Right Lines to the Eye Point in V, or to any Point in the Horizontal Line: Those Lines AV and VB will constitute a Triangle with A B, within which all the Points of Altitude will be contained. Thro the Points o, n, and m, draw parallels to the Fundamental Line, as you fee, and from the Points a, a, a, ered Perpendiculars to those Parallels, and where they Intersect the two Lines A V and B V; as in the Points a, a, a, and b, b, b, &c. they will determine the apparent height of the Solid in that Scenographick Position to the Eye at V. And in Practice these Parallels and Perpendiculars are to be easily described by the help of a good Drawing - Board or Table fitted for this purpose, and others of this nature. perspectivelineal.c: PERSPECTIVE Lineal, is the Diminution of those Lines in the Plan of a Picture, which are the Representation of other Lines very remote.

perspectiveaereal.c: PERSPECTIVE Aereal, is a Proportional Di - minution of the Teints and Colours of a PiCture, when the ObjeCts are supposed to be very re - mote.

perspectivemilitary.c: PERSPECTIVE Military, is when the Eye is supposed to be infinitely remote from the Table or Plain.

perspicuous.c: PERSPICUOUS, is that which is clear and transparent, as that the Light may be seen freely thro ’ it. See Diaphanous.

perspiration.c: PERSPIRATION, a breathing through, as Sweat through the Invisible Pores of the Body.

pertica.c: PERTICA, a fort of Comet, the fame with Veru.

pessary.c: PESSARY, is as Oblong Medicine, which be - ing made of the Length of the Middle Finger, is thrust up into the Neck of the Womb, and is good against several Diseases incident to it.

pestilentialfever.c: PESTILENTIAL Fever, is that which does not only affliCt the Patient with a bare Distemper or Heat arising from Putrefaction, Sc. but also with. a Malignant and Venomous Quality.; It differs ] from the Plague, as a Species or fort from the Genus or Kind; because a Peftilence may some - times happen without a Fever, Blanchard.

pestoloides.c: PESTOLOIDES, is a fort of Urine which seems to have little Leaves or Scales in it. Blan chard. f

petala.c: PETALA, is a Term in Botany signifying those fine coloured Leaves that compose the ‘ Flow - ers of all Plants. And from hence Plants are di - ftinguifhed into Monopetalous, whose Flower is ail in one continued Leaf; and Tripet alous, and Pen - tapetalousj when the Flower consists of three or five Leaves, and Polypetalous when of many, without determining the Number.

petardinfortification.c: PETARD, in Fortification, is an Engine of Metal, in the form of an High - crown ’ d Flat with narrow Brims, which being filled with very fine Powder, well primed, and then fix ’ d with a Ma - drier or Plank, bound fast down, with Ropes running through Handles, which are round the Rim of the Mouth of it, to break down Gates Port - cullices, Draw - bridges, Barriers g, This Engine is from to Inches deep, and broad at the Mouth j the Diameter at the Bottom or Breech, is an Inch and a half, and the Weight of the whole Mass of Metal is from to Pounds generally requiring about Pounds of Powder for the Charge. They are also used in Counter - mines to break through into the Enemies Galleries and to disappoint their Mines.

petechialis.c: PETECHIALIS, is a Malignant Fever, called also Pulicaris, because it makes the Skin look as tho ’ it were Flea - bitten. '

petittreafin.c: PETIT Treafin, in Common Law, is when A Servant kills his Master, a Wife her Husband, a Secular or Religious Man, his Prelate or Supe rior, to whom he owes Faith and Obedience: In how rqany other Cafes it may be committed, fee Cromp. Just of Peace.

petitioprincipii.c: PETITIO Principii, Begging ' of Principles, is & precarious supposing a thing to be true, or taking it for granted when it really remains either Dubi - ous, or else is expressly denied. This frequently is called. Begging the Question, when a Man sup - poses what he should prove.

putrefaction.c: PUTREFACTION, is properly the changing of a mix ’ d Body into a Stony Substance, when it had no such Nature before and the Action by which this is performed, is called,

PUTREFACTION, is a flow kind of Corrup - tion in Bodies, wrought generally by the moisture of the Air, or fame other ambient Fluid, which penetrating unto the Pores of Bodies, and being ai - tated in them, doth fetch or force out some of the more subtil and agile Parts of Bodies, loosen and dis - locate the Parts in general one from another, and thereby quite change the Texture, and sometimes the Figure of the Mixt, from what it was before,

petrification.c: PETRIFICATION, and the Thing so chang ’ d is said to be Petreficd. ’ Tis justly questionable. Whether there be any such thing as this in Nai ture, or not ? PetrefaBion indeed now a - days, is a mighty modifii Word, for every thing aknoft that is found upon - the Surface of dug out of the Earth, passes with some Persons by this Name. But what is there that really and truly deserves the Name of PetrefaBion ? When the the Petrefy - ing Waters, as they are called, ( which are no - thing but Waters impregnated with a great deal of Stony Matter, which in their Passage through the Earth became dissolved in them: ) When these, I fay, Incrustate Rufhes, Grass, or Sticks all over with a Stony Coat, by letting the Stony Parades dissolved in them, by little and little, fall down upon and adhere to them or it may be Infinu - atc into their Pores, and deposita themselves there i And when after this, the Vegetable part inclosed, rots and moulders away, and the Stony Coat, or Substance daily increases; this is not the Trans - mutation of a Vegetable Substance into a Stony iryr P H A P H L or Mineral cne, and therefore the new Body thus formed, is not properly a Petref action in the true Sense of the Word. And when many Bodies are found in the Earth, Which by all possible ways of judging and di - ftinguifhing, approve themselves to be Animal or Vegetable Bodies, such as the. Shells, Teeth, Bones of Animals, the Fossil Trees, Pine - Cones, Hazel Nuts, &c. which are every where found deep in the Earth. It appears odd to call these Petref actions, and more odd to suppose them nothing but the S fort mgs of Nature and to affirm all these things to be nothing but meer Formed Stones, only be - cause we cannot account presently how they came thus into the Earth, or solve all the Objections or Difficulties about them: But every one will have his own way ofExpreffion.

petrosumos.c: PETROSUM Os, is the Internal Process of the Bones of the Temples, so called from its hard - ness and cragginess: ’ is pretty long, jetting out to the Inner Balls of the Skull, within which it hath two Holes, and thro ’ one of them an Artery, and thro ’ the other the Auditory Nerve passes to the Inner Cavities of the Ear, that are excavated in this Process, vi. the Tympanum, Labyrintlm, and Cochlea; and without the Skull it hath three Holes: The first of which is the Meatus Audito - rius: The second is narrow, short, and Oblique, near to the first, and thro ’ it the Jugular Vein en - ters the Inner Cavities: The third is seated be - twixt the Prcceffus Mammillaris, and the Sty hides Appendix, and ends in the Passage which goes from the Ear to the Mouth. PETTERERO. See Pedrero.

pevetts.c: PEVETTS, are the Ends of the Spindle of any WheeLin a Watch; and the Holes into which they run, are called Pevett - holes.

pent.c: PENT / or & dure. See Payne fort & dure.

phacos.c: PHACOS, is a Spot in the Face like a Nit, whence it is called Lenticula and Lentigo.

phagadenickwater.c: PHAGADENICK Water is made by diflol - ving a Dram of Sublimate Corrosive in a Pound of Lime Water on which it will immediately turn Yellow.

phalacrosis.c: PHALACROSIS, is the falling off the Hair.

phalangosis.c: PHALANGOSIS is a fault of the Eye - lids, when there are two rows of Hair, or when the Hair grows inward and offends the Eyes.

phalanx.c: PHALANX, according to some Writers, is rhe Order and Rank observed in the Finger Bones.

PHALANX, among the Macedonians, was an Oblong Square close Battle of Pikemen confiding of in File and in Front, as Polybius faith j and the Soldiers flood so close together, that the Pikes ef the th Rank extended Foot beyond the Front of the Battlp.

phantasy.c: PHANTASY is an Internal Sense or Imagine - tion, whereby any Corporeal thing is represented to the Mind, or impressed on the Brain by its pro - per Image.

phantasticalcolours.c: PHANTASTICAL Colours, are such as are ex - habited by the Rainbow, Triangular Glass Prism, the Surface of very thin Muscovy Glass, &c. They had this Name given ’ em by the PeripatetickPhilo - f others, who supposed them to be no real Colours. This Kircher well Refutes in his Mundus Subter - r emeus. Part z. p.,. and fiiews also the Caule of such Colours.

pharmacum.c: PHARMACUM, is any fort of Medicine a - gainst a Disease,

pharmacy.c: PHARMACY, is an Art of cojleding, causing, and compounding Medicines, vi. the Apotheca - ry ’ s Art; to which may also be added the Ghy mical Analysis of Bodies, in order to prepare good Medicines out of them.

pharyngeerum.c: PHARYNGEERUM is sometimes used for the Pharynx, sometimes for the Bone Hyades.

pharynx.c: PHARYNX, is the upper part of the Gullet, consisting of three pair of Muscles; to which, some add another, making the Number seven; It is continued to the Fauces, ( or indeed is the greatest part thereof ) reaching up behind to the ' Uvula, on the sides to the TonfilU, and before to the Epiglottis: It is Membranous, but not entire - ly so, being in some places Carnous and Thick. Three pair of its Muscles open it in rhe Adion of Swallowing; and the odd one is a SphinElcr which serves to straiten it.

phenomenoninnaturalphilosophy.c: PHENOMENON, in Natural Philosophy, fig - nifies any Appearance, EfFed, or Operation of a Natural Body, which offers its self to the Confide - ration and Solution of an Enquirer into Nature.

phases.c: PHASES, signifies the Appearance or the Man - ner of Things ffiewing themselves, and therefore in Astronomy is used for the several Positions in which the Planets ( especially the Moon ) appear to our Sight: as obscure, horned, half illuminated, or full of Light, which by the help of a Telescope may likewise be observed in Venus and Mars.

PHASES of the Planets: Since all the Planets as well as the Earth are Spherical, Opake and Sca - brous Bodies, they must rested: every way the Sun ’ s Rays which fall upon them; and it will follow al - io from hence, that one half of every Planet, or that Hemisphere which is turned towards the Sun, will be illuminated by him, and the other Hemi - sphere at that time must remain in Darkness. And further, since ’ tis that Hemisphere of any Planet, which is obverted to the Earth, which is confider - ed by any Observator t T The eight little Circles represent the different Phases of Venus, as they will appear to an Eye placed in T on the Earth, while she moves round in her Or - bit A C E G about the Sun. It will be plain then, that when Venus is in A, and the Earth at T; she being then roost retrograde, ( see the Word Di - rei in this Vol. J will least of all appear to us, be - cause her obscure Hemisphere is entirely obverted towards us. And if she happen to be then in either of the Nodes, i. e. in the Plane of the Ecliptick, she will appear like a Spot in the Body of the Sun. But when she gets further to B ( the Eye being still supposed to be in T ) she will still be retro - grade, but fame small part of her illuminated Disk will be visible and she will appear with illume - nated Horns which will be turned from the Sun, or towards the Weft. When she comes to C, one half of her illuminated Disk will be visible to an Eye in T, and then file will appear like an Half - Moon in D file will be gibbous, and in E at full And the fame Phases she will put on as she moves in the other Semicircle from E to A again, only the illuminated Horns will be turned a contrary way as appears by the Second Figure, where the several Phases are delineated -. An P I N A C E And the fame kind of Phases must happen to Mercury in the several parts of his Orbit, regard being had to the Figure of it, and the Time of his Periodical Revolution round the Sun.

pheonsinheraldry.c: PHEONS, in Heraldry, are the Barbed Heads of Darts or Arrows, and are usually of this Figure. Sable, a Sense Ermin between three Phaons, by the Name of Egerton.

philanthropy.c: PHILANTHROPY, is a generous Love for Mankind in General, or an Inclination to promote Publick Good.

philonium.c: PHILONIUM, is an Opiate Medicine; of which they reckon two forts, the Philonium Ro manum, and Perficum.

philosophicalegg.c: PHILOSOPHICAL Egg, among the Chymifts, is a thin Glass Vessel, or Bubble, of the Shape of an Egg, with a long Neck or Stem ’ Tis used in long Digeftions.

philtrum.c: PHILTRUM, is the Hollow dividing the Up: per Lip.

phimosis.c: PHIMOSIS, is the fame with Paraphimojis; al - so the Inversion of the Eye - lids through an In - flammation.

phleborhagia.c: PHLEBORHAGIA, is the breaking of a Vein. ’

phlebotomy.c: PHLEBOTOMY, opening of a Vein, or letting of Blood.

phlegmorwater.c: PHLEGM, or Water, the Fourth of the Five Chymical Principles. See Water. The Insipid Water that comes first in the Di - stellation of Acid Spirits, the Chymifts call the Phlegm: And the more any such Spirit is red - fied, that is, distilled over again, to draw off still more of this Phlegm, they fay ’ tis the better dephlegmated.

phlegmofvitriol.c: PHLEGM of Vitriol, is the Moisture that is first drawn off when Calcined Vitriol is distilled, in order to get it's Spirit and Oil, it comes off with a gentle heat.

phlegmagogues.c: PHLEGMAGOGUES, are Medicines which purge or drain away that Humour which they call Phlegm. PHLEGMON, P H O

phlogosis.c: PHLOGOSIS, is a light Inflammation of the Byes, with a small Pain and Redness; which sometimes turns into a true Opht balmy, and is the Original thereof.

phlyctoena.c: PHLYCTOENA, is a Pimple in the Skin, alio a little Ulcer, like a Bubble or Bladder, in the Corneous Tunick of the Eye, and proceeding from a fliarp Watry Humour. Blanchard. PHQN CKS, the fame with Acoufticks; which

phosphorusachymicalpreparation.c: PHOSPHORUS, a Chymical Preparation, which being exposed to the Light or Air, will shine in the Dark. Of this there are several kinds, Whose Process shall be briefly delivered. To make the Bolonian Phosphorus, fee under the Bolonian Stone. The molt Common Way ( with us ) / is to make the Phosphorus from Humane Urine. And the Hint came first by Chance thus:. One Brand, an Alchymist of Hamburgh, wisely thinking to find the Philosopher ’ s Stone in Hu - man Urine, Work ’ d upon it in a Retort, and so forced over the Phosphorus Matter; yet he would not communicate this Dilcovery to any one, and so the Secret died with him. After his Death, one Kjrkfelius a Saxon Chymist fet himself to find it out, ( having heard of such a thing ) and suc - weeded accordingly; and this Man strewed the Process to several of his Friends. The Honourable Mr. Boyle having ( in part ) had an Account of this Phosphorus, from one Daniel Kjajf, a German, about the Year, published in English an Account of the Way of making this Phosphorus, and several very Curious Experiments upon it, under the Title of NoEliluca. And since that, Mr. Homberg hath written largely about it, as you may see in the Memoirs ( for the Months March and April ) qf the Royal Academy of Sci - ences at Paris,. /,... The Way of Preparing it, is this z Take a good large Quantity of the New - made Urine of Beer - drinkers, and evaporate it gently, to the. Consistence of Honey Then put it in an Earthen Vessel, cover, and place it in a Cellar for three or four Months, that it may throughly fer - ment and putrefied. Then mix a double Quantity of Sand, or Pouder of Pots, with one part of this corrupted Urine, and put it into an Earthen Re - tort or Glass one Coated; and fitting it to a large long - neck ’ d Glass Receiver, in which was before put two or three Quarts of Water, distil it in a na - ked Fire, in a Reverberatory Furnace, gently at first, for about two Hours; afterwards augment the Fire gradually, ’ till all the Volatile Salt and black Foetid Oil be drawn off. Then raise the Fire to the highest Degree, and white Clouds will come into the Receiver, and fix it by little and little, on one side of it, in the form of a yet - lowilh Skin, and another part will precipitate to the bottom in Pouder. Keep the Fire thus vio - lent for three Hours, ’ till no more Fumes will come. Let all cool,, and unlute ths Vessels and P H O throwing more Water into the Receiver, shake all well about to loosen what will stick to the sides and then pour it all into a large Glass Vessel, where it will settle; the Volatile Salt will dis - solve in the Water, but the Phosphorus and, the Oil will sink to the bottom. Pour off the Wa - ter, and gathering the remaining Matter together / put it into a little Glass Vessel, with a little frefti Water, and digest it in a Sand - heat, stirring the Matter about from time to time with a Wooden Spatula; the Phosphorus by this means will sea - rate from the Oil, and sink to the bottom. Pour away the Oil, and make the Phosphorus up, while hot, into little Sticks or Pieces, which must be kept in a Viol of Water close stopt. This is the Solid Phosphorus, With which, if you ' write any Letters on Paper, or on a Wall, they will appear Luminous in the Dark, and continue so a good While. If you cut off a little bit of it and rub it strongly along a piece of Paper, With a Knife, it Will actually enkindle the Paper. The Liquid Phosphorus is made by digesting in Horse - dung a little bit, or some Scrapings of the Solid, for two Days, in Oil or Essence of Cloves Oil of Turpentine, &c. For after it is dissolved in the Oil, it will impregnate it so, that as soon as ever you open the Bottle, the Matter will appear ' all in a Flame. If you put a little of the Solid Phosphorus into a Viol, with a little Oil Of Vitriol, that is very strong and well dephlegmated, and then add to it about half as much common Water as there was Oil of Vitriol, the Mixture will grow very hot, and stoak; and if you carry the Viol into the Dark, you will see the Phosphorus enkindled, and sparkle in many places of the Viol, like Meteors or little Falling - stars: Ann if a small Quantity of Oil of Turpentine be added, it will produce an a & ual Flame. Lemery mentions a New - invented Phosphorus of Mr. Homberg s, being made of one part of Salt Armoniack, and two of QuiCk - Time slack by the Air; which are fluxed together in a Crucible into a kind of Gray Glass, which when it is struck with a Hammer appears presently of a light Fire; Phosphorus Balduini, called the Her me tick, Phofl phorus, is thus made; Heat red - hot about two pounds of Chalk, let it cool, and pouder it. Then take a pint of Aqua fortis, and put into it a fpoonfnl of you pou dered Chalk; a great Ebullition will arise: Re - peat this till the throwing in of the Pouder makes no Ebullition at all / After this, let the Liquor settle, and decant it into an Earthen Pan placed in Sand, and evaporate all the Liquor, so there will remain a kind of Salt at the bottom. Put this Salt into a Copper, or a strong Earthen un glazed Pan; fet it in a gentle Sand - heat, and the Matter will swell. Continue this gentle Fire ’ till it be funk down a little towards the bottom then cover the Pan or Coppel with a Lid that hath two or three Holes in it, and encrease the Fire gradually, ’ till i t be strong enough to melt the Matter; and when ’ tis melted, a yellow Va - pour will exhale through the Holes in the Cover. Then take the Vessel presently off the Fire, and putting on another Earthen Lid, which hath no Holes in it, fet it by to cool. Round about the a Q " sides I P I C sides of the Pan you will find a Crust of yellow Matter, that is the Pofpherus: Itmuft be kept - in a Box well stopt, in a dark place. When ’ tis design ’ d to be rendred Luminous, you must expose it, like the Boloninn Stone, to the Light, for a small Space; and then removed into the Dark, it will shine there. If it be left in the Dark, exposed to the Air for about Fifteen Days, it will shine all that while, but after that, go out, and never be Luminous more. Mr. Boyle, in his Aereal NoSliluca, p. x. de - fcribesa Phosphorus Balduini much like this; and in Phil. Trans N, there is of his a yet more accurate Process for this Thing. The Learned Dr. SI are, in Phil. Trans No., makes an Ingenious Comparison between Light - ning, and the Flafhes which in Warm Weather he had often observed ( by Night ) to arise from feme pieces of the Solid Phosphorus, kept in long Glass Bottles of Water about filled.

PH RENICK VeJJels, are the Veins and Arte - teries that run through the Diaphragm, Mediafli - num, and Pericardium.

phrenitisorphrenzj.c: PHRENITIS, or Phrenzj, is a Dottage with a continued Fever, often accompanied with Mad - ness and Anger; proceeding from too much Heat in the Animal Spirits, not from the Inflammation of the Brain, as the Ancients thought. Willis thus defines it, namely, an Inflammation of the whole Sensitive Soul and Animal Spirits.

phricodes.c: PHRICODES, is a dreadful Fever, in which Men are apt to fanfie terrible things.

phrocyonafix.c: PHROCYON, a Fix ’ d Star of the Second Magnitude, in the Constellation Canis minor, Whose Longitude is hi Degrees Minutes, Latitude Degrees Minutes.

phthiriasis.c: PHTHIRIASIS, is the Loufie Disease; al - io a Scaly Scab on the Eye - brows. Blanchard.

phthisis.c: PHTHISIS, is a Consumption of the whole Body, riling from an Ulcer in the Lungs, accoy - panied with a flow continued Fever, ill scented Breath, and a Cough. Blanchard.

phygethlon.c: PHYGETHLON, is a Swelling proceeding from an Inflammation of the Glandules, wherein Nature expels something j as in the Plague, about the Groins. Blanchard.

phyma.c: PHYMA, is a Swelling: There are Five forts, Verruca, Calli, Vari, Furunculi, and Hydroa, or Defudationes; of which, fee under those Words. Others reckon it a Tumour in the Glandules only, which quickly separates. Blanchard.

physemaaninflammation.c: PHYSEMA, an Inflammation in any Part of the Body, as a Tympany. Blanchard.

physiologyphyfickj.c: PHYSIOLOGY, Phyfickj, or Natural Philofo - phy, is the Science of Natural Bodies, and their various Affdlions, Motions, and Operations. This is either General, which relates to the Properties and Af - sections of Matter or Body in general. Or, Special and Particular, which considers Mat - ter as formed, or distinguished into such and such Species, or determinate Combinations.

physiology.c: PHYSIOLOGY, is by some also accounted a part of Physick, that teaches the Constitution of the Body so far as it is found, or in its Natural State; and endeavours to find Reasons for its Functions and Operations, by the Help of Ana - tomy and Natural Philosophy. Mr. KfH, in his IniroduBio ad Phy ficam, reck - ons Four Classes or Sorts of Philosophers which have treated of Physicks or Natural Philosophy. . Those who delivered the Properties of Na - tural Bodies under Geometrical and Numeral Sum - bols; as the Phythagoreans and Platonifis . The Peripatetickj, who explained the Na - tures of Things by Matter, Form, and Priva - tion; by Elementary and Occult Qualities; by Sympathies, Antipathies, Faculties, and Attracti - ons, &c. And these did not so much endeavour to find out the true Reasons and Causes of Things as to give them proper Names and Terms ‘ so that their Physicks is a kind of Metaphyficks. . The Experimental Philosophers, who by fre - quent and well - shade Trials and Experiments, as by Chymistry, &c. fought into the Natures and Causes of Things: And to these almost all our Discoveries and Improvements are due; and much more would they have done, if they had uot fallen into Theories and Hypothcfes, which they forced oftentimes their Experiments to maintain, whether they could or not. . The Mechanical Philosophers, who explicate all the Phenomena of Nature by Matter and Mo - tion, by the Texture of Bodies, and the Figure of their Parts; by Effluvia, and other subtile Particles, &c. And in sliort, would account for all EffeCts and Phenomena, by the known and established Laws of Motion and Mechanickj: And these are, in Conjunction with the last named, The Only True Philosophers.

piedoucheinarchitecture.c: PIEDOUCHE, in Architecture, is a litt Square Base smoothed, and wrought with Mould - ings, which serves to support a Buss or Statue drawn half way, or any small Figure in Re - lief.

picketinfortification.c: PICKET, in Fortification, is sometimes used for a Stake, sharp at one end, to mark out the Ground and Angles of a Fortification, when the Engineer is laying down the Plan of it; thele are usually pointed with Iron. There are also larger PickctSf Pickets, which are drove inch the Earth, to hold together Fafcincs or Faggots; in any Work cast up in haste. And Pickets also are Stakes drove into the Ground, by the Tents of the Horse in a Camp, to tie their Horses to. And Pickets are also drove into the Ground before the Tents of the Foot, where they reft their Muskets or Pikes round about them in a Ring. When an Korferhan hath committed some considerable Offence, he is often center. ced to stand on the Picket which is, to have one Hand drawn up as high as it can be stretch, and then he is to stand on the Point of a Picket or Stake only with the Toe of his opposite Foot; so that he can neither stand, or hang well, nor ease himself by changing Feet.

pied.c: PIED - DROIT, in Architecture, is a Square Pillar, differing from a Pillafter in this refpeeft, that it hath no Base nor Capital: It is taken al - so for part of the Jaumbs of a Door or Win - dow.

pigments.c: PIGMENTS, are such prepared Materials as Painters, Dyers, ( c. make use of, to impart to Bodies, or to imitate particular Colours. When ' Glass is stain ’ d or coloured, as in painting on Glass, or for the Counterfeiting of Gems or Pre - cious Stones, the Pigment is usually of a Metal - ine or a Mineral Nature.

pileinheraldry.c: PILE, in Heraldry, lignifies an Ordinary, consisting of a Two - fold Line, formed after the man - ner of a Wedge; being probably something like the Figure of the Roman Pilum, which was a ta - pering Dart, about five Foot long, and fharpened at the Point with Steel. The Pile is born invested, en - grailed, cc. like other Ordinaries and issues in - differently from any Point of the Verge of the Escocheon. He beareth a Pile Gules, by the Name of Shandois.

pillarorcolumn.c: PILLAR or Column, in Architecture, is one of the principal Things in which the Beauty and Proportion of a Fabrick doth consist. A Pillar hath Three Parts, the Pedefial, the Shaft or Pil - lar it self, and the Ornaments: And each of these is again subdivided into Three other Parts; the PedeJlal hath its Base, Dye, and Cornich the Pillar its Base, Shaft, and Capital ', and the Ornaments have their Architrave, Frieze, and Cornich.

pilastersinarchitecture.c: PILASTERS, in Architecture, signifie Square Pillars, that usually stand behind Columns to bear up Arches: They have the very fame Dimension, Chapiter, and Base, with the Columns, according to their several Order. When these PiUafters do not stand alone by themselves, they are usually made to jet out of the W all, a Third part or a Quarter of their Breadth, with respect to the Va - piety of different Works: So that some of them projeeft out only a Sixth or an Eighth part, and they are generally as broad at top as at bottom.

pillow.c: PILLOW, is that piece of Timber in a Ship whereon the Boltfprit beareth or resteth at its coming out of the Hull, aloft, close by the Stem.

pinguedo.c: PINGUEDO, the fame with Adeps, or the Fat of Animals. See Adeps.

pinion.c: PINION, in a Watch, is that lesser Wheel; which plays in the Teeth of another. Its Not - ches ( which are commonly,,,, &c. ) are called Leaves, and no t Teeth, as in other Wheels.

pinnaauris.c: PINNA Auris is the upper and broader part of the Ear called the Wing.

pinnatafolia.c: PINNATA Folia, in Botany are such Leaves of Plants as are deeply jagged, cut, or indented in, and which have their. Parts resembling Sea - thers.

pioneers.c: PIONEERS, are such kinds of Labourers as are taken up for use of an Army, to cast up Trenches; and undermine Forts.

pipeinlaw.c: PIPE, in Law, is a Roll in the Exchequer, o - otherwise called the Great Roll. See Clerk of thd Pipe.

pithiasorpi.c: PITHIAS or Pi t bites, with some ' Writers, is the Name of a Comet or rather Meteor of form of a Tub; of these there are divers Kinds, vi; some of an Oval Figure, others like a Tun or Barrel fet Perpendicular, and some like one inclined, or cut short off; others having a Hairy Train or Bush, &c.

pintles.c: PINTLES in a Ship, are those Hooks by which the Rudder hangs to ' the Stern - post.

pisces.c: PISCES, is the Twelfth and last Sign of the - Kpdiackf being a Gonfteljation consisting of Stars; PI Sf PL A P L A

placard.c: PLACARD, is a License whereby a Man is permitted to Ihoot in a Gun, or use Unlawful Games.

place.c: PLACE, is that part of Space which any Bo - dy takes up; and with relation to Space is either absolute or relative. As Mr. Lock, observes.

PLACE also is sometimes taken for that Por - tion of Infinite Space, which is possessed by, and Comprehended within the Material World, and which is thereby diftiriguilhed from the reft of the Expansion

PLACE is usually distinguished into Internal Place, which properly speaking, is that part of Space which any Body takes up or fills; and Ex - ternal Place, which according to Arifiotle, is De - terminer by the Surfaces or Confines of the Ad - joining or Ambient Bodies: But it is better divi - ded into Absolute, Which is the former Internal Place; and into Relative Place, which Is the Ap - parent Secondary or Sensible Position of any Body, according to the Determination of our Senles, with fefped to other Contiguous or Adjoining Bo - dies -.,

PLACE of the Sun, Star, or Planet, is the Sign of the Zodiack, and Degree of it, which the Planet is in or it is that Degree of the Ecliptic reckoned from the beginning of Aries, which the Planets or Stars Circle of Longitude cutteth and therefore is often called. The Longitude of the Sun, Planet, or Stan And ’ tis found by this Proportion: As Sine of Sun ’ s greatest DecIina - - tion is ! - j - o f ToSineof this present Deck -. So is Radius To the Sine of his Longitude, -. i ' j Which if the Declination were North, will be in ' of Gemini - but if the Sun had South Declination, his Place would be in ' of Capricorn.

placeofarms.c: PLACE of Arms, when taken in the General, is a strong City which is pitch ’ d upon for the Ma - gazing of an Army. But a

PLACE of Arms in a Garrison, is a large open Spot of Ground in the middle of the City, where the great Streets meet, or else between the Ramparts and the Houses, for the Garrison to Rendezvous in, upon any sudden Alarm, or other Occasion. And the

PLACE of Arms of a Trench, or of an Attack, is a Post near it, shelter ’ d by a Parapet or Epaule - tent, for Horse and Foot to be at their Arms, to make good the Trenches against the Sallies of the Enemy. - These Places of Arms are sometimes covered by a Rideau or Rising Ground, or else by a Gain or Deep Valley, which saves the trouble of Fortifying them by means of Parapets, fascines, Gabions, c. They are always open m the Rear, for their better Communication with the Camp. When the Trench is carried on as far as to the Glacis, they make it very wide, that it may serve for a Place of Arms. Also the
PLACE of Arms of a Camp, is a spacious piece bf Ground at the Head of the Camp, to draw outahe Army in Order of Battle. But the
PLACE of Arms of a Troop of Horse, or of a Company of Foot in the Camp, is that Spot of Ground on which - the Troops or Company draws out.

As, To find the Centre of a Circle, whose Periphery ( hall pass thro the Ends of a Right Line given in Mag - nitude and Position: For such Centre wifi be in a Right Line. But a

placentavterina.c: PLACENTA Vterina, called by som tUepar Uterinum, from its Colour, which is like that of the Liver; as it is also something in Substance; But it comes nearer to that of the Spleen, it is soft, and hath innumerable Fibres, and small Ves - self, and its Parenchyma is Glandulous almost every where: In Women it is Circular, but with some inequality in its Circumference; in the mid - dle it is about two Fingers thick, but is thinner towards the Edges, and is about a Span, or a quarter of a Yard over, from one side to the other, when the Foetus is Mature for the Birth: Ic is hollowed and smooth within, next the Foetus, and grows every where firmly to the Chorion; but without next the Womb, tis very unequal having many Protuberances, by which it adheres to the Womb, tho ’ to what part of it, is not agreed. When there is more than one Foetus, ’ tis sometimes double, treble, c. and sometimes bur one with so many distend Partitions so it. It grows P L A grows nor from the Womb Originally, but its Rife is from the Chorion, which about the th Week, in Women, fends forth a downy Substance, which soon grows into Knobs, turns Reddish, and then adheres to the Womb conspicuously, about the twelfth or thirteenth Week. It hath Vessels from a double Original, some from the Womb, and some from the Chorion, im - mediately, and mediately from the Foetus. From the Womb it receives Arteries, Veins, Nerves, and Lymphatducfls; all which tho ’ they be very large and conspicuous in the Womb, and even in that place where the Placenta joyns to it, yet they are but very small Capillaries in the Placenta it self, and are dispersed only thro ’ that side of it which is next the Womb. The Vessels that come from the Chorion, are Arteries and Veins and as Dr. Wharton faith, Lymphaeducfls also. From the Foetus thro ’ the Chorion, it receives the Umbilical Vessels of the Foetus: For the first Months of the Pregnancy it sticks most firmly to the Womb but as the Foetus grows mature for the Birth, it loolens by degrees, and at last, like ripe Fruit from the Tree, falls off from the Womb, and makes part of the After Burden or Birth.

pladarosis.c: PLADAROSIS are little soft Tumors which grow under the Eye - lids.

plainscale.c: PLAIN Scale, is a thin Ruler, either of Wood or Brass, whereon are graduated the Lines of Chords, Sines, Tangents, Secants, Leagues, Jgumbs, cc. and is of ready use in moil part of the Ma theniaticks, chiefly in Navigation: A Description thereof fee under the Word Scale.

plaintable.c: PLAIN Table, is an Xnfcrument used in Sur - vexing of Land. r. The Table it self is a Parallelogram of Wood, Inches and a half long, and In - ches broad, or thereabouts i. A Frame of Wood fixed to it, so as a Sheet of Paper being laid on the Table, and the Frame being forced down upon it, ( queezeth in all the Edges, - and makes it lie firm and even, - so as: a P L A P L A Plot may be conveniently drawn upon it. Upon one side of this Frame should be equal Divisions, for Drawing Parallel Lines both long - wife and cross - wife ( as Occasion may require / over your Paper; and on the other side the Degrees of a Circle, projected from a Brass Centre convent - ently placed in the Table. . A Box with a Needle and Card, to be fixed with two Screws to the Table; very useful for placing the Instrument in the fame Position upon every Remove, . A Three - legged Staff to support it, the Head being made so as to fill the Socket of the Table, yet so as the Table may be easily turned round upon it, when ’ tis not fixed by the Screw. . An Index, which is a large Ruler of Wood, ( or Brass ) at the least Inches long, and two Inches broad, and so thick as to make it strong and firm; having a soaped Edge, called the Fi - ducal Edge, and two Sights of one Height, ( whereof the one hath a Sit above, and a Thread below; and the other a Thread above, and a Slit below ) so fet in the Ruler, as to be perfectly of the fame Distance from the Fiducial Edge. Upon this Index ’ tis usual to have many Scales of equal Parts, as also Diagonals, and Lines of Chords. To take the Quantity of an Angle by the Plain Table. As suppose A B and A C were two Hedges or Fences of a Field, and it were required to take the Angle A. Plant your Table ( fitted with the Sheet upon it ) as nigh to the Angle as you can, the North end of the Needle hanging directly over the Flow - er - de - luce; then make a Mark upon the Sheet of Paper at any convenient place for the Angle A, and lay the end of the Index to the Mark, turning it about ’ till through the Sights you espy B; then draw the Line A B by the Edge of the Index. Do the fame for the Line AC, keeping the Index upon the first Mark: Then will you have upon your Table an Angle equal to the Angle in the Field. When you have more Angles to take, the Me - tho is the fame. The Distances from the Angles to the Instru - ment are measured by the Chain, and fet off on the Table with a Scale and Compares, a Whence ’ tis so easie to take the Plot of a Field at one Station, by the Plain Table, that there needs no other Direction. See Surveying

PLANE, is an Instrument used in Joinery to make Boards Plane, Try and Smooth, or in order to joint or frame them together, ( c, These are of several Names and Sorts according to the see - ral LTes; as,. The Fore - Plane, which is a long Plane, and uled first of all before either Smooth - Plane or Jointer, The Edge of the Iron of this Plane is not ground streight, but riling with a Con - vex Arch in the middle of it, that its Edge may bear to be fet the Ranker, for its use is to take off the Irregularities of the Stuff as soon as may be, in order to prepare it for the Smoothing - Plane or Jointer. If the Stuff be free and frowy that is, even tempered all over, you may then fet the Plane so rank, as that you may take off a Shaving of the thickness of an old Shilling; but if it be hard or curling, you can ’ t take off one thicker than an old Groat.. The Smoothing - Plane, is a short small Plane, whose Iron is fet very fine, and its use is to take off the Irregularities of the Fore - Plane, or those which it hath left.. The Jointer is a Plane longer than the Fore - Plane, and hath its Sole perfedHy strait from End to End; it comes after the Fore - Plane and Smoothing - Plane, and is design ’ d to sliort an Edge of a Board perfectly P L A streight ih order to jointing, as also Boards of any thickness; for ’ tis used to Try, as they call it, that is, smooth Tables with, whether large of small: Wherefore its Iron must be fet very fine, little above an Hair ’ s breadth above the Sole of the Plane, and the length of the Edge of it exaCtly strait, or parallel to the Plain of the Sole or Bot - tom of the Plane.; The Strike Block, is a Plane made as true as the Jointer, and like it, only short - er; being used to ftioot a short Joint, which it doth more handily and readily than the long Join - ter. ’ Tis used also for framing and fitting the Joints of Mitres and Bevels, bu t then the piece of Wood Is drawn by hand over the Plane several times till ’ tis shot true.. The Rabbet Plate, is used to cut part of the upper Edge of a Board strait or square down into the Stuff, so that the Edge of another Board cut down after the fame manner may fit and join in with it on the Square; and when two Boards are thus cut away this lap - king over is called Rabbeting. The Rabbet - Plane is sometimes used also to strike a Fascia in a piece of Moulding. The Iron of this Plane is full as broad as the Stock is thick ( usually about an Inch ) that the Angles of the Edge may cut down exactly strait; and it delivers its Shavings at the Side and not out of a Mouth at the Top, like other Planes.. The Plow, is a narrow Rabbet - Plane, with the addition of two Staves with Shoulders to them and on the Bottom of the Shoulders a Fence: Its use is to plow a narrow square Groove on the Edge of any Board, of any proper depth.. Moulding - Planes, of which are several kinds, as the Round Plane, the Hollow, the O G, the Snipes Bill, &c. and these of several Sizes, as from half an Inch to an Inch and half. When these Planes are ' Used on soft Wood, as Deal, Pear - Tree, Maple, the Iron is fet to an Angle of Degr. with the Sole or Base of the Plane; but if it be very hard Wood, as Box, Ebony, Lignum Vice, it is fet to Degr. and sometimes quite upright. There is also some difference in the grinding of the Basil or the Slope of the Edge of the Iron of the Plane; for in working on hard Wood this is ground to anAngle of about or Degrees; but in so t Wood, not to one above Degrees; for the more acute the Basil is the better and soother the Iron cuts, but the more obtuse and thicker it is, the stronger is the Edge to cut upon hard Work.

PLANE of the ProjeBicn, in the Astronomical Perspective or Stereograph ick Projedion, is a Plane which passes thro ’ the Centre of the Sphere, the being supposed the Pole of or in a Point in the Axis of that Plane, and degrees above it or the Surface of the Sphere; thus, if the Eye be in the Zenith or Nadir Points, the Horizon will be a Plane on which the Circles of the Sphere may be projeded Stereographically: And from hence it will follow, that all great Circles of the Sphere passing through the Eye - point, must be at Right Angles to the Plane of the Projedion, because they pass thro ’ its Poles. See Sphcrick Geometry or Pro - jeBion in Vol. I.

planeproblem.c: PLANE Problem, in Mathematicks, is luch an one as cannot be solved Geometrically, but by the Intersection either of a Right Line and a Circle; or of the Circumferences of two Circles; As, Having the greatejl Side given, and the Sum of the other Two, of a Bight - angled Triangle; to find the Triangle. To describe a Trapezium that shall make a Given Area of Four Given Lines. And such a Problem can have but two Solutions, because a Right Line can cut a Circle, or one Circle ano - ther, but into Points. Ozanam.

planegeometrical.c: PLANE Geometrical, in Perfpedtive, is a Plain Surface, parallel to the Horizon, placed lower than the Eye; wherein the visible Objects are imagined without any Alteration, except that they are sometimes reduced from a greater to a lesser Size.

planeofbefieblion.c: PLANE of Befieblion, in Catoptricks, is that which passeth thro ’ the Point of fiejlefticn, and is always perpendicular to the Plane of the Glass, or Refledting Body.
