planesurface.c: PLANE Surface, is that which lies even be - tween its bounding Lines; and as a Right Line is the shortest Extension from one Point to another, so a Plane Surface is the shortest Extension from one Line to another.

planevertical.c: PLANE Vertical, in Opticks and Perfpedtive, is a Plane Surface which passeth along the Prin - cial Ray, and consequently thro ’ the Eye, and is perpendicular to the Geometrical Plane.

planets.c: PLANETS, are the Erratic. or Wandring Stars, and which are not like the Fixed ones al - ways in the fame Position to one another. We now number the Earth among the Primary ru - P L A P L A Planets, because we know ic moves round the Sun, as Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, and Mercury do, and that in a Path or Circle be - tween Mars and Venus. And the Moon is ac - counted among the Secondary Planets, or Satelli - tes of the Primary, since slie moves round the Earth as Jupiter's Four Moons or Satellites do round him, and Saturn ’ s Five round about him; if Cajjini ’ s Eyes may be credited. But I could ne - ver fee my self, or meet with any one die who ever did fee any but the Hugenian Satellite. All the Planets, as far as we can find, have be - sides their Motion round the Sun, which makes their Year; also a Motion round their own Axes, which makes their Day; as the Earth ’ s revolving so, makes our Day and Night. It ’ s more than probable that the Diameters of all the Planets are longer than their Axes: We know ’ tis so in our Earth, and Mr. Flamfteed and Mr. CaJJini both found it to be lo in Jupiter. And therefore ’ twas a great Mistake in the Ingenious Dr. Burnet, to assert, as he doth in his Hypothecs, the Polar Diameter of the Earth to exceed the other. Sir isaac Nevoton asserts our Earth ’ s Equatorial Diameter to exceed the other by about Miles: And indeed else the Motion of the Earth would make the Sea rife so high at the Equator, as to rown all the Parts thereabout. he Learned Mr. Whifton, Profejfor of Mathematicks in the Univerjity of Cambridge, in his Nero Theory of the Earth, accounts ( from the Admirable Sir If. Newton ’ / Principles ) for the Motion and Revolution of the Planets, thus: LEMMA X. From the uniform ProjeCtile Motion of Bodies ih Straight Lines, and theuniverfal Power of At - traction or Gravitation, the Curvilinear Motion of all the Heavenly Bodies do ’ s arise. If a Body, as B, be moving uniformly along the Line D C from D to C, and another Body A be present; this latter Body A must draw the former B from its Straight Line D C: And by doing so continually, while at the fame time the Body B retains its Projectile Force along a Straight Line in every Point of its Course, must make the Line of its real Motion become a Bent one, and change its Rectilinear into a Curvilinear Trajectory. Hence may be learnt what is that Conatus rdi cedendi, a centre motus in Revolving Bodies anct in what Sense, ’ tis be under flood. For since all Bodies have a vis centripeta, or Propension to - wards one another, ’ tis impossible they should. of themselves, in as proper a manner, have a contra ry Propension, or vis centrifugal, an Endeavour of avoiding one another. The true meaning therefore of this Attempt or Endeavour to get farther off the Centre of Motion, is only this, That all Bodies being purely Passive, and so uncapable of altering, their uniform Motion along those Straight Lines or Tangents, to their Curves, in which they are every Moment; do still tend onwards inthe fame Lines, and retain their Propension or Effort to - wards that ReCtilinear Motion all the time: they are obliged to move in Curves; and consequent - ly at every Point of their Cotirfe, endeavour to fly off by their Tangents. Now the Parts of the Tangent, to which this Endeavour is, being farther from the Centre than those of the Curves to which the Bodies are a & ually forced, an At - tempt to go on in the Tangent may be, and is stile an Attempt to, go farther, off, or recede from that Centre; tho from no other AffeCtion than that of Inactivity, or of persevering in a ReCtilinear Mo - tion: So that tho the vis centripeta, or Power of Gravitation, be an Active and Positive Force, continually renew ’ d and impress ’ d on Bodies - yet the vis centrifugal, or conatus recedendi a centre motus, is not so, but the meer Consequence and Refull of their Inactivity. This is evident in Bodies revolving in Ellipses about one of the Foci, in their Descent towards it; where. the Tangent being oblique to the Radius, or Line from the Point of Contact to the Focus this very conatus recedendi a centre motus car - rying it along the Tangent, will for some time make it approach nearer to the Focus; tho ’ not so much near as by its revolving in the Ellipsis it self. For let a Stone be let loose from the Sling, or any Revolving Body be disengaged from the Force which retained it in its Curve, and it will not go from the Centre, but only pass along the Tan - gent in which it was moving, as if there were no such Centre near it at all. When the ProjeCtile Motion of the Planets is in its Direction perpendicular to a Line from the Sun, and in its Degree of Velocity, so nicely dap - ted and contemper ’ d to the Quantity of the Sun's Attraction there, that neither can overcome ' the; other, ( the Force of Gravitation towards the Sun, and the Celerity of the Planers proper Motions, being perfectly in ( equilibria ) the Orbits of such Revolving Planets will be Compleat Circles; them - selves neither approaching to, nor receding from the Sun, the Centre of their Motions. And the Case is the fame in the Secondary Planets about their Primary ones. Thus ’ tis supposable, That thf Velocity of all the Planets about the Sun, was exactly accoy - nodated originally to his Power of Attraction; and that their Primitive Orbits were PerfeCt Circles; from which at this Day they do hot much differ. Thus however, Jupiter ’ s Four Satellites or little Moons have their Motions so exactly proportion - ned to their Gravitation to him, that their Or - bits, as far as the most nice Observations can judge, are perfect Circles, they keeping at an e - qual Distance from his Centre in all the Points of their Cowries about him,. PL A P L A " When the ProjeCtile Motion is not adapted to, but is either too swift or too flow for the Attra - ction towards the Central Body, the Orbits de - scribed will be Ellipses and in the former Case, when the ProjeCtile Motion is too swift, the Or - bit will be bigger. than the Circle, and the nearer Focus of the Ellipsis will be coincident with the Central Body. And in the latter Case, the Orbit will be less than the Circle, and the farther Focus of the El - Hpfis will be coincident with that Central Body. Thus, if the Celerity of B be exactly corse - ipondent to the Attractive Force of the Central Body A, neither will prevail and the Body pre - serving an equal Distance from the Centre, will describe the Circle Been If the Celerity be greater, it will overcome the Attraction, and call it self farther off the Cen - tre for some time, and so revolve about it in the larger Ellipsis B HS; the Central Body pos - feffing that Focus A which is nearest the Point, B, where the Attraction began. But if the Celerity be smaller, the Attraction of the Central Body A will be too hard for it, will force it for some time to come nearer, and to describe the lesser Ellipsis BKL I; the Central Body possessing that Focus A which is farthest from the Point B, where the Attraction began: As will be very plain from the Consideration of the Figure re - latin thereto. ’ Tis indeed possible that the Celerity of Bo - dies may be so great, compared with the Force of Attraction to the Central Body, as to cast them off with such Violence, that the Attraction will never be able to bring them round, or make them revolve about it: In which Case the Orbits de - scribed will be one of the other Conick SeCtions, either Parabolas or Hyperbolas, according to the less or greater Violence with which the Bodies are thrown and the Central Body will possess the Focus of fitch a Figure. But no Phenomena of Nature persuading us that de facto any of the Heavenly Bodies do describe either of those Lines, tho ” Comets Ellipses come near to Parabola's; ) ' several Bodies moving about the fame Central one, tho their Primitive Velocity Were equal, and Di - section alike, yet if they be at different Distances from it, they will describe Figures of different Species about it. For when that determinate De - gree of Velocity, which at one Distance were just Commensurate to the Central Bodies Attraction, and so would produce a Circular Orbit, must at a farther Distance be too hard for it, by reason of the Dimunition of the Attraction there; an Elliptical Orbit must be described, whole nearer Focus would be coincident with the Central Body. In like manner, when the fame determinate De - gree of Velocity were at a nearer Distance, where the Central Attraction is augmented, it would be too little for the fame; and an Elliptical Or - bit must be described, Whose farthest ] Focus would be coincident With the Central Body. This can - not be difficult, if you consider, that the Species of the Planetary Orbits depends solely on the Pro - portion between the Attraction towards the Cen - tral Body, and the Velocity of the ProjeCtile Mo - tion j as that Proportion remaining at any Di - stance whatsoever, the Bigness of the Orbits will be various, but the Species the fame: So when that Proportion is changed, the Species of the Fi - gures must be chang ’ d also which being done, the Velocity given, by the various Force of At - traction in several Distances from the Centre, as well as by the various Velocities at a given Di - stance, of which before; ’ tis evident the Species of the Orbits will be different in this as well as in the former Case. And the greater Disproportion there is between the Quantity of Attraction and the Velocity of the Revolving Bodies, the farther from a Circu - lar; and the more Oblong and Eccentrical will the Orbits described be. And the greater Ap - roach to Correspondence there is, the nearer to Circular, and the less Oblong and Eccentrical will the fame Orbits be. The Circular Orbits of Planets depend not only on the exaCt Adjustment of the ProjeCtile Velo - city to the Attractive Power of the Sun, but up - on the Direction of the fame ProjeCtile Motion, at the Original Commencing of the Attraction. Thus where the Planet is in its own Tangent, neither Ascending nor Descending, and the pre - ceding Angle C B A is a Right one, which we have hitherto supposed; from the Correspondence of the Velocity to the Attraction, the Orbits will be perfeCt Circles. Otherwise, when the Dire - ction of the Motion is Oblique, in any measure ascending from or descending to the Central Body, and the preceding Angle C B A Obtuse or Acute the Planet, tho ’ its Velocity were exactly adapted to the Attraction of the Central Body, would revolve in an Ellipsis; and the Point B, where the Attraction began, would be the end of the lesser Axis thereof. If a Planet describe an Ellipsis about its Central Body in the Focus thereof, it will move fafteft when ’ tis nearest to, and lowest when tis far - theft: from the said Central Body or Focus, and a - agreeably in the intermediate Places. For seeing wheresoever the Revolving Body is, the Area is still proportionable to the Tim, and b in equal Tynes Times always equal; ’ tis evident by how much the Distance is less, and the Line from the Focus is hotter, by so much must the Bodies Motion be swifter to compensate the fame; and vice versa, by how much the Former is longer, by so much must the Latter be flower to allow for it. If the Planet B describe an Ellipsis about the Central Body in the Focus H, as the Area defend - ded by the Line B H, will be. exadlly Uniform and Proportional to the Time of Description so the Angular Motion, or Velocity of the Line from the other Focus B I, will be Proportional to the Time, and Uniform also, tho ’ not so Exa & ly and Geo - metrically. The Law of Gravitation being supposed, if one Planet describe an Ellipsis about the Central Body in the Focus H, and another describe a Circle a - bout the fame in its Centre; If the Semi - diameter of the Circle be equal to H E, the middle Di - stance in the Ellipsis from the fame Centre or So - cus, their Periodical Times of Revolving will be the fame; and when the Distances are equal, their Velocity will be so too. Therefore tho ’ the Planets revolve in Ellipses of several Species, yet their Periodical Times may be as well compared with one another, and with their Distances from the Central Bodies, as if they all revolved in Compleat Circles.

PLANETS. The Motions of the Six Primary Planets round the Sun is so adjusted, that the Square of the Times of their Periodical Revoluti - ons are as the Cubes of their Distances from the ' Sun: And ths fame thing is found by all Aftrono - mers to be true, with regard to the Motions of the Secondary Planets or Satellites round their Primary ones. Greg. Ajlron. p.. The The Forces with which the Primary Planets are continually drawn from a ReCtilineal Motion, and by that means are retained in their Orbits, are re - ciprocally as the Squares of their Distances from the Centre of the Sun. Id. p.. The Forces with which the Secondary Planets are retained in their Orbits, are reciprocally as the Squares of their Distances from the Centres of their Primary Planets about whom they revolve, p.. The Nodes and Apfides of all the Planetary Or - bits are at reft and do not move progressively. P - The Planets and Comets are retained in their Orbits by the force of Gravity; the fame Law prevailing thro ’ all the Solar System. p.. If a Primary Planet revolving round the Sun as its Centre, carry round with him a Satellite which revolves also round the Planet; the Motion of this Satellite will be accelerated all the while it is moving from the Quadratures to the Syzygies, and retarded all the while it is in moving from the Syzygies to the Quadratures: So that it will move f after near either its Conjunction or Opposition, and J lover near the Quadratures. The Figure of its Orbit will al - so be more Curvilineal in the Quadratures than in the Syzygies, and consequently the Satellite will be or recede farther from the Primary Planet, in the Quadratures than in the Syzygies, so as that the Orbit will be an Ellipsis, whose Centre is the Primary Planet, and whose greater Axis lies at Right Angles to a Line drawn from the Sun; and the lesser Axis is coincident with that Line. This Dr. Gregory demonstrates in his Aftron. p., Sc. But if the Orbit of the Satellite Planet, instead of being a Circle be an Ellipsis, in whose Focus the Primary Planet is supposed to be placed, then will the greater Axis of this Elliptical Orbit, twice ad - vance forward, vi in the z Quadratures, and twice recede backward, vi. in the Syzygies, of every Revolution of the Satellite round the Pla - net. p.. In each Revolution of the Satellite round the Planet the Apfides will, for the most part, advance more forwards than they recede backwards, and by the excess of this Progression, will move in Confequentia.

Lycopodium, or Wolfs - claw, the Adiantum Aureum, the Lunaria, Equ fe - turn, &c. . Those whose Seeds are not so small as fin - gly to be Invisible, but yet have an Im perfect or Stamineous Flower; i. e. such an one as is with - out the Pet ala, having only the Stamina and the Perianthium; as Hops, Hemp, Mercurialis, Net - tles, Docks, Sorrels, Arfefmart, Knot grass. Pond - weed, Orach, Blite, Beet, Ladies Mantle, &c. . Such as have a Compound Flower, and emit a kind of White Juice or Milk when their Stalks are cut, or their Branches broken off such as Lettuce, Sow - thistle, Hawkweed, Dendelion, Succory, Goats - beard, Nipplewort, Cc. . Such as LaVe a Compound Flower of a Dis cous Figure, the Seed Pappcfe, or winged with Down, but emit no Milk as the former do j as Colts - foor, Fleabane, Golden Rod, Ragweed Groundsel Cudweed, &c. . The Herbs Capitata, or such whose Flower is composed of many small long Fiftulofe or hoi " low Flowers gathered together in a round Button, Ball or Head, which is usually covered with a Squammofe or Scaly Coat, of which kind are the Thistle, the greater Burdock, Blue - Bottle, Knap - weed, Saw - Worth, &c. These have all a Down adhering to their Seeds. . The Corymbiferous Plants, which have a com ' pound Discous Flower, but their Seeds have no Down adhering to them: The Reason of the S Name Name you have under the Word Corymb us of ! this kind, is Corn Marigold, Common Ox - Eye, Yarrow, the Easie, Camomile, Tan fie, Mugwort, Scabious, Teasel, Eryngo ’ s, c. , Plants with a Versed Flower, and having only one single Seed belonging to each single Flower such are Valerian, Corn - pallet, Agrimony, Burnet, Meadow Rue, Fumitory, c. . The Umbelliferous Plants, which have a Pen - iapetalous Flower, ( i. e. one having just final ! Petala or Leaves ) and belonging to each single Flower there are two Seeds lying naked and join - ed together. They are called Umbelliferous, be - cause the Plant, with its Branches and Flowers, hath an Head like a Ladies Umbrella, which they call Umbella. This is a very large Genus of Plants, which therefore he thus subdivided into, . Such as have a broad flat Seed, almost of the Figure of a Leaf, or which are encom - passed round about with something like Leaves as Cow - Parsnep Wild and Garden Parsnep, Hogs Fennel, ( Pucedanum ) &c. . Such as have a longish Seed swelling out in the middle, and larger than the former as Shepherds Needle, Cow - weed, Wild Her - vil Common Speignel or Meu, Y . S uch as have a shorter Seed as Angelica and Alexanders. . Such as have a Tuberous Root, as the Earth Nut, Kipper Nut, or Pig Nut, Water Dropwort and Hemlock Dropwort. . Such as have a small wrinkled channeled, or striated Seed; as Stone Parsley, Water Pars - nep, Burnet, Saxifrage, Caraways, Smallage, Hemlock, Meadow Saxifrage, Sampire, Fen - nel, Rock Parsley, c. . Such as have rough, hairy, or briftlySeed as Mountain Stone Parsley, Wild Carrot or Birdsnest, Hedge and Bastard Parsley, Hem - lock, Chervil, Sea Parsnep. . Such as have their Leaves entire and undivi - ded into Jags, F. as Perfoliata, or ThoroW - wax, Sanicle, the leaf ! Hares Ear, &c. o. The Stellate Plants, which are so called, their because Leaves grow on their Stalks, at certain In - tervals or Distances, in the form of a Radiant Star. Their Flowers are really Monopetalous, but divided into four Segments, which look like so many distinct Petala, or four Leaves and each Flower is fucceded by two Seeds which grow at the bottom of it. Of this Kind is Cross - wort, or Mugweed, with Madder, Ladies Bedstraw, Woodruff, Clea - vers, V. r. The Afperifolia, or Rough - leav'd Plants, They have their Leaves placed alternately, or in no certain Order on their Stalks they have a Monopetalous Flower cut or divided into five Partitions and after every Flower there succeeds usually four Seeds such as Cynogloffa, or Hounds Tongue, Wild Buglofle, Vipers Bugloss, Comfrey, Mouse Ear, Scorpion Grass, N . The Suffrutices or Verticillate Plants i Mr. Pay, in his last Edition of his Synopsis Me - thodic a Stirp. Britann, faith. The more certain. Marks or Charadteriftick Notes of this kind of Plants are, That their Leaves grow by pairs on their Stalks, one Leaf right again ! ! another, their Flower is Monopetalous, and usually in the form of an Helmet or Hood, there succeed four Seeds usually to each Flower, and which have no other SeedVeJfel but the Perianthium: For that Mark of their Flowers growing in Whirls about the Stalk as they do in the Dead Nettle, Hore Hound, &c. is not found in all Plants of this Genus, To this Head belong Mother of Thyme, Mint, Penny - Royal, Vervain, Wood Betony, Selfheal, Alehoofl, Bugle, Scordlum, Motherwort, F. . Such as have many naked Seeds ( at leaf ! more than four ) succeeding their Flower, which ' therefore they call Polysperm e Plantes Semine nudo. By naked Seeds they mean such as are not incle - ded in any Seed Pod, or Case, out of which they spontaneously drop but such as either have no - thing at all covering their Seeds, or else drop off with their Covering upon them. Of this Kind are Pilewort, Crowfoot, Marsh - Mallows, Avens, Strawberries, Cinquefoil, Torment ! !, Meadow - sweet, F. . Bacciferous Plants, or such as bear Berries as Briony, Dwarf Honyfuckle, Butchers - broom, Solomons Seal, Lily of the Valley, Nightshade, Asparagus, Whorts or Whortle - berries, &c. . Must i fill qu ous, or Corniculate Plants or such as have after each Flower, many distinct, long, slender, and many times crooked Gales, or Siliquce, in which their Seed is contained and which, when they are ripe, open of themselves, and let the Seeds drop out: Of this Kind is the Common Houfleek, Orpine, Navelwort, or Wal - pennywort, Bearsfoot, Marfli Marigold, Colum - bines, F. . Such as have a Monopetalous Flower, ei - ther Uniform or Difform, and after each Flower a peculiar Vessel, or Seed Case ( besides the com - mon Calyx ) containing the Seed, and this often divided or parted into many diftindl Cells, These by some are called Vafculiferom Pla ? its, such as common Henbane, Marfli Gentian, Bindweed, Throatwort, Rampions, Toad Flax, Fox Glove, Yellow and Red Rattle, or Cock ’ s - comb, Eye - bright. . Such as have an uniform Tetrapetalous Flower, but bear their Seeds in Oblong Siliquous Cafes as your Stock - gillyflower, Wall - flower, common Whitloe Grass, Jack, by rhe Hedge, or Sauce alone, common Mustard, Charlock or Wild Mustard, Radifli, Wild Rocket, Ladies Smock, Scurvy - grass, Woad, V. . Vasculiferous Plants, with a seemingly Te - trapetalous Flower, but of an Anomalous, or un - certain kind; For this Flower, tho ‘ it be deeply divided PL A F L E divided in four Segments, is yet really Moridpe - any Metal, or such like running Matter,. which fcalous, and falls off all together in one; luch as will afterwards harden, is call. Speedwell or Fluellin, Wild Poppy, Yellow Pop - THAT - BaJlion. See Bast ion. py, Loose Strife, Spurge, and Plantain, ( according PLA - Band, in Architecture, is a ' Square Mould to Mr. Hay. ) I which terminates the Architecture of the Doriff . Leguminous Plants, ( or such as bear Pulfey With a Papilionaceous Flower, Their Flower is Difform, and almost in the form of a Butterfly and Wings expanded, ( whence the Name Papilio - naceous ) consisting of four parts, joined together at the Edges; thele are Pease, Vetches, Tares, Lentils, Beans, Liquorice, Birdsfoot, Trefoil, Reft - harrow, ( c. . Vasculiferous Plants, with a Pentapetalous Blower. These as the th and i th Kind, have besides the common Calyx or Cup of the Flower, a peculiar Case containing the Seed, and their . Flower consisting of Leaves; such as Maiden Pinks, Campions, St. Johns Wort, Male Him - kernel, Chick weed, Cranebill, Flax Primrose, Periwinkle, Centory, Wood Sorrel, March Tre - foil, ( c. . Plants with a true Bulbous Root. A Bul - bous Root consists of but one round Ball or Head, out of whose lower part or Balls there go many Fibres or Strings to keep it firm in the Earth. The Plants of thi. Tdnd, when they first appear, come up with but one Leaf, and the Leaves are nearly approaching to those of the Grals Kind of Plants, for they have no Foot Stalk, and are long and slender: The Seed Vessels are divided into three Partitions; their Flower is usually Hexa - petalous, or seemingly divided into fix Leaves or Segments; such ! as Garlick, Daffodil, Hyacinth, Safffon, ( c. . Such as have their Roots approaching to a Bulbous Form. These emit at first coming up but one Leaf, and in Leaves, Flowers and Roots, resemble the true Bulbous Plants; such as F lower de Lis, Cuckoo - pint, Orchis, Broom Rape, Ba - ftard Hellebore, T way - blade, Winter - green, ( c, .. Culmiferous Plants, with a Graffie Leaf, and an imperfect Flower. Culmiferous Plants are such as have a smooth hollow jointed Stalk, with one long harp - pointed Leaf at each Joint, encom - passing the Stalk, and fet on without any Foot - stalk: Their Seed is contained within a Chaffy Husk; such as Wheat, Barley, Rye, Oats, and most Kinds of Grasses. . Plants with a Graffie Leaf, but not Culmi - serous, with an Imperfect or Staminous Flower; Order, or the Fascia which passeth immediately under the Triglyphs, and serves for the fame Use in this Order, as the Cymatium in the others. It is also the Fascia of the Chdmh'ranles: And the lame Name is also attributed to divers other Members of Archjtediure, which are destitute of Ornaments, having only a certain breadth with - out much Projedhire. PLATES, a Term in Heraldry. See Balls.

platforminfortification.c: PLATFORM, in Fortification, is a Place pre - pared on the Ramparts for the railing of a Bat - tery of Cannon; or it is the whole Piece of Fortification raised in a re - entring Angle. See Battery.

platform.c: PLATFORM; in Architecture, is a row of Beams that support the limber - Work of a Roof, and lie on the top of the Waif where the Ent - blature ought to be raised. Also a kind of Ter - rafs Walk, or even Floor on the top of a Build - ing; from whence we may rake a fair Prolpedt of the adjacent Gardens or Fields. So an Edifice is said to be covered with a Platform, when Jt hath no Arched Roof.

platformororlop.c: PLATFORM, or Orlop, in a Man of War, is a Place on the Lower Deck of her, abaft the Main Malt, and round about the Main Capstan, where, in the Time of Service, Provision " is to take care of the Wounded Men ’ tis between the Main Mast and the Cock - pit.

platisma.c: PLATISMA, is a broad Linen - cloth put up - on Sores.

plattoon.c: PLATTOON, corruptly from the French Word Pelaton, is a small Square Body of Mufqueteers, such as is usually drawn out of a Battalion of Foot, when they form the Hollow Square to Lengthen the Angles; and the Granadeers are generally thus polled.

plants.c: PLANTS in a Ship, are flat Ropes made of Rope - yarn, and weaved one over another; their Use is to save the Cable from Galling in the Haufe, or to wind about the Flukes of " the An - chors to save the Pendant of the Fore - sheet from galling against them.

plantinlaw.c: PLANT, In Law, is the propounding, or ex - hibiting of any Action Real or Personal in Writ ' ung; and the Party making this Plant, is called, T he Party Plaintiff.

plea.c: PLEA, in ' Law, signifies that which either Party allegeth for himself in Court, and are either Pleas of the Crown, or Common - Pleas. Pleas of the Crown, are ail of - them Suits in the Kings as Cyprels Grasses and Rullies, Cats Tail, Burr, Name, against Offences committed against his Reed, ( c. . Plants whose Place of Growth is under - Crown and Dignity, or against his Crown and Peace; and thole seen to be Treasons, Felonies, Mifprifions of either, and Ma ) hem. Ccmntcn - Pleas tain - and various, but chiefly Water Plants, as, be those that are held between Common Persons / the Water Lily, Water Milifoil, Water - wort. Pep - ! yet by the former Definitions, they must comprise ' per - grass, Mouse - tail, Milkwort, Dodder, ( c. I ail other, tho ’ the King be a Party, Plea may j farther be divided into as many Branches as A There is also another usual Division of Plants ' cl ion; which fee, for they signifie ail one. into Trees, Frutices or Shrubs, Suffmtices and Herbs; j Then there is a Foreign Plea, whereby Matter but this is rather Popular and Vulgar, than Just j is alledged in any Court, that may be tried by and Philosophical. ’ another. j PLEADINGS, in Law, are allthe Sayings of LAST, the fame with a Mould in which the Parties to Suits after the Count - or DeclaratL S i t P LI P O I on; to wit, whatever is contained in the Bar, Replication and Rejoynder, and not in the Count ij: less; and therefore Defaults in the Matter of tie Count are not comprised within Mislead - ing, or insufficient Pleading, but only Mi / p lea - ding, or insufficient Pleading committed in the Bar, Replication, or Rejoinder.
PLEA foris faclura, & plea vita. See For - seizure.

pledgesincommonlaw.c: PLEDGES in Common Law, are Sureties, either real or formal, which the Plaintiff finds to prosecute his Suit.

plegiis.c: PLEGIIS acquietandis, is a. Writ that lies for a Surety, against him for whom he is Surety, if he pay not the Money at the Day.

pleiads.c: PLEIADS, the fame with those Seven Stars in the Neck of the Bull, which are usually thus called,

plenartyinlaw.c: PLENARTY, in Law, is when a Benefice is full, dire & ly contrary to Vacation, which signifies the bein ' ?; void of a Benefice.

plenitude.c: PLENITUDE, is when a Man has too much Blood; the fame with Plethora.

pleonsamus.c: PLEONSAMUS, is a Figure in Discourse, when a Word not necessary is added, to express a Vebemency in us, and a greater Certainty in the thing; as when we fay, I saw it with thcfe Eyes: Here, saw it, is really enough in Gram - mar, but with these Eyes, is added, to shew both the Certainty of the Fads, and our Zeal and Ve - hemence in asserting it. PL EROTIC A are Medicines that breed Flesh and fill up Wounds.

plethora.c: PLETHORA, when there ’ s more good Blood than is requisite: It happens either to the Vessels, when they are stretch ’ d out, and cannot hold all; or to the Strength, for sometimes tho ’ the Vessels be not over full, the Strength is over - loaded.

plevinincommonlaw.c: PLEVIN, in Common Law, signifies a War -. rant, or Assurance. See Replevin.

pleura.c: PLEURA, is the Skin or Membrane which covers the inside of the Thorax, adhering to the Ribs.

PLEURA, is a double Membrane, which co - vers all the inward Cavity of the Thorax: It arises from the Vertebra of the Back, and ascends on each side upon the Ribs, to the middle of the Ster - num. It is fix ’ d to the Periofieum of the Ribs, and to the internal Intercostal Muscles, and it co - vers the Midriff. Its Side towards the Cavity is smooth and equal, but that which is fixed to the Ribs is rough.

pleuritisapleurifie.c: PLEURITIS, a Pleurifie, is an Inflammation of the Membrane Pleura, and the Intercostal Mu - ides, attended with - a continual Fever, and Stitch - es in the Side, Difficulty of Breathing, and some - times Spitting of Blood; and it ’ s either a true Pleurifie, as this which we have described, or a Ba - ftard Pleurifie, whose Symptoms are not so violent, and in some things different from the former.

plexus.c: PLEXUS choroides seems to hang over the Pi - neal Glandule, as it were over a Button. It is an admirable Contexture of small Arteries in the Brain like a Net.

plexusnervcfus.c: PLEXUS Nervcfus, is when two or three Nerves meet tegetherand jut out.

plica.c: PLICA, is an Epidemical Disease in Poland, when their Hairs grow together like a Cows Tail; besides, they are Crooked - back ’ d, have loose Joints, it wrenches their Limbs and loofens them, - breeds. Lice, with other Symptoms. PL NTHUS or Plintbis, in Architecture, is taken for that Square Member which serves as a Foundation ' to the Base of a Pillar: But Vitruvius calls the upper part, or Abacus of the tuscan Pil - lar, a Plinth, because it resembles a square Tile. Moreover, the fame Denomination is some - times attributed to a thick Wall, wherein there are two or three Row's of Bricks advanced in form of a Plat - band, This

plinthpalladio.c: PLINTH Palladio calls the Orle, and Blended the Abacus. The Word is also used for a like Member about the Capital of a Pillar, but then ’ tis called always the Plinth of the Capital, and is placed just above the Echinus in the Dorick and above the Ovolo, or quarter Round, in the other Orders.

plow.c: PLOW, is an Instrument made of Bpx or Pear - tree, used by Seamen to take the Height of the Sun or Stars, in order to find the Latitude It admits of the Degrees to be very large, and is much esteem ’ d by many Artifts.

PLOW - Land, Carucata, was formerly as much Arable Land as one Plow could plough up in one: Year. This in the beginning of the Reign of Rich. I. was accounted at Acres; and in the th of Rich I. ioo Acres is allowed for a Plow - Land. And this Measure was very different ac - cording to Time and Place.

plum.c: PLUM B - Line, the fame with Perpend cular.

plumbum.c: PLUMBUM ujlum, is a Composition of two Parts of Lead melted in a Pot or Crucible, with one Part of Sulphur then added to it, and kept o ’ er the Fire till they be burnt all out; the Mat - ter will then be turned into a Black Powder, which they properly call by this Name Plumbum Ujlum.

plume.c: PLUME, is the Term used by Botanists for that Part of the Seed of a Plant, which in it ’ s Growth becomes the Trunk; ’ tis inclosed in two small Cavities formed in the Lobes for its Recep - tion; and is not like the Radicle an entire Body, but divided at its loose end into divers pieces all closely bound together like a bunch of Feathers whence Dr. Grew very properly gives it the Name of Plume. In Corn it is that part, which after the Radicle is hot forth, hoots out towards the smaller end of the Seed, and therefore is by some called the Acrospire.

pluries.c: PLURIES, is a Writ that goeth out in the third place, - after two former Writs that had no effeeft: For first the Original Capias issues, and if that speed not, then goeth out the Alias, and if that also fails, then the Pluries.

pneumatickengine.c: PNEUMATICK Engine, the lame with the Air Pump.

pneumatocele.c: PNEUMATOCELE, is a Windy Rupture, when the Skin of the Scrotum is distended with Wind.

pneumatodes.c: PNEUMATODES, is a short Breathing. PNEUM AT ONIPHALUS, is a Swelling in the Navel, got by Wind.

pneumatosis.c: PNEUMATOSIS, is the Generation of Ani - mal Spirits, which is performed in the Cortical Substance of the Brain; the little Arteries there are emptied, and the Spirits distil, which after they are come as far as the middle of the Brain, they Acftuate and Invigorate all the Nerves.

podagra.c: PODAGRA, vid. Arthritis, The Gout in the Feet.

poeticalrisingandsetting.c: POETICAL Rising and Setting of the Stars: This is peculiar to the Ancient Poetical Writers, for they refer the Rising and Setting of the Stars, always to that of the Sun; and accordingly make three forts of Poetical Rising and Setting. Ccfmi - cal, Acronycal, ( or as some write it, Acronyclal ) and Heliacal. See those Words.

pointapointingeometry.c: POINT, a Point in Geometry, is that which is supposed to have no manner of Dimensions, but to be Indivisible in every rested:. The Ends or Extremities of Lines, are Points. If a Point be supposed to be moved any way, it will by its Motion describe a Line.

pointblank.c: POINT Blank, a Term in Gunnery, dignify - ing that a Shot, or Bullet goes directly for - ward to the Mark, and doth not move in a Curve as Bombs and highly elevated Random - Shots do. POINT

pointinnavigation.c: POINT in Navigation, signifies i r Degrees Minutes, or one zdpartof rhe Compass: The half of which is Degrees Minutes, which they Call a Half Point; and the half of this, which is z Degrees Minutes, they call a Quar - ter Point. The Seamen also call the Extremity of any Promontory ( which is a Piece of Land running out into the Sea ) a Point; which is of much the fame Sense with them as the Word Cape. They fay two Points of Land are one in ano - ther, when they are so in a Right Line one against another, as that the Innermost is hindered from being seen by the Outermost.

pointofconcourse.c: POINT of Concourse, in Opticks, is that Point where the Visual Rays, being reciprocally inclip - ned, and sufficiently prolong ’ d, meet together, are united in the middle, and cross the Axis. This point is most usually cased the Focus,; and some - times the Point of Convergence.

pointofconcurrence.c: POINT of Concurrence -, a Term in Perfpedtive. See Principal Point.

pointofincidence.c: POINT of Incidence, in Opticks, is that Point on the Surface of a Glass, or other Body on which any Ray of Light falls: And as some also word themselves, That Point of the Glass, which a Ray parts from, after its Refra & ion, and when ’ tis re - turning into the Ra re Medium again.

pointofinflexion.c: POINT of Inflexion of a Curve. See Inflexion.

pointprincipal.c: POINT Principal, a Term in Perfpe & ive. See Principal Point.

pointsensible.c: POINT Sensible, according to Mr. Lock., is the least Particle of Matter or Space which we can discern; and to the sharpest Eyes, is seldom lets than thirty Seconds of a Circle, whereof the Eye is the Center.

pointingthecable.c: POINTING the Cable, is when the Strands about two Foot from the end are untwisted, in Order to make Sinnet of the Rope - yarn, and then to lay them one over the other again, making it less towards the End, where all is made fait toge - ther with a piece of Marlin, the Design of which is partly to keep the Cable from Raveling out, but chiefly chat none of the Cable may be cut ossa and Hole away.

point.c: POINT In, when two Piles, are born in a Coat of Arms, so as to have their Points meet together in any part of the Escutcheon. They fay, He bea - Ireth two Piles in Point.

pointsinheraldry.c: POINTS in Heraldry, are several Places in an Escutcheon, diversly Named according to their Situation. See the Word Escutcheon. pointsofstation.c: POINTS of Station, in Astronomy are those Degrees of the Zodiack, in which a Planet seems to stand quite still, and not to move at all.

Circle, because opposite to the former.

polarprojection.c: POLAR Projection, is a Representation of the Earth, or of the Heavens, projected on the Plane of one of the Polar Circles.

polarity.c: POLARITY, is the Property of the Magnet, or of a piece of Oblong Iron touch ’ d by a Mag - net, to point toward the Poles of the World.

poleinmeasuring.c: POLE, in Measuring, is the fame with Perch or Pod, or as feme call it, Lugg. By our Statute Law, ( Ann. Elis '. Cap.. ) this Measure is a Length of Feet and an half, but it varies by the Usage of some Countries; being in some Pla - ces. of Feet, which they call Woodland Men - sure; in some places of ax Feet, which is called Church Measure ( i. e. of such Lands as did or do belong to the Church ) and in others of Feet, and this is called Forefl Measure.

poleinmathematicks.c: POLE in Mathematicks, is a Point De - grees distant from the Plane of any Circle, and in a Line perpendicularly ere died in its Centre; which Line is called the Axis. And from this Polar Point may Circles be described on the Glebe or Sphere, as they are on the Plane from their Centre.

polestar.c: POLE Star, is a Star in the Tail of the Lit - tle Bear, ( a Constellation of Stars which is cal - led Cynosura ) and is very near the ead North Pole of the World. The right Ascension of this Pole Star for this Year, is o Hours Minutes o Seconds of Time; and it Increases x Minute Seconds every Years: Therefore having at any time this Stars Right Ascension, and the Right Ascension of the Sun ( both in time ) if you Subtrad the latter from the former, ( adding Hours to the Right Ascension of the Pole Star when it is less than the Suns ) the Remainder will be the Time when the Pole Star is in the Meridian, Then Hang up two Strings and Plummets between the Pole Star and your Eye, and you will have a true Meridian Line, which will be of great - ule to redifie a Clock or Watch. And you may find the Meridian very nicely, if instead of the Strings above mentioned, you use the Sights of a good Circumferenter, or other Surveying Instrument. Some Persons have been mighty apt to imagine ’ F at the Efei ht or Elevation of the Pole, and also the Position of the Circles of the Heavens, in rested of thole on the Earth, hath much changed and varied: But Mr. Caffini is doubtless right in his Assertion, That there is no just ground for any such Surmise: And that all the Difference which we find now in the Latitudes of Places, in re - sped of the Ancient Accounts, arises from the former Observations not being well made; as in - deed we may judge they cannot have been, since they had no luch good Instruments to do it withal, as the Modern Astronomers have. Yet he thinks it very probable, that there may be some little Variation in the Height of the Pole in one. and the fame place; but this not exceeding two Minutes, and which will in process of Time quite vanish, after ’ tis arrived to its highest Diffe - rence. Vid. Memoir es dc Mathemat. & de Physique, July.

pole.c: POLE of a Glass ( in Opticks ) is the thickest part of a Convex, but the thinnest of a Concave Glass, and if the Glass be truly ground, will be exactly in the middle of its Surface: This is some - times called, The Vertex of the Glass.

poles.c: POLES of the World, are two Points in the Axis of the / Equator, c ach Degrees Distant from its Plane one pointing North, which therefore is called, The North or ArBick Pole the other South - ward,, which therefore is called, the South or An - tar ’ click, Pole. Whether any People live directly under the Pole or not, is a Question; but Mr, Halley hath proved. That the Solstitial Bay, under the Pole, is ' as hot as under the Equinodia !, when the Sun is Verti - cal to them, or in their Zenith; because for all the Hours of that Day under the Pole, the Suns Beams are inclined to the Horizon with an Angle of i Degrees: Whereas under the Equi - nomial, tho ’ he become Vertical, yet he shines no more than, Hours, and is absent Hours: And besides, for Hours Minutes of that iz Hours he is above the Horizon there, he is not so much Elevated as under the Pole.

POLES of the Ecliptic are Points in the Solfii - till Colure. Degr. Minut. distant from the Poles of the World; and thro ’ these all Circles of Longitude in the Heavens do pass, as the Hour Circles do thro ’ the Poles of the Equator. To find the Pole of any Circle. See Spheric Geometry.

polemical.c: POLEMICAL, is a Word used in Reference to that part of Theology which relates to Controver - fie; which because of the Wars, Jars, and Squab - bles that usually arise about Controverted Points,, is called Polemical Divinity. POLICY P - L

policyofajfurance.c: POLICY of Ajfurance, is a Form of Security, mentioned in - Eli cap. iz. and and al - io in Car. z. cap., arid given by a certain Society of Men formed into a kind of Corpora - tion, to any Person to Insure the safe Return of the Whole or any part of a Ship to Insure Houses against Fire so that if they are Burnt down, they shall be Rebuilt at the proper Charge of the InfurCfs and to Insure Mens " Lives in Of - fices when they have paid great Sums for the fame and lastly, to Inlure to Persons paying so much Money at Once, or becoming constant Con - tributors to the Office or Society of A ffiirance, a Remainder of so much Money after the said Con - tributor or Subscriber ’ s Death. This Policy of Assurance is under the Seal of the Office, " and entitles the Person Benefitted by it, to make good his Claim according to the I nor of the Art - cles, or By - Laws of that Society of which he was a Member.

pollux.c: POLLUX a fix ’ d Star in the Twins, of the Second Magnitude, whose Longitude is ' De - grees Minutes, Latitude Degrees Mi - nutes,

polyacousticks.c: POLYACOUSTICKS, are Instruments con - tried to Multiply Sounds, as Multiply in g - glalles or Polyfcopes do Images of Objects.

For its Superficial Content, fee Area, Every Polygon may be divided into as many - triangles as it hath Sides. If you take a Point, ' as a, any where within the Polygon, and from thence draw Lines to every Angle a b, a c, ad, &c. for they shall make as many Triangles as the Figure hath Sides. The Angles of any Polygon takeg together will make twice as many Right ones except four as the Figure hath Sides. Thus: If the Polygon hive fix Sides, fas ill the Figure above ) the double of that, is ix. whence take, there remains. I fay that all the Angles b, c, d, e, f, g, of that Polygon taken to - gether, are equal to Right Angles. For the Polygon having Sides, is divided iritd Triangles and the Angles of each, by. e Eucl. are equal to z Right ones so that all the Angles together make z Right ones: But eacli of these Triangles Jxaxh. one Angle in the Point a and by it they compleat the Space round the said Point and all the Angles about a Point are knowii to be equal to Right ones wherefore those taken from iz, leave, the Sum of the Right Angles of the Hexagon. So that tis plain, the Figure hath tWiCe M many Right Angles, as it hath Sides, except Every Polygon circumscribed about a Circle ? is equal to a Re & angled Triangle, one of whose Legs shall be the Radius of the Circle, and the other the Perimeter ( or Sum of all the Sides ) of the Polygon. So that all these Triangles taken together, will be equ / l to all these in the Poly - gon, or to the whole Polygon. But the A F A A is equal to all the Tri - angles within the Parallels; because drawing the Lines B j F, C F, D F, ( c. The A SAY, will be equal to the A F A B; the A F C B A F C B, ( c. Wherefore the Tri - angle F A A is equal to thsfipeiygon, which was to be proved. COROLLARY I. Hence every Jugular Polygon is equal to a He - ll angle Triangle, one of whose Legs is the Pe - trimeter of the Polygon, and the other a Perpendicular drawn from the Centre to one of the Sides of the Polygon. COROLLARY II. And every Polygon circumscribed about a Circle, is bigger than it; and every Polygon insert - bed, is less than the Circle, as is manifest; because the thing containing, is always greater than the thing contained. COROLLARY III. The Perimeter of every Polygon circumscribed about a Circle, is greater than the Circumfe - rence of that Circle and the Perimeter of every Polygon inscribed is less. Hence, A Circle is equal to a Hight Angled Triangle B whole Base is the Circumference of the Circle, and its Height the Radius of it. For this Triangle will be lesser than any Poly - gon confcribed, and greater than any inscribed, ( because the Circumference of the Circle, which is the Base of the Triangle, is greater than the Compass of any inscribed: ) Therefore it will be equal to the Circle. For if this Triangle be great - ter than any thing chat is bigger than the Circle, and lesser than any thing that is lesser than the Circle; it follows, that it mull be equal to the Circle. This is called the Quadrature or Squaring of the Circle; that is, to find a Right - lined Figure equal to a Circle; upon this Supposition, That the Rafis given, is equal to the Circumference of the Circle but actually to find the Right Line equal to the Circumference of a Circle, is not yet discovered Geometrically. So is the Chord a p the Side of the Polygon required; which here is a Pentagon. POLYGON,

polygonexterior.c: POLYGON Exterior, in Fortification; is the Distance of one Point of a Bastion from the Point of another, reckoned all round the W ork.

polygoninterior.c: POLYGON Interior, is the Distance between the Centres of any two Bastions, reckon ’ d all round as before.

polygonal.c: POLYGONAL ' Numbers, are such as are the Sums or Aggregates of Series of Numbers in A - rixhmetical Progression, beginning with Unity; and lb placed, that they repreieni the Form of a Poly - gon Thus, / o n - O O O o i IO are Triangular Numbers, because they are the Ag - gregates of a certain Number of Points placed in the Form of Triangles, &c. o a o a ooo r. a o o ooo I are Quadrangular Numbers, &c.

polygram.c: POLYGRAM, is a Geometrical Figure consist - ing of many Lines.

polyhedrousfigure.c: POLYHEDROUS Figure, in Geometry, is a Solid contained under of consisting of many Sides; which, if they are Regular Polygons, all Similar and Equal, and the Body be inferibable within the Surface of the Sphere, ’ tis then called a Regular Body. See that " Word.

polynomeal.c: POLYNOME AL, or Multinomial Root r, - in Ma - thematicks, are such as are composed of many Nomes, Parts, or Members; as, a - f b d - f - c. each Flower, and this without any certain Order or Number.. These Mr, Ray makes to be a diftincfc kind of Herbs, calling them Herb seine nudo Polysperm s Where by Semine nudo he means such Seeds as do not put off spontaneously the Integuments of Coverings which they either have, or appear to have, but fall covered with it from the Mother - Plant. These kind of Herbs he divides into Two forts. I. Such as have a Calyx or Perianthium to their Flower; and this consisting either of, r. Three Leaves; the Flower alio being Tripe - talous, or having but Three Leaves: As, the Plantago Aquatica, and the Sagittdria, both Water - Plants. Or where the Flower is Polypetalous, and the Calyx falling together with the Flower j as in the Chelidonium minus: or remaining af - ter the Flower is dropt, as in the Hepaticit Nobilis. Zi Five Leaves; in some Deciduous with the Flower, as in the Ranunculus: In others Pe - rennial, as in the He / leborus nicer ferulaceus or Annual, as in the Flos Adonis. . Eight Leaves as the Malva and Alee a. Tew Leaves; as the Caryophylla, Fragraria, Pcntaphyllum, Tormentilla, Argentina, Althaea, and Pentaphylloides. II. Such as have no Calyx or. Perianthium a the Clematis, Filipendula, Vlmaria, Anemone Ne - morum, Pulfatilla, See. In Philof. Trans, N. z o. you have a curious Method of Railing an Infinite Multinomial to any Given Power; or of Extracting any Given Root out of such Power: Which was discovered from Sir isaac Newtons Theorem for Railing a Binomial to any Given Power, or Extracting the Root of the fame, by that Ingenious and Excellent Alge - wrist Mr. Abr. de Moivre.

polypetalousflower.c: POLYPETALOUS Flower, is the Term in Bo - any lor the Slow'er of a Plant which consists of more than Six distend Flower - leaves fet round to form it; and which fall off singly.

polypus.c: POLYPUS, is a Swelling in the Hollow of the Nostrils, and is Two - fold; either like a Tent, and then it goes by the general Name of Sarcoma; or such an one that has a great many distend Branches or Feet, which extend either to the Out - side of the Nose, or the In - side of the Mouth. Their. Colour is White, oftentimes Reddish, and fotnetimes Black and Livid. Excrefcencies of this Nature happen not only in the Nostrils, but fotnetimes in the Heart, and in the Cavities of the thicker Membrane of the Brain. Blanchard.

polyscopesormultiplyinggl.c: POLYSCOPES, or Multiplying Gl iffcs, are such as represent to the Eye one Qbjed as many.

polyspastumaterminmechanicks.c: POLYSPASTUM, a Term in Mechanicks, the fame with the Trochlea or Pully. POLYSPERMiE Plant, are such Herbs or Plants as have more than Four Seeds succeeding

pomiferousherbs.c: POMIFEROUS Herbs, are ( according to Mr. Ray ) such as have the largest of Fruit of any Plants whatever, and this covered with a thick hard Rind or Bark; by which they are distinguished from the Bacciferous Herbs, which only have a thin Skin over the Fruit. These kind of Plants have a naked Monopeta - lous Flower, divided into Five Jaggs or Partitions, and growing on the top of the succeeding Frffit. And these either are, i . Capreolate, or creeping along the Ground, &c. by means of their Tendrils, ( Capreoli ) as the Cucurbita, Melt, Cucumis, Cepo, Belfamina P Anguria, and Colocynthis. Or, z. Without Capreoli or Tendrils; as the Cucur - bita Clypeata, or Mele - Cepo, Clypeiformis.

pomiferoustrees.c: POMIFEROUS Trees, ( ' fee Trees ) are such as have their Flower on the top of the Fruit, and their Fruit in the Form of an Apple or Pear.

pompholigodesurine.c: POMPHOLIGODES, Urine with many Bub - bles upon it; which are frequent, if the Body be must up or pained. Blanchard.

pomumadami.c: POMUM Adami, i s a Protuberance in the Fere - side of the Throat; so called, because ’ tis - foolishly thought a piece of the Apple stuck in Adams Throat, as part of his Punishment, and hence de - rived to his Posterity. Blanchard - p O R In Reality ’ tis only the Convex part of the first Cartilage of the Larynx, called Scufiformis. This is greater in Men than Women.

pone.c: PONE, is a Writ, whereby a Cause depending in the County Court, or other Inferior Court, is removed into the Common - Pleas.

ponepervadium.c: PONE per Vadium, is a Writ to the Sheriff to take Surety of one for his Appearance at a Day assigned.

ponendisinaffifis.c: PONENDIS in Affifis, is a Writ founded up - on the Statute of Weft. cap.. and upon, the Statute Articuli Super Chartas, cap.. Which Sta - tutes shew what Persons Sheriffs ought to im - pannel upon Affifes and Juries, and what not.

ponenduminballium.c: PONENDUM in Ballium, is a Writ command - ing a Prisoner to be bailed, in Cafes Bailable.

ponendumsigillum.c: PONENDUM Sigillum ad exceptionem, is a Writ whereby the King willeth the Justices, ac - cording to the Statute of West.. to put their Seals to Exceptions laid in by the Defendant against the Plaintiff ’ s Declarations, or against the Evidence, Verdidl, or other Proceedings before the Justices -

ponscerebri.c: PONS Cerebri, ( by ffimej is a Congeries or Heap of innumerable Filaments divaricated out of the Solider Substance of the Brain, whence all the Nerves take their Rife.

pontage.c: PONTAGE, is a Contribution towards the Maintenance or Re - edifying of Bridges. It may also signifie Toll taken to this Purpose of those that pass over Bridges.

pontibus.c: PONTIBUS J eparandis, is a Writ directed to the Sheriff, G ? c. willing him to charge one or more to Repair a Bridge, to whom it belongeth.

pontoninfortification.c: PONTON, in Fortification, is a Bridge made of two Boats, at some Distance one from another, both covered with Planks; as also the Internal Space betwixt them. They have Props and Rails on each side; and the whole Structure ought to be so solid, as to be able to transport the Horse, to - gether with Cannon and Baggage, as well as the Infantry.

pontvolant.c: PONT Volant, or the Flying Bridge, used in Sieges, is made of two, small Bridges laid one o - ver another; and so contrived, by the means of Cords and Pulleys placed along the fades of the Under Bridge, that the Upper can be pushed for - wards ’ till it joins the Place where it is to be fixed: But however the whole Length of both these Bridges must not be above Four or Five Fathom long, left they should break with the Weight of the Men. These are chiefly used to surprise Out - works or Posts that have but narrow Moats.

poop.c: POOP of a Ship, is the Floor or Deck over the Round - house or Matter's Cabin, being the highest or uppermost part of her Hull, a - stern.

popliteavena.c: POPLITEA Vena, is the Vein of the Ham, and sometimes reaches down the back of the Leg even to the Heel. This comes from the Iliacal Branches of the Vena Cava; which, after they descend as low as the Thighs, are called Crurales.

popliteus.c: POPLITEUS, by some called Subpopliteus, is a. Muscle of the Leg, which ariseth with a sliort strong Tendon from the External Head of the In - senior Appendix of the Os Femoris from whence defending obliquely over the Juncture, becomes Fleshy, and expanding it self, is so inserted to the Superior part of the Tibia internally, immediate - ly below its Superior Appendix. This assists the other Muscles in bending the Tibia, and also An - tagonizeth the Biceps, by turning the Foot and Toes outwards when we fit with our Knees bended.

pores.c: PORES, are small Interstices, Spaces, or Va - cities between the Particles of Matter that con - statute every Body, or between certain Aggregates or Combinations of them. Thus, for Instance, those little imperceptible Holes in the Skin, thro ’ which the Sweat and Vapours inffinfibly breath out of the Body, are called Pores j and the having of such Holes or Pores in any Body, is called Pe - rosiny or Poroufnejs, The Honourable Mr. Boyle has written a Pam -; cular EJftay on the Porosity of Bodies; in which he proves. That the most, Solid Bodies that are have some kind of Pores. And indeed, if they had not all Bodies would be alike Specifically weighty.

PORES. Sir If. Newton in his Opticky hews, that Bodies are much more rare and porous than is commonly believed. Water is times lighter and consequently rare than Gold; and Gold is so rare as very readily and without the last oppose - tion to transmit the Magnetick Effluvia, and easily to admit Quick - silver into its Pores, and to let Water pass through it; for a Concave Sphere of Gold hath, when filled with Water and folder ’ d up, upon preftlng with great force, let the Wa - ter squeeze through it, and stand all over its out - side in multitudes of small Drops like Dew, with - out bursting or cracking the Gold, as he was in - formed by an Eye - witness. Whence we may con - crude, that Gold hath more Pores than solid Parts, and by consequence, that Water hath above times more Pores than Parts. And he that hall find out an Hypothesis to fosse how Water can be thus rare, and yet not be capable of compression by force, may doubtless by the fame Hypothesis make Gold and Water, and all other Bodies, as much rare as he pleases. So that Light may find a ready passage through transparent Substances, there being open and free Space sufficient for such a Passage. We find that the Magnet tranlmits its Vertue without any fen - sable diminution or alteration, through all cold Bodies that are not Magnetick, as Gold, Silver, Brass, Glass, Water, &c. The gravitating Pow - er of the Sun ( If you will explain it Mechanically ) is transmitted entire through all the vast Planetary Bodies, so that with an equable force it ads thro ’ all their Parts, even to their very Centres; i. e. ac - cording to the quantity of Matter in each part. The Pvays of Light, let ’ em be either Bodies act - ally coming to us from the Sun, or only Motions or Imprefllons upon the Medium, move in Right - Lines, and are hardly ever, unless by great chance, reflected back again in the fame Right - Line after their Impingence on ObjeCts; and yet we fee that Light is transmitted to the greatest distances thro ’ Pellucid Bodies, and that in Right - Lines. Now how Bodies should have Pores sufficient for these Effects is hard to conceive, but yet not impossible. For Sir If. Newton hath shewn, That the Colours P O R of all Bodies arise from their Particles being of such a determinate Size or Magnitude: ( " See Co - lours. ) Wherefore if we conceive those Particles to be so disposed, as that there is as much of Porosity or Space interspersed between them as the Quan - tity of these Particles amounts to. And in like manner, if you suppose these Particles to be com - posed of others much less, and that these have as much interspersed Vacuity as their Quantity a - mounts to; and so on till at last you come to So - lid Particles without any Pores: Then if in any Body there be ( for Inftancej of these Sizes of Particles, and that the last be of the solid or least fort; that Body will have times as much Vacui - ty as Solid Matter. If you suppose such De - grees or Sizes of Particles, and that the last and least be solid; the Body will have times as much Pores as Solidity. If you imagine any Body to have such Degrees or Sizes of Particles, it will have times as much Space as Solidity in - terfperfed: And if it have such Sizes of Particles as before, it will have times as much Vacuity as Solid Matter, and so on. And perhaps in the wonderful confirmation g. nd Fabrick of Natural Bodies there may be other Proportions of Space to Matter ito us wholly unknown, whence ’ tis pos - sable there may be yet far greater quantities of Va - city interspersed in Bodies.

porime.c: PORIME, ( Gr. in Geometry, is a The - rem or Proposition so easie to be demonstrated, that ’ tis almost self - evident; as, That a Chord is all of it within the Circle. And on the contrary they call that an Aporime, which is so difficult as to be almost impossible to be demonstrated - as the Quadrature of the Circle, is now,, and as the Squaring of any Assigned Portion of Hippocrates his Lunes was, ’ till a little while ago.

porisme.c: PORISME. Proclus and Pappus define this Geo - metrical Term to signifie a kind of Theorem, in the form of a Corollary, which is dependant up - on, or deduced from some other Theorem area - dy demonstrated. And ’ tis commonly used to fig - nisi some General Theorem, which is discovered from finding out some Geometrical Place: As, for Instance, if a Man hath found out by Alge - bra, or any other Method how to Conftrud: a Local Problem and from that Place so constructed and demonstrated, hath deduced some General Theorem, that Theorem is by the Geometrick Writers called a Porism, Of these Poriftms, Mr. Q - s anam, in his French Mathematical. Dictionary, gives many useful Instances; which fee.

poristickadethod.c: PORISTICK Adethod, in Mathemadcks, is that which determines when, by what way, and how many different ways, a Problem may be resolved.

porocele.c: POROCELE, is a Rupture proceeding from Callous Matter, or the Stone. Blanchard.

porotica.c: POROTICA, are Medicines, which, by dry - ing, thickening, and astringent Qualities, turn part of the Nouriffiment into Brawny, Callous Mat - ter Blanchard.

portthehelm.c: PORT the Helm, a Sea - Term, signifying to put the Helm to the Left or Larboard side of the Ship; but however they never fay Larboard the Helm, but always Port it; tho ’ they fay Starboard the Helm, when it is to be put to the Right side of the Ship. A Ship is said to Heel a - port, when five swims not upright, but leans to the Left side. The Word '

port.c: PORT, also signifies a Haven or Harbour; as also the Holes in a Ship ’ s side, thro ’ which her Great Guns are put out.
PORT - NAILS, are such Nails as are used to fasten the Hinges to the Ports of Ships.

portablebarometer.c: PORTABLE Barometer, was first invented by the Honourable Mr. Boyle, and was effected by making the Torricellian Experiment in a long Glass Tube, sealed at the top, and bent near the bottom up again, parallel to the longer Leg: For by this means the Quicksilver in the open and shorter Leg, supplied the Place of the ftagn'ant Mercury in the Baffin or Ciitern, The Instru - ment P O S anent was all of one piece, and might easily be earned from Place to Place without Ipilling the Mercury. By which means, Observations of the W eight of the Atmosphere might be readily made on the Tops of Hills, Bottoms of Mines, &c. But this Open Tube could not be carried about ' with lo much Ease and Safety as those Portable Barometers which are now in Use, and which are made by Mr. John Patrick Torricellian Operator in the Old Pally i with very great Exa & ness and Neatness: For in thele there is an Invention to screw the Mercury quite up to the Sealed end of the Tube, by which means it will not swag up and down in the Carriage and lo by its great Weight endanger the breaking of the Tube.

portculliceherse.c: PORTCULLICE, Herse, or Sara fine, in For - tification, ( signifie several great Pieces of Wood laid or joined across one another like an Harrow, and at the Bottom it is pointed at the end of each Bar. with Iron. These formerly uled to hang over the Gate - ways of Fortified Places, to be ready to let down in Case of a Surprize, when the Enemy should come so soon, as that there is not Time to Ihut up the Gates. But now adays the Orgues are more generally used. as being found to be much better. See Orgues,

porticoorporch.c: PORTICO, or Porch, in Architecture, is a long Place cover ’ d either with a Vaulted Roof, or an even Floor, supported by Pillars But this Word may be applied to signifie all manner of Dis - positions of Columns in a Gallery.

portioner.c: PORTIONER, where a Parsonage is served j sometimes by two, or sometimes by three Mini - stars alternately. The Ministers are called Porti - cners, because they have but their Portion or Pro - portion of Tythes or Profits of the Living.

portmote.c: PORTMOTE, lignifies a Court kept in Ha - yen Towns, as Swainemote in the Forest, and is called the Portmote Court.
PORTMOTE, is a Convention or Meeting of the Inhabitants of a Pori - or Burgh, in which some Customary Duties were anciently paid to the Lord of the Fee,

porusbilarius.c: PORUS Bilarius, or Meatus Hejraticus, is a Pipe or Channel paying directly from the Liver to the Du Hus Communis, and which transmit the Bile from the Liver by the Intervention of some small Glandules. Within the Liver, its Trunk and Branches are invested with a double Coat: A Proper one, which it retains also without the Liver; and another Common to it and the Porta, called Capsul a Communis, which it hath from the Membrane of the Liver. In this Common Coat, this Porus and the Porta are so closely enwrapped, that at first they appear but one Vessel i but if you Fold them up to the Light, you will discover Ves - iels of two Colours and then you may dexter - roufly rip up the Capsula, and so lay them open. Its Roots within the Liver are equally divided with thole of the Porta every where, except in that little Space where the Roots of the Vesica are spread in the Right side of the Liver and they are both larger arid more numerous than those of the ! Vesica, drawing Choler from all Parts of the Liver almost: And this Porus Bilarius seems to be a more necessary Part than the Gall - Bladder, or Ve - sic; because in many Creatures, as Red and Sal - low Deer, Holes, &c. the Vesica is wanting, but none want this. Without the Liver, tis as wide again as the Meatus Cysticus, with which it joins at two Inches Distance from the Liver - and so both make up the Dublus Choledochus Communis. The Porus hath no Valve in its whole Progress only the Ductus Communis, at its Entrance into; the Intestines,. having pierced the Outer Coat, passes between that and the Middlemost Coat for about the th part of an Inch; and then piercing that alio, marches down farther between it and the Inner Coat of the Gut, for about half an Inch ' and at last opens with a round Mouth into thelnte ftine: So that this Oblique Insertion ( like that of the Ureters into the Urinary Bladder ) serves instead of a V the, to hinder any thing from Rcgur - Skating out of the Guts into this Dud: And this is farther prevented also by the flaggy, loose Con - ftitution of the Inner Tumck of the Guts which, when any thing would enter the Mouth of the Po rus, claps close upon it, and stops it. There are no Anajhmofes between the Roots of this Dud and those of the Porta, as have been often said: For the Extreme Capillary Twigs of the Porus term - name in the Parenchyma of the Liver, out of whole Glandules they imbibe the Choler, there lepara - ted from the Blood.

positionorsite.c: POSITION, or Site, in Affedion of Place, and expresses the manner of any Bodies being in a Place: this therefore is not Place, nor indeed hath it any Quantity; as Sr. If. Newton well ob Princip. Mathem. p..

position.c: POSITION, or the Pule of P stion, otherwise cabled the Pule of Falfhood, is a Rule in Arithme - tic wherein any Number is taken to work the Question by, instead of the Number fought; and so by the Error or Errors found, we find the Num - ber required. This Pule of Fa ’ fe Position is of Two kinds, viz. Single and Double.

positionsingle.c: POSITION Single, is when there happens in the Proposition some Partition of Numbers into Parts Proportional; and then at one Operation the Que - stion may be resolved, by this Rule. Imagine a Number at pleasure, and Work there ' with according to the Tenor of the Question, as if it were the true Number; and what Proper - tion there is between the False Conclusion and the False Position, such Proportion hath the Gi - ven Number to the Number fought: Therefore the Number found by Argumentation shall be the first Term of the Pule of Three, arid the Number supposed Shall be the second Term, and the Given Number shall be the third Term. Example, Three Men, A. B. and C. content to buy d Ship for /, So that B. must pay twice as much as A. and C. four times as much as B. Hovtf much must each Man pay ? Answer. positiveofdegreeofcompanioningram.h: POSITIVE of Degree of Companion in Gram
positiveofdegreeofcompanioningram.c: POSITIVE of Degree of Companion in Gram - mar, is that which signifies the Thing limply and absolutely, without comparing it with others; it belongs only to Adjectives,

positivequantitiesinalgebra.c: POSITIVE Quantities in Algebra, are such as & re of a Real and Affirmative Nature, and ei - ther have, or are supposed to have the Affirma - tive or Positive Sign - before them, and ns al - ways used in opposition to the Negative Quanti - ties, which are defective, and have this Sign before them,

posecomitatus.c: POSE Comitatus, a Term in Law, signifying the Aid and Attendance of all Knights, Gentle - men, Yeomen, Labourers, Servants, Apprenti - ces, and all others, above the Age of Fifteen Years within the County; except Women, Ecclesiastical Persons, and such as are decrepit, or labour of an Infirmity: And the Statute of z H.. cap.. lays, T, hat Persons able to Travel, fioall be as - slant in this Service, which is used where a Pos - session is kept upon a Forcible Entry, or any Force of Rescue used, contrary to the Command of the King ’ s Writ, or in opposition to the Eye - cution of Justice.

possession.c: POSSESSION, in a Legal Sense, is taken twofold, Actual and in Law: ACiual Pojfejfon is, when a Man actually enters into Lands and Te - onements to him descended. PcJJ'eJJion in Law, is when Lands or Tenements are descended to a Man, and he hath not as yet a & ually entred into them. As for Example. Before or until an Office be found of Lands Escheated by an Attainder, the King hath only a Pojfejfion in Law, and not in Deed: There is also a Unity of Pcjfeffon, which the Civilians call Con - folidationem. If the Lord purchase the Tenancy held by Heriot Service, then the Heriot is extends by Unity of Pojfejfion; that is because the Seigniory and the Tenancy are now in one Man ’ s Pojfejfion,

possessivesingrammar.c: POSSESSIVES, in Grammar, are such Ad - jectives as signifie the Possession of, or Property in some Thing,

posteainlaw.c: POSTEA in Law, is the Return of the Proceed - ing by Nijt prius, into the Court of Common - Pleas, after a Verdict, and there afterwards Recorded.

post.c: POST ATiE, Adjl antes, or Corpora Glandulofa, are two Glandules placed near the Passage of the Seed; which ( as may be guess ’ d ) lubricate the common Passage of the Seed and Urine, and af - ford a kind of a Vehicle to the Seminal Matter, and are laid to provoke the Titillation in Coition: Their Moisture being conveyed by certain little Tubes, which terminate in the Passage near where the Seed is ejected, and is emitted at the fame time with it. The Learned Bartholine has observed some such thing in Women,

POST, in the Art military, is used for any fort of Ground or Place, whether fortified or not, where a Body of men can make a Hand, fortify themselves, or be in a condition to fight an enemy; and There - fore they Say the Poji was relieved, the Post was quitted, the Poji was Taken Sword in hand, cc. A Spot of ground Seized by a Party to Secure the front of an Army and to cover the Polls that are behind, They call an Advanced Poji: and The Ad - vance Guard or the Right of the z lines of an Army, &c. they call the Poji of Honour.

postdiem.c: POST Diem, is the Return of a Writ after the Day assigned, for which the Cufios Brevium hath four Pence, whereas he hath nothing if it be re - turn ’ d at the Day; sometimes it is taken for the Fee it self,

postdijfeijin.c: POST Dijfeijin, is a Writ given by the Sta - tute of Weftminjl. z. cap. z - and lies for him that having recovered Lands or Tenements by Pracipe quod reddat, upon the Default or Reddition, is again disseised by the former Diifeifor.

postfine.c: POST Fine, in Law, is a Duty belonging to the King, for a Fine formerly acknowledged before him in his Court, which is paid by the Cognilee, after the fame is fully passed, all and things person - med touching the fame; the Rate thereof is so much, and half so much as was paid to the King for the Fine, and is Collected by the Sheriff of the County, where the Land, &c. lies, whereof the Fine was levied, to be answer - red by him into the Exchequer.

postterme.c: POST Terme, is a Return of a Writ, not only after the Day assigned for the Return thereof, but after the Term also; for which, the Cufios arc. vium takes the Fee of Twenty Pence; Sometimes also. it is taken for the Fee it self

posterninfortification.c: POSTERN, in Fortification, is a false Door usually made in the Angle off the Flank, and of the Curtain, or near the Orillon for private Sallies.

posticum.c: POSTICUM, is the Pojlern - Gate, or Back - Doct of any Fabrick.

postulatesordemandsinmathematical.c: POSTULATES, or Demands in Mathematical See. are such easy and self evident Suppositions as aeed no Explication or Illustration to render them Intelligible. As, That a Bight Line may be drawn from one Point to another. That a Circle may be described on any Centre gi - ven, of any Magnitude, See.

postulation.c: POSTULATION, ( in the Law ) is made up - on the Unanimous Voting of any Person to a Dig - nity or Office, of which he is not capable by the Ordinary Canons or Statutes, without special Dispensation.

potansorpotence.c: POTANS, or Potence, a Part of a Watch; lee under Balance.

potentorpotence.c: POTENT, or Potence, the Term for a Cross in Heraldry, formed into this Figure. He beareth Sable, a Croft Potent, Or, by the Name of Aleyn. This form represents the upper end of a Crutch; for Anciently Crutches were called Patents,

potentcounterpotent.c: POTENT, Counter Potent, a Term in Heral - dry: See Vairy Copy.

potentialcoldness.c: POTENTIAL Coldness, is a Relative Quality which some Drugs, Simples, or Compound Me - dicines are supposed to be endowed with: And therefore you will find frequently in some Old Books, or in the Writings of such as follow the Old Physicians, that such a Plant or Drug, is cold in the d or d Degree: The meaning of which, is, not that such a Plant is actually Cold to die Touch, but that it is Cold in its Effects and Operations, if taken Iwardly. And whenever such an Effcdt doth follow the taking of such a Medicine, Mr. Boyle thus accounts for it according to the Mecha - nical Philosophy, vi. That this Body, which they call Potentially Cold, is made up of Corpvfdes of of such a Size, Shape, &c. that being disjoined and resolved by the Mcnftruum of the Stomach, or the Fluids it may elsewhere meet with, they do lo intimately associate themselves with the small parts of the Blood and other Liquors, as by clogging and impeding them to lessen their wonted Agitation; and perhaps also to make them at in a peculiar way, as well as less briskly on the Nervous and Fibrous parts of the Body: The Perception of which Imminution, or perhaps Change of Motion in the Organs of Feeling, is that, which being referred to the Body that produced it, is called Potential Coldness. Hence, if it be supposed that in Agues some Morbifick Matter of a vifeous, or not easily dis sizable Texture, be harboured in some part of the Body, and requires such a Time to be made fluid and resolvable, which is an Hypothesis, generally received, the Cold Fits in tfaefe Diseases, will be plausibly accounted for. Also the Shiverings and Cold arising from the taking of most Poisons, may hence be solved; and that lesser Degree of it which seizes Hypechcn - driacl and Hysterical Persons,

potentialmeedingrammar.c: POTENTIAL Meed in Grammar, is the fame, in form with the Subjunctive; but differs in this Than I I P O W P R A That it hath always Implied in it, either Poffum, Volo, or Debeo; as Roget Quis, that is, Rogare po - test, a Man may ask. ' Tis sometimes called, The Permissive Mood, because it implies often a Per - mission or Conceftion to do a thing: As Habeas, talent, viva cum ilia. Terent.

pour.c: POUR fair proc dee, que null inject sims ou ordures en fojfes, on rivers pres Cityes, &c. is a Writ di reded to the Mayor, Sheriff, or Bailiff, of a City or Town, commanding them to pro - claim, That none cast Filth into the Ditches or Places near adjoining, and if any cast already to remove it.

pourparty.c: POUR Party, is a Term in Law, contrary to pro indiviso - for to make Pour party, is to divide and fever the Lands that fall to Parcener, which before Partition they hold jointly, and pro indi - vis.

pourseifirtorres.c: POUR Seifir Torres la feme que tient en Dower, kc. was a Writ whereby the King Seised upon the Land, which the Wife of his Tenant that held in Cnpite, deceased, hath for her Dowry, if she Married without his Leave; and is grounded up - on the Statute of the King ’ s Prerogative.

poursuivant.c: POUR Suivant, signifies the King ’ s Messenger attending upon him in his Wars, or at the Coun - cil Table, Exchequer, in his Court, or his Cham - ber, to be sent upon any Occasion or Message; as for the Apprehending of a Person Accused, or Suspended of any Offence: Those that be used in Martial Causes, are call ’ d Pursuivant at Arms, others are used upon Meffages in time of Peace, and especially in Matters touching Jurifdidtion.

pourveyance.c: POURVEYANCE, is the providing. Corn, Fuel, Victual, and other Necessaries for the King ’ s House.

pourveyor.c: POURVEYOR, signifies an Officer of the King or Queen, or other great Personage, that provideth Corn and other Victual for their House.

powches.c: POWCHES, so the Seamen call frnall Bulk - heads made in the Hold of a Ship, to stow Corn, Goods, or the like, that it do not shoot from one side to the other.

powersinalgebra.c: POWERS in Algebra, are Numbers arising from the Squaring or Multiplication of any Num - ber or Quantity by it self, and then that Product by the Root or first Number again; and this Third Product by the Root again; and so on ad Infinitum i as,,,,,,,,, &c. Where a is called the Root or First Power, is the Square or Second Power, is the Cube or, Third Power, is the Biquadrate or Fourth Pow - er, &c. And these Powers in Letters or Species, are expressed by repeating the Root as often as the Index of the Power expresses, thus; a is the Root or First Power, a a the Square or Second Power, a a a the Cube, a a a a the Biquadrate or Fourth Power. And to avoid the tediousnes of repeat - ing the Root so often when the Powers are high, we only put down the Root with the Index of the Power over it, thus: a, that is the ninth Power of a; b's, b are the sixteenth or the ninety fourth Powers of b.

powersinmechanickj.c: POWERS, in Mechanickj, are the Six Mecha - nical Faculties; the Ballance, the Leaver, the Wheel, the Pulley, the Wedge, and the Screw; which are usually stile the Six Mechanic Pow - ers. The Force also or Strength brought for the moving of any Weight by any Engine, is called the Power. And the design of Mechanicks, is to teach Men how to add such a fitting Supplement to the Power, as that it may move any Weight, required, with facility and cheapness, and in as lit - tle room as may be. See Vol. II.

powersoflines.c: POWERS of Lines, or Quantities are ' their Squares, Cubes, or other Multiplications of the parts into the whole, or of one part into another. POYNlNG'r Law, is an Adi of Parliament made in Ireland by Hen.. and so called, because Sir Edward Poyning was Lieutenant there, when it was made; whereby all the Statutes in England were made of force in Ireland, which before that time were not, neither are any now in force there which were made in England since that time.
