proprietateprobanda.c: PROPRIETATE Probanda, is a Writ that lies for him that would prove a Property before the She - riff For where a Property is alledged, a Replegiare lieth not.

proptosis.c: PROPTOSIS, is the Fallowing - down of some Part; as of the Eye, the Cable, ( c.

prorata.c: PRO Rata. See Qneranda pro rata portionis.

prorogue.c: PROROGUE, signifies to prolong, or put off to another Day. The Difference between a Proroga - tion and an Adjournment, or Continuance of the Parliament, is, That by the Prorogation in open Court, there is a Session; and then such Bills as pa ( Ted in either House, or both Houses, and had not the Assent to them, muff at the next Assembly begin again: For every Session of Parliament is in Law a several Parliament; but if it be but Ad - journey or Continued, then there is no Session, and consequently all things continued in the fame State they were in before the Adjournment.

prosecutorinlaw.c: PROSECUTOR, in Law, is he that follows a Cause in another ’ s Name. See Promoters.

prosodia.c: PROSODIA, is that Part of Grammar which teaches the Quantity of Syllables, distinguishing Into Long and Short, ( c.

prosopopeia.c: PROSOPOPEIA, is a violent Rhetorical Figure, wherein the Speaker addreffeshimfelf to inanimate Things as if they were living, and makes them speak as if they had Souls.

prosphys.c: PROSPHYS S, is a Coalition, or growing to - gether, as when two Fingers are connected to each other.

postapheresis.c: POST APHERESIS, in Astronomy,. is the fame with the Equation of the Orbit, or limply the Equation and is the Difference between the True and Mean Motion of a Planet. The Angle also made by the Lines of the Planets Mean and True Motion, is called the Projlapherefis.

prostasisapartofsurgery.c: PROSTASIS, a Part of Surgery, which fills up what is wanting; as we see in hollow and fistulous Ulcers filled up with Flesh by Surgery. Blanchard.

prosthesisingrammar.c: PROSTHESIS, in Grammar, is in the General a Metaplasm, and in Particular an Addition of some Letter or Letters to the Beginning of a Word as Gnavus pro navus. This is also called Appofi - tion.

prostomiathered.c: PROSTOMIA, the Red - tinctured part of the Lips. Blanchard.

protectioninlaw.c: PROTECTION, in Law, hath a general and a special Signification: In the General, it is used for that Benefit and Safety which every Subject, Denifon, or Alien, especially secured, hath by the King ’ s Laws. Protection, in the Special Significa - tion, is used for an Exemption or Immunity given by the King to a Person against Suits in Law, or other Vexations, upon Reasonable Causes moving him thereto. Of this, Fit - Herbert m aketh two kinds; the First he - calls a Protection, cum claufula volumus, whereof he mentions Four Particulars: i. A Protection quia profeCiurus, for him that is to pass over Sea in the King ’ s Service,; A Prote - ction quia moraturus, for him that is Abroad in the King ’ s Service upon the Sea, or in the Marches.. A Protection for the King ’ s Debtor; that he be not sued or attached ’ till the King be paid his Debt: This the Civilians call Moratcriam.. A Protection in the King ’ s Service beyond Sea, or in the Marches of Scotland. The Second Form of Protection is cum claufula nolumus, which is granted most commonly to a Spiritual Company for their Immunity, from ta - king their Cattle by the King ’ s Ministers: But it ' may be granted also to one Man Spiritual or Tem - coral.

protestinlaw.c: PROTEST, in Law, hath two divers Applica - tions; One is by way of Caution, to call witness, ( as it were ) or openly to affirm, That he doth either not at all, or but conditionally yield his Con - sent to any A ft, or unto the Proceeding of any Judge in a Court wherein his Jurifdi & ion is doubt - ful, or to answer upon his Oath further than by Law he is bound. The other is by way of Com - plaint, to Protest a Man ’ s Bill j For Example; If I give Money to a Merchant in Prance, taking his Bill of Exchange to be repaid ia England by one whom he affigneth; if at my Coming, I find not my self satisfied, but either delay ’ d or deny ’ d, then I go to the Exchange, or other open Concourse of Merchants, and Protest, That I am not Paid: And thereupon, if he hath any Goods remaining in any Man ’ s Hands within the Realm, the Laves of Mer - chants is, That I be paid out of them to my full Satisfaction.

protestationinlaw.c: PROTESTATION, in Law, is a Defence of Safeguard to the Party which maketh it, from be - ing concluded by the ACt he is about to do, that Issue cannot be joined by it.

protopathia.c: PROTOPATHIA, is a Primary Dileaf e, not caused by another.

protracting.c: PROTRACTING - P / w, is a fine Needle fast - ned in a piece of Wood, Ivory, ( c. used to prick off any Degrees and Minutes from the ProtraCior.

protractor.c: PROTRACTOR, is an Inftrutnent used in Sur - vexing: It is commonly made of a well polish ’ d thin piece of Brass, and consisteth of a Semi - circle divided into Degrees, and a Parallelogram with Scales upon it, and may be of any Bigness desire ’ d. But this Inftrutnent is so well known, that there needs no further Description. Its Use is chiefly. To lay down an Angle of any assigned Quantity of Degrees: Or, an Angle be - ing Protracted, to find the Quantity of Degrees it contains P T A contains readily; which is of great life in Plot - ting, and making of Draughts,

proviso.c: PROVISO, is a Condition inserted into any Deed, upon the Observance whereof the Validity of the Deed depends; but sometimes it is only a Co - venant. It hath also another Signification in Mat - ters Judicial, as if the Plaintiff or Demandant de - iift in prosecuting an Action, by bringing it to a Trial; the Defendant or Tenant may take out a Venire facias to the Sheriff, which hath in it these Words, Prcvifo quod, &c. to this End, That if the Plaintiff take out any Writ to that Purpose, the Sheriff shall summon but one Jury upon them both: In which Case, we call it going to Trial by Proviso.
PROVISO, in the Sea Phrase, for a Ship to Moor a Proviso, is for her to have one Anchor out, and also a Hawser ashore, and so file is moored with her Head to the Shore with two Cables.

prow.c: PROW of a Ship, is that part of her Fore - castle which is Aloft, and not in the Hold; and is pro - perly that which is between the Chafe and the Loaf. PRUNELLiE Sal. See Sal PrunelU. r

psammismusabath.c: PSAMMISMUS, a Bath of dry and warm Sand, wherewith the Feet of Men in the Dropsy re dried. Blanchard.

pseudodipteron.c: PSEUDODIPTERON, is an ancient form of a Temple, compassed about with but one row of Pillars, and which Row from the Wall, is at the di - stance usually of two Rows of Pillars.

pseudqstellainastronomy.c: PSEUDQSTELLA, in Astronomy, signifies any kind of Comet or Phenomenon newly appearing in the Heavens like a Star.

psoasmagnus.c: PSOAS Magnus, or Lumhalis, is a Muscle of the Loins, which proceeds from all the Vertebres of the Loins and their transverse Processes inter - nally and laterally, within the Cavity of the Ab - women from thence descending over the superior Part of the Os Sacrum and Spine of the Ilium, where it ’ s joined with the fleshy Fibres of the Iliacus In - terms, with which it ’ s infeparablely united to their partly Fleshy and partly Tendinous Insertions in the inferior part of the lesser Trochanter of the Thigh - Bone: Its use is, together with the Iliacus Internus, to move the Thigh forwards.

psoasparvus.c: PSOAS Parvus, is a Muscle of the Thigh, which arises fleshy from the superior Part of the first Ver - terra of the Loins, internally and laterally within the Abdomen, immediately below the Cavity of the Diaphragm, whence descending obliquely inwards towards the Pelvis Abdominis, ( where it ceases to be Fleshy ) in a manner embracing the Psoas Mag - nus, and is inserted with a thin, broad, strong Ten - don, to that of Sart of the / Pubis, where it ’ s join ’ d to the Os Ilium: This Muscle, with its Partner Adting, assist the Recti Abdominis in drawing the Off Pubis upwards, as in raising our selves from a decumbent Pollute. Thus Rope - Dancers hang by their Hands, and raise the inferior Parts of their Bodies, to take hold of a Rope with their Feet. Tho ’ their proper Action is to bend the Loins, yet their Tendons embracing the Psoas Magnus and Iliacus Internus, ( which we have frequently obfer - ved to extend over the inferior Parts ) not unlike the Fascia Temdinofa Cubiti and Lata of the Thigh, do also Corroborate them in their Action. Cowper.

psorophthalmyanophthalmy.c: PSOROPHTHALMY, an Ophthalmy, or In - flammation of f. he Eyes with itching. Blanchard.

psyctica.c: PSYCTICA, ate cooling Medicines against the Scab. Blanchard.

ptarmicaorsternutatoria.c: PTARMICA, or Sternutatoria, are those things which being endowed with a more piercing AcrL many than the Errhinaceous Medicines, do so ex - treamly irritate and fiirivel up the Membranes of the Brain, thfit it fends forth the pituitous Humour at the Nostrils, in an extraordinary measure, and so cause Sneezing. Blanchard. ' PTERIGOPALATINUS, or Sphcenopterigopnla - - tinus, is a Muscle of the Gargareon, whose former Appellation intimates its Progress and Infer non - the latter its Origin also. This arises from the Process of the QsSphcencides, and descends accord - ing to the length of the Interstice made by the in - ternal Ala of the Os Spbcenoides and Musculus Pteri - goidaws Internus of the lower Jaw - and becoming Tendinous, marches over the i - rccejjus Pterigoi des, and is Inserted to the Fore - part of the Gargareon, The Tendon of this passes over the Ptetigoidal Process, which, like a Pully, gives it a different Power from that of the Sphanopalatinus, tho ’ they have both their Origin from the Place. Wherefore, contrary to that, This draws the Gargareon down - wards; which Contrivance in Nature is no less remarkable, than any of those where the like Ar - tisic of a Trochlea is made use of. PTERIGOPHARYNGiEUS, is a Muscle which arifesthin and fleshy from both the Prerigoidal Pro - ceases of the Os Cuneiforme also from the Root of the Tongue, and Extremities of the Os By aides from these places its fleshy Fibres run in a semi - circular manner, embracing the superior and back Part of the glandulous Membrane of the Fauces, where they meet in a middle Line. When this - Muscle ads, it brings the middle or back Part of the Fauces towards a Plain, by which means, the TonfilU, together with the reft of the Glandules, are comprest in the Evacuation of their Mucus, to join with the Aliment in its descent into the Stomach in Deglutition; and at other times to promote Screw - ticn, in which this Muscle is the chief Instrument i That the Ton fi lie approach towards each other, is observable, when we infpedl these Parts in living Persons.

pterigostaphilinu.c: PTERIGOST APHILINU S Externus, is a Muscle which moves the Vvula, arising from a small Protuberance upon the under side of the Body of the Os Spbcenoides, and goes directly to be inserted into the hinder part of the Vvula - PTERIGOST APHILINUS Internus, is a Mu - ch which moves the Vvula, arising from a small Protuberance of the Os Sphcenoides, and growing into a small round Tendon, which passes cvefm. small Process like a Hook, of the P rocejfus Pteri - goidieus, from thence reverting, it ’ s inserted into the Fore - part of the Vvula.

pterygium.c: PTERYGIUM, is the wing or round rising of the Nose or Eye, or the process of the Bone Space - noides, which is like a Wing, Also a membranous Excrescence above the honey Tunic of the Eye, call ’ d Vnguis and Vngula, growing for the ns oft part from the inner Corner, towards the Apple of. the Eye, and often obscuring it, Blanchard.

pterygoidausinternusandexternus.c: PTERYGOID AUS Internus and Externus, are two Muscles arising from the Procejfus Pterygcides, or Aliformis of the Os Sphc. nodes. Their use is to move the Jaw from side to side.

pterystaphylini.c: PTERYST APHYLINI, are Muscles oftheTA - la or Gargareon, and were so named by Riclanus; but the Accurate Dr. Crown changed their fasces into Sphcenopalatinus and Fterigopalatinus, or Space - nopterigopalatinus. ( See those Words. ) Their use is to give various Motions to the Vvula, PUS ANA,

ptisanptisan.c: PTISAN, Ptisan, is a Deco & ion of Pearl - Barley, Liquorifti, Raifins, &c. being a cooling pleasant Drink for one in a Fever, and much used by the French.

ptylosis.c: PTYLOSIS, is a Disease when the Brims of the Eye - lids being grown thick, the Hairs of the Eye - brows fall off. Blanchard.

puddings.c: PUDDINGS, in a Ship, are Ropes nailed to the Arms of the Main and Fore - Yards, near the ends, and then at or due distances inwards one from another, in order to keep the Robbins from galling or wearing asunder upon the Yards, when the Topfai - Sheets are haled home. They callalfo those Ropes which are - wound a - bout the Rings of Anchors to lave the Clinch of the Cable from being galled with the Iron, by this name. So that when the Ring is so served, ris called the Pudding of the Anchor.

pudcmplants.c: PUD CM Plants, the fame with sensitive Plants, which fee.

pugillus.c: PUGILLUS, is an handful of any Herbs. Ci - thers Interpret it, as much as may be taken up with the Thumb a - nd two Fingers.

puisneorpuny.c: PUISNE, or Puny - the Lawyers term for Younger.

pulmonariaarteria.c: PULMONARIA Arteria, or Vena Arteriosa, is a Vessel in the Breast, arising immediately out of the Right Ventricle of the Heart; its Mouth is not so large as that of the Cava; it has three Valves, called Segmoidales or Semilunar es. Its use is to car - ry the Blood from the right Ventricle of the Heart to the Lungs, and its Coat is double, like that of the Arteries.

pulmonariavena.c: PULMONARIA Vena, or Arteria Vencfa, is a Veil'd of the Heart, which discharges it self thro ’ the left Auricle into the Ventricle of the fame side; for after it has accompanied the Wind - pipe an Arteria Pulmonaris in all their branchings in the Lungs j and by its small twigs, has received the Blood out of the Artery, all these twigs are united first into two Trunks ( vi. the Right and Left ) af - terwards into one, which opens into the left Ven - triple of the Heart. This Vein hath no valve in it, except that at its opening into the left Ventri - cle, where at its Orifice are placed two Membra - nous Valves, called Mitrales from their form resembling, when joined, something of a Nitre. These are very strong and firm, to sustain the violent mo - tion of the Blood, and to hinder it from returning back again into this Vein, and to dired its course to the Aorta, whose Orifice opens in the Syfiole of the Ventricle.

pulmonaryvessels.c: PULMONARY Vessels, are those which carry the Blood from the Heart to the Lungs, and back a - gain, being two in number, vis the Pulmonary Vein, and the Pulmonary Artery, which fee.

pulp.c: PULP, is the fieftty part of Fruits, Roots, or other Bodies, which is Extracted by Infusion or Boiling, and passing through a Sieve; as the Pulp of Tamarinds, CaJJia, Althea, Dates, &c.

pulse.c: PULSE, by the Mathematical Naturalists, is the term used for that Stroak with which any Me dium is affedcd by the motion of Light, Sound, & c. through it. And the Admirable Sir If. Nevoton demonstrates, lib.. mop.. Princip. That the Velocities of the Pulses, J in an Elastick Fluid Medium ( whose Ela - fticity is proportionable to its Density ) are in a Ratio, compounded of half the Ratio of the Ela - stick force - directly, and half the Ratio of the Den - fity Inversely. So that in a Medium, whose Ela - fticity is equal to its Density, all Pulses will be e qually swift.

pulsusthepulse.c: PULSUS, the Pulse, is the immediate Index of the Heart, by the mediation whereof, the Blood is diffused through the whole Body, and is different - ly affected thereby, according to the different In - flux of the Animal Spirits; the Motion whereof is chiefly to be attributed to the circular and dired Fibres. Others affirm it to be the dilatation and contradion of the Heart and Blood. A Pulse is either natural or preternatural of the former we have spoken already; the latter is such as is dis - ferent, according to the different Circumstances of the Fibres and Animal Spirits; to wit, strong, veeak. v swift, flow, equal, unequal, intermittent, &c.

pulses.c: PULSES, according to Dr. Ahercromhy, are ei - ther, Pulse Unequal, is either in helped of time or strength; that is, either it strikes quicker and flower, orelfe ftrongerand weaker. Pulse Interrupted, is when the flfoaks are much Smaller than usual, or their Intervals much great - ter. Pulse Intense, is that whose ftroakis very hard, ' ( the parts as it were upon a bent ) or else this strength is made up with the multiplicity and fre - quench of less Mications, as in the heights of Fe - vers. Pulse remiss, is that whose stroaks are less quick, or less strong, and in Sickness slews more danger than the other. Pulse Superficial, is that which slews an ead Temperament of Body, as also a free and merry Temper of Mind. Pulse Deep, shews a disposition to Melancholy, Asthma ’ s, Lethargy, ( fc. and is more frequent in the Aged than the Young. Pulse Leaping, is said to portend no great danger. Pulse Trembling, shews great Extremity. Pulse Wandring, is that which is sometimes felt in one place, and sometimes in another, and some - times no where, and is never but a few Minutes before Death.

pulsion.c: PULSION, is the driving or impelling of any thing forward. See Attraction.

pulverization.c: PULVERIZATION, is reducing any Body in - to a fine Pouder, which is done by beating Friable Bodies in a Mortar; but to Pulverize Malleable ones, or such as will spread under the Hammer, some other Helps and Artifices must be made use of. To Pulverise Tin and Lead, proceed thus r Get a round wooden Box, which rub well with Chalk all over on the inside; then melt the Metal, and pouring a little of it nimbly into the Box, fhuc the Lid, and shake the Box strongly and quick, and the Metal will be reduced by it into a Pou - der. And this is a very useful thing to know, thos it be plain and easie; because by this means, these Metals are rendred fit for several Operations, and will easily be mixed with Salts or other things.

pulvisfulminans.c: PULVIS Fulminans. Mix well together three Parts of common Salt - petre, two parts of Salt of Tartar, and one of common Brimiione, all finely pondered. Take half a Dram or a Dram of this Mixture, put it upon a Fire - shovel over a gentle Fire, so that it may hear, and appear to melt and change Colour gently, and in about half a quarter of an Hour it will go off with a terrible Noise, as great I PUR PUR great as that of a Musket, and yet without dan - ger to any Person in the Room for its force is chiefly downwards. The reason of this Effect ap - pears to be, that the Fixt Salt of Tartar doth so lock up the Spirits of the Nitre and Sulphur, that they cannot get loose without breaking their Pri - sons, which when the Fire hath assisted and enabled them to do, they do it with very great violence and noise.

pumpbrake.c: PUMP Brake, at Sea, is the Handle of the Pump, as

pumpcan.c: PUMP Can, is the Bucket whereby they pour Water into the Pump to fetch it and make it work when they intend to use it. And.

pumpvale.c: PUMP Vale, is the Trough by which the Water runs from the Pump along the Ship - fid es, that it may go out at the Scorer - holes.

punctumsaliens.c: PUNCTUM Saliens: In the growth of an Egg, you fee a little Speck or Cloud as it were in the innermost Tunic of it, called Amnios, which grow - ing gradually thicker, acquires a kind of slimy Mat - ter, in the middle whereof you fee first this Pun - Bum Saliens, ( a little e Speck thatfeemsto leap ) after - ward the rude body of an Embryo, which tends every day more and more to Perfection. Blanchard.

pupillaorpupula.c: PUPILLA, or Pupula is the opening of the Tu - nic of the Eye, called " Uvea, or Choroides it is round in a Man, and is capable of being contracted or dilated like a Muscle, according to the different degree of Light the eye is exposed to.

puppisvena.c: PUPPIS Vena, is that Vein which spreads it self about the hinder part of the Head.

purchase.c: PURCHASE: This word hath the fame fence at Sea as Draw has a - Shore; thus they fay, The Cap ft an Purchafes apace; that is, draws in the Ca - ble apace. And when they cannot draw or hale in any thing with the Tackle, they fay, The Tackle mill not Purchase.

purflew.c: PURFLEW; the term in Heraldy to express Ermines, Pean, or any of the Furrs when they com - pose a Bordure round a court of Arms. Thus they fay he Beareth Gules, a Bordure Purflew, Verry meaning that the Bordure is Verry.

pureation.c: PURE ATION, Purging, is an Excretory Mo -,, tion quick and frequent, proceeding from a quick and orderly Contraction of the Carneous Fibres of the Stomach and Intestines, whereby the Chyle and Excrements, and corrupted Humors, either bred or sent there from other Parts are protruded from Part to Part, till they be quite excluded the Body. Blanchard.

purgationinlaw.c: PURGATION, in Law, is the clearing of a Man ’ s self of a Crime whereof he is generally fuf - peated, and of the fame accused before the Judge; and is either Canonical or Vulgar. The Canonical, is that which is prescribed by Canon - Lam, the Form thereof is usually thus in the Spiritual Court: The Man suspended takes his Oath, that he is clear of the Fault objeCted, and brings so many of his honest Neighbours, being not above Twelve, as the Court ( hall assign him, to Swear upon their Conscience and Credulity, that he Sweareth truly. Vulgar Purgation, was by Fire or Water, or by Combat, used both by Infidels and Chriftians, till by the Canon Law abolished: But Combat may be still practised by the Laws of the Realm in Cau - fes doubtful, and where there is want of Evidence and other Proof, if the Defendant chuse rather the Combat than other Tryah

purification.c: PURIFICATION of a Metal, in Cymiltryv signifies its being purged or cleansed from the mix - ture of all other Metals. ' Tis chiefly used about Gold and Silver. The belt Purification of Gold, is by Antimony, in this manner: Put the Gold in a Crucible, make it red hot, and when it begins to melt,, pour upon it by degrees four times its weight of Antimony in Pow - der; the Gold will presently melt; continue a very strong Fire till you perceive the Metal to sparkle; then take the Crucible out of the Fire, and knock it, that the Gold may sink to the bottom; break it when ’ tis cold, and separate the fine Gold, Which is called the Regule, from the drossy Part. After this melt the Regule again over a strong Fire in a Crucible, and when it begins to melt, throw into it, by little and little, three times its weight of Salt - Peter continue a very strong Fire to keep the matter in constant Fusion; and when the Fumes are all gone, and the Metal appears. bright and clear, cast it into an Iron Mortar greased and warmed; or else if you don ’ t value the Crucible, leave it in that to cool, and break the Crucible be - fore ’ tis quite cold, and then separate the Regule from its Dross remaining at the top, the Gold will be very pure. There are several other ways of Purifying Gold, as the Depart and Cementation, which fee under those words: But this is the best of all. Red Gold is less valuable, as containing most Copper; the Yellow is better, and it should re - main Yellow while ’ tis in the Fire. Purif cation of Silver, is made in the Coppel thus: Heat the Coppel gently and by degrees, till it grow red hot, then cast into it four or five times as - much Lead as you design to Purifie Silver: The Lead will loon melt and fill the sides of the Cop -: el; then put the Silver into the midst of the mel - ted Lead, and it also will presently melt; then lay Wood all about and over the Coppel, and blow the Flame so thatit may reverberate on the Mat - ter, the Impurities of which, will by this means mix with the Lead, and the Silver will remain pure and unmixed in the middle of the Coppel; and the Lead, mixed with the Drossy Parts of the Silver, will lie on the sides like a Scum: This Scum is to be ta - ked off with a Spoon or other Instrument, and is what is called Litharge, which according to the degree of the Calcination it hath endured, is of di - vers Colours, and sometimes is called Litharge of Gold, and sometimes Litharge of Silver.

pursueorpurlieu.c: PURSUE, or Purlieu, from the French Pur, i e. Purus, and Lieu, i. e. Locus, is all that Ground near any Forest, which being anciently made Forest, is afterwards, by Perambulations, severed again from the fame, and exempted from that Servitude that was formerly laid upon it: And he that Walketh or Gourfeth within that Circuit, is not liable to the Laws and Penalties incurred by them which Hunt within the Precindts of the Forest.

purpuretheheraldsterra.c: PURPURE, the Heralds Terra for a Colour consisting of much Red and a little Black: And this Term is used in the Coats of all Persons below the degree of No - ble; but in the Coats of Noble - men, ’ tis called Amethifl; and in those of Sovereign Princes, ’ tis ’ Tis expressed in Engraving by Lines called Mercury. Lines drawn athwart the Escutcheon, beginning at the Dexter Point.

purseranofficer.c: PURSER, an Officer in a King ’ s Ship, who re - chives her Victuals from the Victualler, and is to take care that it be in good Condition, and well laid up and lowed: His Office is alio to keep a Lift of the Men and boys belonging to tfye Ship, and to fet down exactly the Days of each Man ’ s admittance into Pay, that so the Pay - Master or Treasurer of the Navy may issue out his Disburse - ments, and Pay Men off according to the Purfers Books.

puttocksorputtock.c: PUTTOCKS, or Puttock. Shrowds, are small Shrowds which go from the Shrowds of the Main - Mast, Fore malt, and Missen - Mast, to the Top - Malt Shrowds. And if there be any Top Gallant - Masts on the Top - Masts, there are Puttockj to go from the Top - Mast Shrowds into those. These Puttockj are at the Bottom seized to a Staff or to some Rope which is seized to a Plate of Iron, or to a Dead - man ’ s Eye, to which the Laniards of the Fore - Mast Shrowds do come.

pycnostyleinarchitecture.c: PYCNOSTYLE, in Architecture, is a Building where the Pillars Hand very close one to another, one diameter and a half of the Column being only allowed for the Inter calumniation.

pylorusorjanitor.c: PYLORUS, or Janitor, is the lower Orifice of the Ventricle, which lets the Meat out of the Sto - mach into the Intestines; Dr kVAlis calls the be - ginning of the Pylorus, where its Coats are thickest, the Antrum.

pyramidingeometry.c: PYRAMID, in Geometry, is a Solid Figure whose Base is a Polygon, and whose Sides are plain Triangles, their several Tops Meeting together in one Point. The So ' id Content of A Pyramid, is to f of the Perpendicular Al - titude multiplied by the Base; because a Pyra - mid is of a Prism of the fame Height and Base. e ii Eucl. which fee also proved under the Word Parallelepiped ( the fame with Prism J The superficial Area of a Pyramid, is found by adding the Area of all the Triangles, whereof the Sides of the Pyramid consist, into one sum: For, the whole external Surface ( except the Base ) of any Pyramid, is nothing but a System of as many Tri - angles, as the Pyramid has Sides. If a Pyramid be cut with a Plane Parallel to the Base, the Surface of that Truncated Pyramid com - pretended between the Parallel lanes, is found by SubftraCHng the Surface of the Pyramid cut off front the Surface of the whole Pyramid. Also, the external Surface of a right Pyramid, that stands on a regular Polygon Bale, is equal ter a Triangle, whose Altitude is equal to the Altitude of one of the Triangles which compose it, and its Base to the whole Circumference of the Base of the Pyramid. Whence therefore the Surface of a right Cones ( for a Cone is but a Pyramid of infinite Sides ) is equal to a Triangle, whose Height is the side of the Cone and the Base equal to the Circumference of the Base of the Cone.

pyramidalia.c: PYRAMIDALIA, are Vessels which prepare the Seed, of which in their proper Place. Also Mu - ffles of the Nostrils, and of the Abdomen, called Pyramidales, or of a Pyramidical Figure. Also two Strings of Marrow about the Basis of the oblong - ted Marrow.

pyramidalisjivesuccenturiatusmuf.c: PYRAMIDALIS, Jive Succenturiatus Muf cuius, one of the Muffles of the Abdomen, lying on the ReCtus, helping in conjunction with the reft, to compress the Abdomen, and to exclude its Con - tents: Mr. Cowper thinks it to have also a peculiar use in compressing the Bladder.

pyramidoid.c: PYRAMIDOID, is what is sometimes called d Parabolic Spindle and is a solid Figure formed by the Revolution of a Parabola round its Safe or greatest Ordinate and if you confider it according to the method of Indivisibles, you may conceive its Solidity to consist of an infinite series of Circles whole Diameters are all parallel to the Axis of the Revolving Parabola.

pyrifomisseuiliacuyexternus.c: PYRIFOMIS, Seu Iliacuy Externus, is a Mu - ffles of the Thigh which receives itsfirftName from its Figure, the second from its Situation; Its be - ginning is round and fleshy from the inferior and internal Part of the Os Sacrum, where it relpedts the Pelvis of the Abdomen, and descending obliquely in the great Sinus of the Os Ilium, above the Acute Process of the Ischium, and joining with the Glu - teus Medius, it ’ s inferred by a round Tendon to the superior Part of the Root of the Great Trochanter. This moves the Os Femoris somewhat upwards and turns it outwards.

pyrotechnick.c: PYROTECHNICK - ART, is the Art of Chymi - stry, so called from the Greek Tug Fire, and Tzyya Art because Fire is the chief Instrument the Chy - mist makes use of in the separating and collecting the purer Substances of mixt Bodies.

pyroticorvrentia.c: PYROTIC, or Vrentia, are Medicines vir - tually Hot, which being applied to humane Bodies, grow extreamly hot j because that having Particles and Pores so ordered, that Vapours and Humours insinuating into them, the subtil Matter finds such Passages, that it being moved extream violently, forces certain earthy, hard, and acute Particles, which float in the Passages upon the Neighbouring Parts with great Impetuosity, and so excites an Heat which corrupts or changes differently, accord - ding to the diversity of its Motion and the Particles, that are moved. Such are things that cause Red - ness, that Blister, that Ripen or Rot, that close up, and bring Wounds to a Crust, and that pull Hairs out of the Body. Blanchard.

pyrrichius.c: PYRRI CHIUS, is the foot of a Latin Verse consisting of two Syllables, and both short. PYTHA - r Q U A

pythagoreansyfiem.c: PYTHAGOREAN Syfiem, is the fame with the Copernican but is so called, as being maintained by Pythagoras and his Followers, and therefore is the most ancient of any. In this the Sun is suppo - fed at reft in the Centre of our System of Planets, and the Earth to be carried round him annually in a Track or Path between Venus and Mars. I still only add here an account how The Phenomena of Day and Night, and the ’ viciffitud. es of Seasons are accounted for, according to the Pythagorean System, where the Earth moves round the Sun. Let T & VS repreleht the Earth ’ s Annual Orbit Round the Sun at. The Plane of which Orbit if Infinitely produced among the Fixt Stars, will describe that Circle which we call the Ecliptic. In this Orbit, let the Earth be supposed to move from T to Q next to ir, and let the Earth be Represented by the Epicicles NAiESQN, in which N and are S the North and South Poles, and the Line N S the Earth ’ s Axis always keeping Parallel to it self; and M Q, the Equator, whole Plane is inclined to the Ecliptick With an Angle of ', which is the Complement of ', the Angle that the Earth ’ s Axis ( perpendicular to rhe Plane of the Equator ) makes with the Ecliptic. Suppose then the Earth in ( then will the Sun appear to be in Y, the first Point of its Annual Orbit ) and the Earth io turning it self to the Sun that the Axis of its motion may be Per endiculaf to a Line drawn from the Center of the Sun to that of the Earth, then will the Earth ’ s Equator appear Coincident with the Celestial Equinoctial j and will the Sun appear to be just in the middle between the two Poles, and to fend his Light equally towards both of them, and as far as both of them ( for the Sun always Illuminates one half of the Globe. ) Wherefore as that Hemisphere of it ( vi. TNLCP ) which is now turned to - wards him, is Enlightned, so the other ( behind ) is now supposed to be in Darkness. And fcecaufe the Earth revolves round its Axis N S in Hours,, which Axis is how at Right - Angles With the Line T G A connecting the Centres of the Earth and Sun. Every Point of the Equator JE ( S, and of the Tropicks T C and G P, and of all other Parallels to the Equator, will be as much in the Light as in the Dark in every Diurnal Revolution; and consequently the Days and Nights will be Equal, at that Time, all over the Earth. - But as the Earth moves further on in the Annual Orbit towards T and the Plane of the Terre - trial Equator will - be then no more direct to the Sun, but will Subside towards the South, and therefore the Sun will appear ro go as much to - ward the North Pole, and as it were from the Equator in the Heavens; for the Earth being ap Z patently QU A Parently at Reft, its Equator will be so too, and consequently the Celestial Equinoctial will appeal to change from its position by a diurnal Motion and the Sun will appear to move also, because it Changes its position in respect to the Equinoctial in the Heavens. And the Sun ’ s Light which be - fore reached just as far as the Poles N and S, will now go beyond N, and will fall as much short of S. But when the Earth is come to VS, the Sun then will appear to be in ?, where he will seem most of all to decline from the Equator towards the North, vi. as much as is the Angle of Inclination between the Plane of the Equator and that of the Ecliptick; and the Sun will then seem to move all Day in the Circle T C, which is a Parallel to the Equator, at distance, and is called the To - pick of. The Earth being thus posited, ’ tis ap - parent that the Sun ’ s Rays enligthning always one half of it will now reach beyond the Pole N, as far as L, and fall short of the Southern Pole S, by the Ark S M to L N to ' the Incli - nation of the Ecliptick to the Equator; and there - fore if lesser Circles are imagined to be there drawn on the Earth, they will be the Polar Circles as A L and M G: And ’ tis plain that that part of the Earth which lies between the Polar Circle A L and the Pole will enjoy perpetual Day, notwith - standing the Earch ’ s diurnal Motion, as the op - posited Part within the AntarClick Circle M G will be in continual Darkness. The Earth being thus in VS, and the G appearing in S, ’ tis plain also that of every Circleparallelto the Equator in the North - ern Hemisphere, the greatest Part or more than a Semicircle will be Illuminated; but from the E quator towards the South Pole, the greatest Part of every Parallel will be in Darkness: Wherefore in all Places lying to the Northward of the Equator, the Days will be longer than the Nights; that is, it will be Summer; as in the Southern Hemisphere the Nights will be longer than the Days, where it will be Winter and this in proportion to the Place s distance from the Equator: But to those who Live under the Equator, or the Line, ( as the Seamen call it ) the Days and Nights will be Equal now, and at all times of the Year. The Earth moving on in its Annual Orbit from VS into ) X, and so to T it will arrive at the other Equinoctial Point, and then the Sun will ap - pear to be in and all things will be the fame as when the Earth was in s, which hath been above deliver ’ d. The Earth going on in its Orbit from Q, to I and so to, the Sun will then appear to be in VS and consequently in the Winter Tropick, as we call it in reference to our Position toward the Sun: And now the state of things with us will be the Reverie of what it was when the Earth was in VS, our Nights will be longer than our Days, &c. as appears from the Figure; and it will fare with us Inhabitants of the Northern He - mifphere, in all refpedls, as it did then with the Inhabitants of the Southern.

Which Changes leem to be effected by the exhaling of the Moisture, which may leave the tinging Corpuscles more dense, and something also augmented by the Accretion of the Oily and Ear - thy Part of that Moisture. Now the Green is without doubt of the fame Order with those Co - lours into which it changes, because the Changes are gradual, and thele Colours, though ufuallynot very full, yet are often too full and lively to be of the fourth Order. . Blues and Purples may be either of the second or third Order, but the best are of the third., Thus the Colour of Violets seems to be of that Order, because their Syrup by Acid Liquors turns Bed, and by Urinous and Alkalizate turns Greens For since ’ tis the Nature of Acids to dissolve and attenuate, and of Alkalies to precipitate and in - cassate; if the Purple ' Colour of the Syrup was of the second Order, an Acid Liquor, by attend - ating its tinging Corpuscles, would change it to a Red of the first Order; and an Alkali, by incraf - fating them, would change it to a Green of the fe - cond Order: Which Red and Green, especially the Green, seem too immersed to be the Colours produced by these Changes. But if the said Pur - ple be supposed to be of the third Order; its Change to Red of the second, and Green of the third, may without any Inconveniency be allowed. If there be any Body of a deeper and less red - dish Purple than that of Violets, ’ tis probable its Colour is that of the second Order. The Blue of the first Order, though Very faint and little, may possibly be the Colour of some Substances; and particularly the Azure Colour of the Sky seems to be of this Order. For aft Va - pours, when they begin to condense and coalesce into small Parcels, become first of that Bigness whereby such an Assure must be refkded before they v: V. Whiteness, if most intense and luminous, is that of the first Order; if less strong and lum - nous, ’ tis a Mixture of the Colours of several Or - ders. The Ancient Britains seem to have had no such AfFemblies; but that the Saxons had something like it appears from King Inn ’ s Laws, who flourish ’ d An.. pariicles.c: PARI ICLES, are the very small parts of which any Natural Body is supposed to be compounded j and these are often called the Confiituent or Compo - next Particles of any Natural Body. That these are almost infinitely small, the continual Effluvia which some Bodies do continually emit, and this without any sensible diminution of their Bulk or Weight, as well as some other Experiments and Observations do plainly slew. But how to make any Conjecture at the several Sizes of these Component Particles of Bodies, whether they are all equal in Bulk, or which are greater and how much they are so, than others, is what Phi - lofophers have hardly yet had Data or Discoveries enough to determine. But the wonderful Sir If. Newton in his excellent Book of Optickj, hath o - pened a Door into this new World, and hath given some very good Rules whereby to guess at ' the Bigness of the Component Parts of Natural Bodies. For he having shewn in Prop.. Bock. r. Part. That the transparent parts of all Bodies do most probably exhibit the fame Colours with thin Plates of Glass or thin Bubbles of Water, and on the fame grounds; provided they are of the fame thickness and of the fame density with them. And since their Parts seem for the most part to have the fame density with Water or Glass, as by many Circumstances ’ tis obvious to collect. To determine the Sizes of those Parts, you need only have recourse to the Tables in the aforesaid Book for this purpose, in which the thickness of Water or Glass exhibiting any Colour is express ’ d. Thus if it be desired to know the Diameter of a Cor - muscle, which being of equal density with Glass, still reflect Green of the d order ( as he distil - guiihes it ) by looking into the Table, you will find that the Number i shews it to be - parts of an Inch. In the general he proves also, that the Parts of Bodies on which their Colours depend are denser than the Medium, which pervades their Interfiices. Prop,. B,. part, He He Hews also at the end of his Latin Opticas, That the Component Particles of all Bodies mull be hard or solid, or else Fluid Bodies could not congeal; which ’ tis certain that Water, Oyl, Vine - gar, and Spirit or Oyl of Vitriol will do by Cold Quicksilver by the Fumes of Lead; Spirit of Nitre and Quicksilver together by dissolving the Mer - cury and then evaporating the Flegm: Spirit of Wine, or Urine, by first well dephlegmating them, and then mixing them together; and the Spirit of “ Urine and of Salt, by subliming them together to make Sal Armoniack. Nay, the very Particles or Rays of Light seem to be hard Bodies, otherwise they could not in their different Sides have different Properties, as he hath shewn that they have ( fee Light. ) Hardness therefore ought to be accounted as the Property of all Am - ple Matter in the Universe; for all Bodies which we know, are either hard, or may be made so. And if there are many hard Bodies, as we know is the case of most, that have Pores interspersed, or Meatus placed between their Particles; those Par - titles themselves that are devoid of any luch Va - cities must needs be much harder. ’ Tis probable that the moil f, mall Particles of Matter do attrap one another and adhere toge - ther with the greatest force; and that these may combine into larger Particles, whose attracting force is weaker: and many of these latter covering together may form yet greater Particles of Bodies, whole attracting farce shall be yet weaker. And so on by a continual series, ’ till you come to the greatest of those Particles, on which the Chymical Operation;, and the Colours of Bodies depend ( fee Attraction and Colour ) and these covering into MafTes may form Bodies of sufficient magnitude to become perceptible by Sense. It hath been discovered of late by the wonderful Sir Isaac Newton, Mr. J. Veil of Oxon, and such others as have proceeded on his Principles: T hat there is a Power in Nature, by which each Particle of Matter attracts every other Particle with a Force that increafeth in a greater proportion than That by which the Squares of the Distance decree fe; viz. in a Reciprocal Triplicate or Quadruplicate Ratio of the Distance s: For, were it not so, the attradion of these small Particles would not be much greater at the Point of ContaCl, than at some determinate di - stance from it; as is evident in the case of the Gra - city of greater Bodies, whose power of attradion is only reciprocally as the Square of the Distance; for we find that Bodies are of the fame weight, when at the Earth ’ s Surface, or when at ioo Feet distance. But when a little Salt is dissolved in a large quantity of Water, there is no attradion of the Particles towards one another, till by evapo - rating part of the Water, they are brought within a due distance; and then they presently run to - wards one another, unite, and form Chrystals, whose Parts have a strong Cohesion. ( See Attracti - on in thisko /, ) ’ Tis plain also, that the Attractive Force in these Particles is ( csteris paribus ) proportionable to their Solidity; for it must be compounded of the Sumrns of all the Parts of each Particle, and thole Parts will be most numerous in such Particles as are most solid; i. e. in such as have feweft and least Pores or Interstices between their Parts. For Particles or Corpuscles may be so compounded, that the most solid and compad Particles may constitute the lighcell Corpuscle: That is, if the interspersed Vacuities between the Particles of Matter be large ) lo that few of them may be diffused thro ’ a large Space. And such a Corpuscle, tho ’ consisting of Parts endued with a strong attradive power, may yet be Tpecifxcally lighter than another, which may con - lift of Particles not so solid; but yet much closer put together. And because this Natural Philosophy of Particles is of the greatest use to be fully understood, I stall here give you ( from Dr. Keil ’ s Book, of Animal Se - creation, &c. ) some further Propositions about this matter. I fay then, That if any Particles of Matter attraCt each other with a Force that is in a Triple case or yet greater Reciprocal Proportion of their Di - fauces: The force by which a Corpuscle is drawn to a Body, made up of such Attractive Particles, is in - finitely greater at the ContaCt, or extreamly nearer it, than at any determined distance from it. Prop. VI. A large Particle attraBs not more strongly than a ftfnall one of the fame Solidity, but a diversity of Figures causes different Degrees of At tra - ct ion in Particles, that are otherwise the fame. This attradive Power ads only on such Particles as are extremely near and therefore of a large Particle, the remotest parts conduce nothing to At - tradion: and for the fame Reason the attradive Force varies, according as the Particles are Cones, Cylinders, Cubes, or Spheres: and cateris paribus a Spherical Particle has the strongest attradive Power. Prop. VII. If Particles swimming in a Fluid, at - traB one another more strongly than they do the Par - titles of the Fluid, the Force, by which they come to each other, will be that by which their attractive Force exceeds the attracting Force of the Fluid. For the Particles of the Fluid, that lie di redly between the attrading Particles, being more pores - fed than the other ambient Particles they will from the Nature of Fluidity, with that excess of Pressure, drive the other Particles out of their places, and make way for the attrading Particles to come together Prop VIII. If Particles swimming in a Fluid are more attraBed by the Fluid, than by one another, they will recede from one another, with a Force that will be equal to the difference of their mutual Attra - Bion, and the AttraBion of the Fluid. For the Ambient Particles of the Fluid attrading more strongly, will with their excess of Force draw the other Particles to themselves and make them to recede from one another. Prop. IX. The Force, by which Particles attraBing one another cohere, is greater, ceteris paribus, where the ContaB is greater. For the parts that are farther remove ’ d from the Contact, conduce nothing to the Force of the Co - lesion j and a greater Power must be requisite to separate two Particles, which cohere in twopoinrs, than two Particles which cohere only in one point if the Degree of Cohesion be equal in each point. Thus two polished Marble - stones ( suppose a Foot square ) adhere more strongly than any other two Bodies of a Foot square, which are not so solid, but have more Pores and Interstices between their Parts, and which will not receive so good a polilh, by which the parts come to a close contact with one another. Prop. X. If the attraBing Corpuscles are elaftieg, they must necessarily produce an intestine Motion, greater or lejftcr, according to the Degrees of their E - elasticity and attraBive Forces. For after meeting they will fly from one ano - ther with the fame Degree of Velocity ( abating the resistance of the Medium ) that; they met together with but when they approach other Particles ia their RefiJition, their Velocity must increase, be - cause they are afresh attraded, and therefore meet - ing a second time, they will recede with a greater Velocity than they did at their first Concurfion: and so their Velocities will be increas ’ d By every Concurfion and Resilition, which must necessarily produce a sensible intestine Motion and the stronger their attradive Force, and the greater their Elaftieity, their Concurfions and Refiiitions will be the more sensible. XL Particles attracting one another in a Fluid, moving either with a swift or flow progressive Motion, attruEl one another just the fame, as if the Fluid was at reft, if all the Particles move equally hut an unequal Velocity of the Particles does migh - tily disturb their Attractions. The Parades do all by Hypothesis move equal - ly, and consequently the progressive Motion of the Fluid does not alter their distances, that is to fay, it does not repel them from one another; and con - sequently they must attraeft one another with the fame Facility, as if the Fluid was at reft. And therefore according to the several Degrees or Quantities oi xz Contact ot Particles, there will arise several degrees of the firmness or cohesion of Bodies. And the greatest force or degree of Co - helion, will be when the Surfaces of the covering Particles are perse & ly plane; for there the Force by which any Corpulcle adheres to another, will ( cater is paribus ) be as the Parts of the Superficies which do adhere to, or touch One another. And from hence, and I believe hence only ? can that hitherto difficult Problem, about the Cause of the Cohesion of the Parts of Matter in solid and firm Bodies be solved. . Those Corpuscles or Particles of Matter are most easily sep arable one from another, whof'e Contacts with other Particles are sewel and leaf; as will be the case of exceeding Particles of a Spherical Figure. And from hence, and hence only, can the True and Primary Reason of Fluidity arise. Mr. J. Keil of Oxford in Phil. TranfaCl. iV.. advances these other Theorems about the small Particles of Matter. i. That the leaf Particle of Matter assignable, may so fill any large assigned Space, that the Diameters of the Pores, Int erf ices, or Meatus between its Parts may he all less than any given Bight Line; or, so that all the Parts of such a Particle, shall be nearer to each other than any given Bight Line. See his LeClure de Divifibilitate Materice, in his LeCliones Physica. . Two Bodies may be assigned or given equal in Bulk., but yet any how unequal in SpecificfiGravity, or in the Quantity of Matter in each so that the Summs of the Pores or Meatus in each, Shall be nearly e - qual. V. gr. Let there be a Cubick Inch of Gold and another of Air: Tho ’ the Quantity of Matter in the former may be times as great as that in the latter: Yet the Vacuities in the Gold, may be to those in the Air, as to i. e. very nearly equal. . Those Particles which constitute Water, Air, or any other Fluid ( if they touch one another ) are not absolutely solid; but are compounded of other Par - titles, which do contain within them many Pores or Vacuities. And he thinks that such Particles of Matter as are the leaf of all others, andjwhich are perse & ly solid and devoid of all interspersed Vacuities, may be called The First or Primary component Particles of Matter, or Particles of the first Composition. Such MolecuU as are compounded by the Coa - lefcence of many of these first Particles ( only ) may be called Particles of the d, Composition. And such Moles as are compounded of these second Mo - recule by several of them coalescing together may be called Particles of the third Composition: And so on till you come to Particles out of which the last Composition of Bodies is made, and into which they are primarily dissolved. a. If a Particle of Matter pouch any Body, the Force with which it tends toward the Body, or by which it adheres to it, is proportionable to the Quan - tity of the Contact, for such Particles as lie remote . If the Texture of a Body be such, that its Pari, tides of the last Composition ( fee Prop.. J can be moved a little from their primary flats of Cohesion or ContaPl by some external force ( such as the weight and ccmprejfure, or thefiroke or shock, of feme other Body. ) But yet so as that the Particles of the Body don ’ t by this pressure or stroke, run into any new Contacts or Cohefions Then, I fay, they will recover again their former Contacts, by the power of Attraction, or by a Force ' that will make them tend towards one a - nother: And consequently - such a Body, will, after the pressure or firefe, recover again its former Figure and Position of its Particles. And this is the reason of the Elaflicity of Bodies . But if the Texture of a Body be such, that when its Particles are by feme external Force removed from their former CcntaBs and Cohefions, they go im - mediately into others of the fame degree that Body cannot recover its former Figure and Position of Parts. And this is the Texture of such Bodies as are soft, and herein the Reason of their softness con - fists. . As Particles which are perfectly solid will at - tract one another the most strongly; and as in all other Particles the power of their Attraction is pro - portionable to their Density or Solidity - so the at - tractile forces of even Particles perfectly Dense or Solid, depend much upon their Figures. For if a ( mall Particle of Matter be supposed to be formed into an indefinitely small Plate or Lame - na, of a Figure perfectly circular; and if another Particle of Matter be supposed to be in a Right Line passing through the Centre of that Plate, and at Right Angles to its Plane: Then if you suppose that Particle to be distant from ! the circular Plate a tenth part of the Radius of that Circle; I fay, the Force by which that Corpuscle is attrap & ed by the Plate is times less than if the attracting Matter had coalesce into a Spherical Figure: So that the Virtue of the whole Particle had been dis fused, as it we re from one Physical Point. But yet this circular Plate will more strongly at - tract the Particle than any other Particle of the fame weight with it, that shall be formed into a long and slender Cylinder . Salts . Salts are Bodies, whose Particles of the - last Composition are endowed with a very great attractive force: But yet between those Particles, there are very many Pores or Meatus, which are pervious to the Par - titles of the laji Composition of Water; which Aque - ous Particles being strongly attracted by the Saline ones, do rush towards them with an Impetuosity, do disjoin their mutual ContaCt, and dissolve their Co - lesion, i o. A Body fpecificully heavier than Water, may have its Magnitude so diminished, that it shall be suspended by or swim in Water, and not descend by its own weight. And this is the reason that the small Particles of Salts and Metals will swim in such Menstruums as will dissolve those Metals, &c. , Greater Bodies attraCt one another with a less force than Lesser ones do. For the Force with which the Bodies A and B attraCt one another, exerts it self only in thole Par - titles which are neat one to another, the remote ones having no such force; wherefore there is no greater Attractive Force required to move the Bo - dies A and B towards one another, than to move c and d. But the Velocity of Bodies moved by the fame Force, are reciprocally proportional to those Bodies: Wherefore the Velocity by which A tends towards B, will be to the Velocity with which the Particle c, apart from the Body, tends towards B:: as the Particle c to the Body A much less therefore is the Velocity of the Body, than that of c would be, if it were separated from it. From hence it comes to pass that the Motion of the Greater Bodies is naturally so flow and gentle, that ’ tis usually impeded by an Ambient Fluid or other Bodies round about them. But in Lesser Bo - dies, this Attractive Force is very alive and vi - gorous, and is the cause of a great many Noble EffeCts. . Two Particles of Matter thd, they do not touch, may yet come so near one to another, as that their mutual AttraEiive Force shall much exceed the Force of Gravity. . If a Particle placed in a Fluid be equally at - tracted every where by all the ambient Particles of the Fluid, no motion of the Particle will arise from thence: But if it be attracted by some Particles more, and by others less, it will move that way, where the Attraction is greatest, and the Motion produced will be answerable to the Inequality of the Attraction j ( i. e. ) it will be greater, where there is a greater In - equality, and lesser, where there is less. . If a Body be placed in a Fluid, and its Par - tides do more attract the Particles of the Fluid, than the Particles of the Fluid do one another and if there be also in that Body any Pores or Meatus, per - vious to the Particles of the Fluid then the Particles Vel. XL of the Fluid will soon disuse them / elves thro ’ those Meatus: and if the Cchejion or Connection of the parts of the Body be not so strong, but that it may be surmounted by the Impetus of the Particles of the Fluid rushing upon it, and every way into its Pores; there will arise from thence a Dijfolution of that Body. And from hence you may see the Reason of the Dissolution of Bodies in Menstruums In order to which, Three things are always necessary: . That the Particles of the Body to be dissolved, do more strongly attraCt those of the Menstruum, than those of the Menstruum do one another. . That the Bodies have Pores pervious to the Particles of the Menstruum. . That the Cohesion of the Constituent Par - titles of the Body be not so strong, but that it may be broken by the violent aCtion of the Particles of the Menstruum upon it. . If Particles mutually attracting each other do also mutually touch one another, no Motion can arise for they can come ho nearer to each other; But if the / are separated from one another a very small distance, a Motion must arise from their mutual Attraction. Tho ' if they are farther from one another than that they cannot attraCt one another more than they will the Particles of the Fluid in which they are, and so no Motion also will be produced. From these Principles all the Phenomena of Fer - tentation, and of all Ejfervefcences do proceed. And from hence you may see the Reason why Oyl of Vitriol when mingled with a little Water, hath so great an Effervescence and Ebullition: For by the Infusion of the Water the Saline Particles are a little disjoined from their mutual ContaCt; but flee they do much more attraCt one another than they do the Particles of the Water, and fincethey are not every way equally attracted a considerable Motion must from thence arise. And from hence also you may see the Reason why so great an Ebullition arises from putting Fi - lings of Steel or Iron into the former mixture of Oyl of Vitriol with a little Water; for the Par - titles of the Steel have a very great degree of E - Iafticity, and from thence a strong Inflection must arise. And from hence also ’ tis that some Men - ftruums ad with a greater force and will sooner dissolve Metals, when mingled with a little Water, than when pure and without such mixture. . If the Particles which do mutually attraCt each other have no Elasticity, then they are not Reflected each, from one another, but will form Congeries, Moleculas, Aggregates or Lumps of Particles from whence what we call a Coagulation arises: And if these Lumps exceed in Specifick k. Gravity that of the Fluid, and are large enough, a Precipitation will succeed. T ho ’ a Precipitation may also arise from the Specifick k. Gravity of the Menstruum in which the Par - titles swim, its being diminijked or increased . If the Figure of Particles mutually attracting each other, when swimming in a Fluid be such, that there is a greater Attracting Force in some of their given Parts than in others, as also a greater ContaCt there; then these Particles will coalesce into Bodies having given Figures; and this way all Chryftalli - nations arise; and you may by Geometry determine the Figures of the Component Particles from having the Figure of the Chrystals given. H a. if PEE ' PER . If between two Particles of a Fluid, another foall interpose, whose two opposite Faces or Sides, have very great attractive Forces; this interpofmg Particle will glew or fafien the other two to it self: and when this is done throughout the whole Fluid, that Fluid Will be frozen or turned into Ice. . If a Body of some Bulk, emit a large quantity of Effluvia, and the Particles of such Effluvia have a very great attracting force; then will these Effluvia, when they come near any lesser or lighter Body, by their attracting force, surmount the Gravity of those Bodies, and lift them up to the Bodies from whence they flow: and since the Effluvia are much more copious and thick, at lesser distances from the E - mii tent Body, than at greater the light Body will be attracted by fill more and more dense Effluvia, and at last be brought to adhere to the Emittent Body. And this way most of the Phenomena of Electri - city may be solved.

pennydenarius.c: PENNY, Denarius, was the first coined piece of Silver we have any account of; and for many Years the only one. In the Reign of H. r. there were Half - pence. Dr. FUcky in his Diff rrtatio Epifiolaris, p. o. faith, that the Anglo - Saxons had but one Silver Coin amongst them, and that was a Penny; and Cambden and Spelman, and most of our good An - tiquaries agree in this. The old Penny before was struck with, a double Cross, so that it might easily be broken in the middle, or into four Quarters; and so made into Halfpence or Far - things, faith Mr. Stow; on which it was then or - dered, that Half - pence and Farthings should be made or coined round, as the Penny was before. The Penny was called Sterling, which lee.

perpetualmotion.c: PERPETUAL Motion by this Term ought to be meant an uninterrupted Communication of the fame degree of Motion from one part of Matter to another, in a Circle ( or such like Curve returning into it self ) so that the fame Quantity of Matter shall return perpetually undiminished upon the first mover: And perhaps if Men had rightly under - stood that this is the true meaning of a perpetual Motion, abundance of Expence both of Money and Reputation might have been saved, by thevain pre - tenders to this piece of impossible Mechanism. For flee by the second Law of Nature or Motion, ( fee Motion ) The changes made in the Motions of Bo - dies are always proportional to the impress s ’ d moving force, and are produced in the fame direction with it, no Motion can be communicated to any Engine or Vol. II. Machine greater than that of the first force impress - fed and therefore since on our Earth, all Motions are performed in a Fluid which refills them, it must of necessity retard them and consequently a con - fiderable quantity of the Motion must be spent up - on the refilling Medium so that ’ tis impossible the fame Quantity of it can return undiminished on the first mover which yet is absolutely necessary for the continuance of the fame Motion perpetually. Besides, in no Engine or Machine whatsoever, can all Friclicn be avoided, there being in Nature no such thing as exadl Smoothness or perfect Congrui - ty: The manner of the Cohesion of the parts of Bodies, the small proportion the solid Matter bears to the Vacuities between them, and the nature of those constituent Particles not admitting it where - fore this FriEHon will also sensibly in time diminifli the impressed or communicated Force, so ’ tis not possible the Motion can be perpetual which Ef - sect can indeed never follow, unless the commu - nicated Force be so much greater than the gent - rating Force, as to recompense the Diminution made therein by all these Causes, in order to the Motions returning undiminished upon the first Mover. But nil dat quod non habet, the genera - ting Force cannot communicate a greater degree of Motion, that it hath it self, and consequently the perpetual Motion is demonstratively impossible. Besides, it being certain that a Body cannot move constantly in any Orbit with the fame de - gree of Motion from one single Impulse since that degree of Motion and Velocity arising from such a single Impulse must by that means continually de - crease, and so at Iaft be quite spent and extineft: From hence it will follow alio, that there can he no Perpetual Motion in any Engine from one single Impulse for this Motion, that it may return a - gain upon the first Mover, must be propagated ia an Orbit and consequently must by degrees cease and flop.

plowanancientinstrument.c: PLOW, an Ancient Instrument, tho ’ now not much used at Sea, mentioned in the former Vo - lame; and its Description is thus given by Sir Jo - nas Moor in his Navigation. There is first a Staff, as A L G, on which a small Arch, as H I, and a Cross, as E F are fitted together with three Vanes; as A an Horizon - Vane, B a Shade - Vane, and C a Sight - Vane which is moveable upon the Staff By this Theorem all the Chances at Hazard may easily be Calculated. plebanus.c: PLEBANUS, was sometimes the Title of a Rural Dean, because the Deanaries were formerly affixed to the Plebanire, or chief Mother Churches within such a District, which at first was usually Ten Parifhes. Sometimes it seems to have been used for a Parish - Priest of such a large Mo - ther Church as was exempt from the Jurifdicti - on of the Ordinary, and therefore he had the Au - thority of a Rural Dean committed to him by the Archbishop, to whom the Church was ime - diately subject. In order to make an Observation of the Sun's Altitude with this Instrument, you must fit on the Horizon Vane, and then you may place the Shade - Vane to any degree of Altitude in the Divi - signs of the Arch, so it exceed not the Altitude to be observed, nor be above io Degrees ( " which a little practice will soon enable you to guess readily at: ) for in both these Cafes the Divisions on the Staff are deficient. Then put on the Sight - Vane, hold up the Instrument, and turn the Back of the Arch to the Sun, and move the Sight - Vane on the Staff backwards and forwards, till the Shade of the upper Edge of the Shade - Vane fall on the upper part of the Slit of the Horizon - Vane; and that at the fame time, looking thro ’ the Sight - Vane, you can see the Horizon thro ’ the Horizon - Vane for then will the Summ of the Degrees on the Arch and on the Staff be the Altitude, allowing for the Height above the Horizon and for R efraction. - For the Height above the Horizon they usually allow or Minutes.

polene.c: POLE NE, was a kind of Shooe with a pick - ed Point turned up at the T oe: These first came into fashion in the Reign of William Rufus, and by degrees came to be of that excessive length, J that in Richard the Second ’ s Time, they were ty ’ d up to the Knees with Silver or Gold Chains, ac - cording to the Dignity of the Wearer. They were forbidden by Edward the Fourth, in the fifth Year of his Reign, under a great Penalty, to be worn so very long; but they were not quite disused till the Reign of Henry the Eighth.

ponton.c: PONTON: The late Invented Fenton is a Boat of T in or rather Latten, eight Yards long and two broad, having a large Ring at each Cor - ner: When the Army marches it is laid on a Carriage, and drawn by five Horses. Each Boat hath an Anchor, and Cable, and Baulfs, and Chejis belonging to it. The Baulks are leven Yards long and about five or fix Inches lquare: The Chests are Boards joined together by Wooden Bars about a Yard broad and four Yards long. When these Pontons are to be used, they are flipp ’ d into the Water, and placed about two Yards a - sunder, having a strong Rope running through the Rings, which is fastened on each side the River you would pass over, to a Tree, Stake, &c. The Baulks or Beams are laid across the Boats at a due distance, and the Chests upon them; and these are joined close to make a Bridge, over which Foot, Horse, and even a Train of Artillery may pass.

portaorvenaporta.c: PORTA or Vena Porta: Dr. Keil in Animal Se - creation, p.,, &c. thinks that he hath found out the true Use of this Vein, ( of which you have a large Description in Vol. I. under Vena Porte ) which is, that the Bile being to be mixed with the Chyle as it comes out of the Stomach into the Duo - denum, could no where be so conveniently secern - ed from the Blood, as where the Liver is placed: But if all the Branches of the Caliacl Artery car - ried all the Blood to the Liver, from which the Gall was to be separated; it is evident, confide - ring the nearness of the Liver to the Heart, and the intestine motion of the Blood, that so viscid a Secretion as the Gall is, could never have been formed in the Blood, and consequently could ne - ver have been secreted by any Gland in that place. In this case Nature is forced to alter her constant method of fending the Blood to all the parts of the Body by the Arteries. Here he forms a Vein, ( which is no Branch of the Cava, as all the others are ) and by it file fends the Blood from the Branch - es of the Mefenterick and Creliack Arteries, ( after it hath passed thro ’ all the Intestines, Stomach, Spleen, Call, and Pancreas ) to the Liver. By this extraordinary Contrivance the Blood is brought a great way about before it arrives at the Liver; and its Celerity is extremely diminifiied; fq that all the Corpuscles which are to form the Bile, may have sufficient time to attract one another, and unite before they come to their Secerning Vessel. And thus, faith sse, have we found out the true Use of the Porta; which he confirms afterwards, by hewing what Nature doth further in profecu - iron of the fame Design; in increasing the Cavities of all the Arteries as they divide, and that as. the Trunk of the Mefenterick Artery bears a lesser proportion to its Branches than the Aorta does to its Branches; so the Branches of the Mefenterick Artery are likewise less in proportion to their Con - jugate Veins than the Aorta is to the Vena Cava. The descending Trunk of the Aorta below the E - emulgents is to the Vena Cava at the fame place. PO Sa PS to r. But a Branch of the Mefenterick Artery is to its corresponding Branch of the Port a as to z i and therefore the Blood in the Bran - j ches of thS Porta moves above times Slower than it does in the Trunk of the Mefentericlg Artery, and then only upon the Account of the Increase of the Diameters of the. Vessels. So necessary is it to abate the Rapid Intestine motion of the Blood which would otherwise hinder the CoalefcencS of I the Particles for the formation of the Ball.

precontract.c: PRECONTRACT, is a contra, ( usually un dies as Refled and Refrad it: and if it consisted, in an Instantaneous Motion, or one propagated to all distances, in an Instant; as some have advan - ced j there would be required an Infinite vis or Force, to produce that motion, every moment, in every Lucent Particle. And if Light confined either in Pressure, or in Motion propagated in a Fluid Medium, whether instantaneously or in Time, it must from thence come to pass, that it should infled it self in umbram. For Pressure or Motion in a Fluid Medium cannot be propagated in Right Lines, beyond any Obstacle which fiiail hinder any part of the Motion; but will infled and disuse ic self every way into those Parts of the Quiefcens Medium which lie beyond the said Obstacle. Thus the Force of Gravity tends downward, but the Pressure, which arises from that Force of Gra - city tends every way with an Equable Force: and with equal Ease and Force, is propagated in Crook - ed Lines as in Straight. Waves on the Surface of Water while they Aide by the sides of any Large Obstacle, do infled, dilate and diffuse themselves by degrees, into the Quiescent water lying beyond the Obstacle. The waves, Pulses, or Vibrations of our Air in which sounds consist, do manifestly infled themselves, tho ’ not so much as the waves of water; for the Sound of a Bell or of a Cannon, cao be heard over a Hill, which intercepts the Sono - rous object from our Sight; and Sounds will be propagated as easily thro ’ Crooked Tubes, as thro, Straight: But Light isneverobferved to go in Curve ’ Lines nor to infled it self in Vmbram. For the fixed Stars do immediately disappear on the In - terpofition of any of the Planets, as well as some parts of the Suns Body, by the Interposition of the Moon, Venus or Adercury.
