printing.c: PRINTING. There is a dispute between the Towns of Harlem in Holland, and Ment in Ger - many, about the Invention of this Noble Art. The Harlemers fay that Laurents Jarirs Rafter of Harlem was the first Inventer of Printing, A. D.. But that at first he used only wooden Blocks or Plates, ( ' like those used in China, and some other Eastern Countries, where that kind of Printing hath been much longer in use, and perhaps gave the first hint to our manner of Printing now in ute; ) tho ’ after some time he left those off, and cut Sin - gle Letters in Steel, which he Sunk into Copper Matrices, and fitting them to Iron Molds, c & fk Sin - gle Letters of Metal in these Matrices. They fay also that his Companion John Gutten - burgh Stole his Tools away while he was at Church, and with them went to Ment in Germany: where letting his Stolen Instruments to work, he claim ’ d the first Invention of this Art before Rafter did his. To prove this they fay that one Babbi Joseph a Jew, in his Chronicle mentions aTrinted Book that he saw at Venice in the Year according to the Jewish Account and of ours,. as may be seen in Pet. Scriverius. But notwithstanding all this, and also what they fay further of a Book entitled De Spiegel, which they slew Printed at Harlem in Dutch and Latin, tho ’ without Date, but they pretend it to be the first that ever was printed, notwithstanding this says Moon, Guttenburgh of Ment is more generally taken for the first Inventer of Printing, than Rafter of Harlem. Dr. Wallis faith, This Art was first Invented about the Year, and was pra & ifed in Germany im - mediately, but whether first at Ment or Harlem he determines not. He faith the Book which bears the Repute of being the first that ever was Printed, is Fully s Offices which was printed in the Year or; for the Copy of it in the Bodleian Library in Oxon disagree a Year with that in the Library of C. C. College there. In that Book in the Bodleian Library, is a note written which menti - ons one Johannes Fauftus, as Co - adjutor to Gutten - burgh, as also Peter Scheffer on the fame account and this Scheffer, Job. Arnoldus in Libello De Chal - cographies Inventione, makes the Inventer of the Matrices. Thele three work ’ d together a while, and then parted. There is also another note written, in a later hand, in the said Book, which refers the first Inven - tion of Printing to the Year: but most to the Year above mentioned by Dr. Wallis, vis;.. Next to these Places of Ment and Harlem, it seems to have been practised first at our Univer - fity of Oxon in England: For R. H.. and Thomas Bourchier then A. B. of Canterbury sent William Tur - ner Master of the Robe, and William Caxton Mer - chant of London, over to Harlem to learn this Art, who privately prevailed with one Frederic. Corf eles, ( an Under Workman ) for a Sum of Money to come over hither who did so, and at Oxford fet up the Art of Printing, before it was used any where else, except in Merits ' and Harlem. And there is a Treatise, said to be of S, Jerom, ( because found in his / orks ) but in Reality of Ruffinus on the Creed, Printed at Oxon in a Broad Odla - vo, in the Year. which is but years after the Edition of Tallies Offices at Menty and per - haps is one of the first Books Printed on Paper, for that of Tally was on Vellum. Soon after this Cax - ton ( who first brought it, as is supposed, to Oxford ) promoted it to London: which Baker in his Thro - nice faith was about: But Moon in his Arc of Printing faith he had not been any Books printed at London bestor: about which time it was received in Italy, Germany, &c. In Philof. TranfaBions, N. and so. There is this further Account of the Rife and Progress of the Art c - f Printing, Boxhornius, Schrevelius, and other Authors, fay. That Roster could not nor did he in fatft Print so large a Book as the Speculum Salutis, without Gra - dual Improvements and his first Elfays were on Small and loose leaves of Paper before he attempt - ed whole Books. In the Bodleian Library at Oxford, are two Books, and in that of Benet Col. in Cambridge ft another very ancient Printed Book Printed only on one Side of the Paper the whole wrought, or Call on Wood, not Set or Composed with Printing Letter, and Printed with Writing Ink. ', which do Sufficiently shew that they were done when this Art was in its Infancy, and are very probably the work of Roster: but they are without date or Prin - ters Name. Roster had an Assistant, whose Name was John Fuji / or as Some write him Fauft or Fauftus from whom he took an oath of Secrecy, as Schrevelius tells us But Fuji tan away with Roster s " fools and Mater - als, & in some Time fet up a Printing Preis at Ment, where he was assisted by his servant John Scheffer, a Young Man of a good Genius, and who after - wards Married his Daughter and became his Part - ner. They tell a Story also of Suff ’ s going to Paris, but whether before or after he Settled at Menrg, ft uncertain, and offering there a great N umber of Prin - ted Bibles to Sale, as if they were Manufcripts I But the French considering the. Number of these Books, and their exact Conformity one to another thro ’ out the whole, to a Line, a word. a Letter, nay even to a Point and that the belt of Book - writers could not be thus exaeft, forced the Secret out of S K him P R I P R I him, by either a & ually Indi & ing him for a Ma - gician, or threatening him at least so to do: and j this ’ tis laid gave the Rife to the Story of Dr. Say - ' ftus. And ’ tis probable about this time many Printed Books were fold up and down for Manuscripts. ’ Tis not certain in what Year Fuji and Scheffer began first to work at Ment. But Schrevciius faith Fauftus, ( as he calls him ) printed Aiexandri Doblrinale cum Petri Hifpani TraBatibus, A. D.. And Lambecius in Comment, de Biblioth. C ef. Lib.. p.. faith, that he brought from Infpruclgxo the Imperial Library at Vienna, a Pf al - ter printed on Parchment, by Fuji and Scheffer. And soon after this Date many Books were Prin - ted, which are still in Being: as the Durandus in the Library of Basil, Printed. Johannis John - nenfis Catholicon, in her Majefties Library, Prin - ted. The Latin Bible of in the French Kings Library, all before the Tallies Offices above mentioned: which was not printed till or. The first Book Printed here in England, was the Ruffinm Printed at Oxford, as was said before. But they Pradlifed the Art earlier in other Countries: and in Particular it was used at Pome in the Palace of the Maximi, A. D. by Conrad Sweynheim and Arnold P anti art both Germans, and who continued Printers there many years after, as Martinellus in his Rotme Sacra af - firms. Some think that Paper, fmadehf Linen Rags ) was first made at Basil, by some Greeks who fled out of their Country after Constantinople was fackt, A. D.: and this in Imitation of the Gotten Paper used in the Levant. Certain it is the Cotten Paper hath been of very ancient use in the East; there being in the Bodleian Library an Arabick Manuscript ( among those the University bought of Dr. Huntingdon ) written in the th. year of the Hegira which is A. D., on this Paper; and some there are without Dates which seem order. And as for the Linen Rag - Paper it must be - touch order than: for in the Archives of the Library of the Dean and Chapter of Canterbury, there is an Inventory, on our Paper, of the Goods of Henry Prior of Chrijls Church there, that is in the th year of Ed.. which is A. D.. and. in. the Cotten Library are several writings, on our Pa - per, as high at least as the th. of Ed.. Some think the Rolling Press was invented by Lipfius; But there is a Printed Book in the Bod - lean Library, ( placed Laud. p. ) being a Assis - sale Secundum ufum Ecclef. Herbipolenjjs, ( i. e. Wurtffurgh ) in Germany. At the beginning of this Book is an Instrument of Rodulfus the A. B. of this Church, containing the Reasons of the Publi - cation of this Miffale, and instead of a Seal there is annexed a Print engraven of the Arms of the See, &c. very finely done ( for that Time, for ’ twas be - fore Durer ) and on which are Evident Marks of the Pressure by the Plate, with some touches of Ink at the Edges, &c. which all that have seen it judge to be plain marks of its being done or wrought off in a Rolling Press. And there are sufficient Reasons to prove that this Book is as ancient as. Mr. Bagford thinks we had not the first hint of Printing from the Chinefes of whom we had no knowledge hardly, when this Art was invented: But rather from Old medals, Seals, cc. and the Letters on them. But if it be certain, as it seems to be, that Cards are as old as H.. nothing seems to give a better hint to the Invention of Printing than Card - making, as is evident by the first Spe - cimen of Printing at Harlem; and by those Books above mention ’ d in the Bodleian Library, and that of Benet College in Cambridge. The cutting of the Molds or Blocks for making our Playing Cards, is after the fame manner as that of the Old Books first printed at Harlem. They lay a Sheet of wet or moist paper on the Form or Block, being first lightly brushed over with Ink made of Lamp Black mixt with Starch and Water Then they rub it off with a round lift with their hand, which is done with great Expedition. They colour the Court Cards by the help of several Pat - terns or Stanefiles as they call them; being Card Paper cut thro ’ with a Penknife for every colour, as Red, &c. ( for at The first Printing, the Card hath only a Meer out - line. ) These Patterns are pain - ted with Oil - Colours to keep them from wearing out by the Brufhes: for they lay it upon the Pidlure, and by Aiding a Brush that is full and loose over the Pattern, it fixes the Colour into the Cut - holes, and leaves it on the Print that is to be a Card: and so they go thro ’ with all the Colours on the Cards: This very probably was the way of their first Printing at Harlem as might have been discovered before this; if they had considered that the Great Letters, in our Old M. SS. ( of years old ) are done by the Illuminators, after this of Card - making. T he next form of Printing at Harlem was by cutting whole Forms in Wood from MSS. exactly written, and without Pictures. Such Perhaps was the Donatus, which might, bear date about.: Some fay. This appears Plain, ( faith Mr. Bagford ) from Copy Bocks which we have seen prin - ted at Rowe, Venice, Switzerland and England, as high as. The third way of Printing was with Single Types made of Wood; but who invented this is not known: it was at first esteemed so great a Rarity, that the Printers carried about their Letters in Baggs at their Backs, and got money at Great mens houses by Printing the Name of the Family, Epitaphs, Songs, and other small Pamphlets. The Fourth Improvement of this noble Art was the Invention of Single Types made of Metal: which is owing to Peter Scheffer, above mentioned, first Servant, and then Son - in - law to Fauftus, who work, d at Ment. Sometimes you have the names of these two men printed at the end of their Books, and sometimes not: Sometimes with Dates as high as the year and as low as. As for John Guttenkurgh, who by many Authors is said to be the first Inventor of Printing, we can - not find one Book with his Name and Printing. As the first Harlem Printing was only a book with Pidlures, and the Impression taken off with a Lift coiled up, as our Card - makers do now use: So when they came to use Single types, they made use of stronger Paper, with vellum and Parchment, and then the Press was first used; tho ’ afterwards much improved; as was their Printing Ink. Rplling - Press Printing was not used in England, rill K ), James I. and then brought hither from Ant - were by our industrious John Speed. As to the Art or Practice of Printing its self ’ tis so useful to the Common - wealth of Learning, to have it better understood by Authors and Editors of Books than it dually is, that I shall here give a full A a full but fuccinbfc Account of the whole matter from Mr. Moxori s Mechanick Exercises of Printing; and from what I could colled: from my own Gb - serration, or get by Information. The principal Officer in this affair is called the Master Printer: who contrives or finds a Room or Rooms, for setting up what they call a Printing House; or who furnifties a proper Place ‘ with all Tools, and Instruments used in Printing. After the Second or Third Proof he has a Rev if e which is also a Proof - Jheet i He examines in this Rev if e Fault by Fault, if all the Faults he markt in the last Proof were carefully mended by the Com - fofitor j if not he marks them in the Revise.

prints.c: PRINTS. The Original of Prints or Cuts, as we sometimes call them, was this; in the Year, one Mafo Finiguerra, a Goldsmith of Flo - rence, graved his Plate; and then calling some of it in melted Brimstone, he perceived, that what came out of the Mold was markt with the fame Prints as his Plate, by the Black which the Sulphur had taken from the Graving: after this he tried to do as much on Silver Plates with wet paper, by rolling it Smoothly with a Roller, and this Suc - weeded. This IN novelty tempted Baccio Baldini, a Goldsmith of the fame City, to attempt the fame thing, which he did with Success; ingravirg Several Plates of Sandro Boticello ’ s Invention and Design; and upon this Andrew Mantegna, who was then at Rome, Set about engraving some of his own Pieces. This knowledge getting into Flan - ders, Martin of Antwerp, a famous Painter, graved abundance of Plates of his own Invention, and sent several Prints into Italy, which were markt thus, M. C. After him the Famous Albert Durer appear ’ d and gave the world a vast number of Prints, both in wood, and copper. About this time one Hugo de Carpi an Italian Painter of no great Capacity, but of a ready Invention, found out a way, by means of several Plates of wood, to make Prints resemble Designs of Claro - Obfcuro: and some Years alter the Invention of Etching was discovered, which Was soon made use of by Par - meggiano.

procurations.c: PROCURATIONS, are a Pecuniary Sum of Composition paid by the Pafilh Priest to an Ordi - nary or some other Ecclesiastical Judge, as an Archdeacon, &c. to commute for the Provision or Entertainment Which was otherwise to have been procured for him; which Entertainment was cal - led a Procuration.

procurator.c: PROCURATOR, is used for one that gather - ed ! the Fruits of a Benefice for another man; R. z Stat. j. c.. as Procuracy was the word for the Instrument imbowering him to do it. In the Weft, such Persons are called Proctors to uus day. Cow el. p R o - -....

prodeshomes.c: PRODES Homes This is a Title often given in our old Books to the Barons or other Military Tenants, who were Called to the King ’ s Council and was no more than Homines discrete & fideles.

proserprofrum.c: PROSER, Profrum vel Proferum; is the Time appointed for the Accounts Of Sheriffs, and other Officers in the Exchequer; which is twice a Year. An. H... In another Sense Proser alio fig - nifies the Officer or Endeavourer to proceed in any Action by any Man concerned so to do.

profileinfortification.c: PROFILE, in Fortification, is the Reprefenta - tion of the Height, Depth and Thickness of any Work; and fiippofe the Work Cut perpendicular - ly down from Top to Bottom; as in the Figure annexed, where you have the Profile of, a Ram - part, FauJJ'ebray, Fojs, Covert - way and Esplenade, ab Ini is the Solidity of the Rampart, a in its Base; b l its Top; be its perpendicular Height; a b its inward Talus or Slope; l m its outward Talus or Slope; h e is the Terre - plain; e l is the Base of the Parapet, ed its Banquet ', fh is the in - ward Talus of the Parapet, i l the outward one, hi its upper one; hi is the inward Height of the Parapet, i k. the outward Height; / the Cor - don; n op q represent ts a Fauffebray with its Ban - quet, &c. q r is its Lipicrc or Term; r s tu x is the Soss or Ditch; r s the Scarpe uy the Coun - terfearpe; t the Lunette; w u the Depth of the Ditch: xy the Covert - way; x the Parapet and Glacis of the Covert - way: y the Height of the Barnquet and Parapet of the Covert - way; x the Basts of the Glacis; the Slope of the Glacis.

prosevicecomitis.c: PROSE Vicecomitis. Tho ’ the certain Debet of the Sheriff could not be known before the fi - wishing his Accounts, yet it seems there was anci - ently an Estimate what this constant Charge of the Annual Revenue amounted to, and what the con - stant Allowances amounted to according to a Me - dium; and those Summs were paid into the Ex - chequer at the Return of the Writ of Summons of the Pipe; and they were and are to this day cal - led by this Name Profre Vicecomitis. But altho ’ these Profers are paid, yet if on conclusion of the Sheriffs Accounts, and after the Allowances and Discharges had by him, it appears that he be in Surplulage, or that he be charged with more than indeed he could receive, he hath his Prefers paid or allowed to him again.

projectiledialling.c: PROJECTILE Dialling, is the way of Draw - ing, by a method of Preje & ion, the true Hour - Lines, Furniture of Dials, &c. on any kind of Surface whatsoever, without any regard had to the Situation of those Surfaces, either as to Declinati - on, Re - or Inclination, This curious and in many Cafes most useful manner of Dialling, seems to have been the Invention of our Mr. Sam. Fojler f formerly Astronomy Professor in Grejham College Something of this was Printed in his Pofihumous Mifcellanies, and more added by Mr. Ley - burn ( in his Dialling ) from a Manuscript which Fefier left behind him. In order to perform this manner of Projective Dialling after Mr. Fojler s way, there is necessary a Semicircle divided into two Quadrants, whole Divisions must begin, and be numbred both ways from the middle Point in the Arch, to the Diame - ter; which Diameter must be made to receive a Ruler into a Grove made in it, so as that the Semi - circle may Hide easily along it, and be fattened by a Serve any where upon it: It will be convenient to have two or more of these Rulers of different Lengths. You may see the Fig. of this Semicircle and Ruler in Leybourns Dialling, p.. But there is no difficulty in understanding the use of it at all; and a Quadrant, divided on both sides, may very well supply the place of the Semicircle. The General Use of this Instrument is; Upon a Line dr awn any where, to projeB an Altitude or De - pression, above or below the Horizon, from a fix ’ d Point placed at a distance from that Line. The manner of doing which is very easie; For if you bold the Edge of the Ruler to the fix ’ d Point, and also apply the Point of that Edge of the Ruler to the Line given, removing it higher of lower ( as occasion requites ) till the Thread and Plummet of the Semicircle or Quadrant fall on the degr of Altitude of Depression intended; for then thS the Ruler lies at the Altitude or Depth, and lo projects it from the fix ’ d Point into a Line, as was designed. Two General and Easie ways to projeB Hour Lines on all Surfaces, Concave, Convex, & e. Inclining, Inclining or Declining. i. Let a Gnomon, being first fharpened into a Point, be shaped, and fastned in such wife, that it no way hinder either the draught of the Horizon - tal Line, or the Point of the Shadow from having free access to the Dial at all times of the Yean z. Draw an Horizontal, Line, by help of your Semicircle in a true Level both in regard of it self, and also to the Point of the Gnomon, through the whole Superficies on which the Dial is to be de - scribed. Or having two Points in the fame Level with the Point of the Gnomon, project it upon your Superficies, if it be a rugged one. And if the Superficies be more than one, or if any of them be very much inclined toward the Horizon, or else be very rugged, or far remote from the Gno - mon, so that it will not at all, or not so well, re - weive an Horizontal Line upon it, you may Either fee up some Board, or such like Objedf, upon which for a time you are to inscribe the Horizontal Line, and by help of which the Hours were to be projected upon the Superficies; Or else ( which perhaps will be better ) you may extend a Thred in the l ( air ( fit matters not which way, nor whether from the Gnomon towards the Sun, or from the Sun: whether stretch out in one length, or with returns, so long as it lieth justly parallel, in every Point of it, to the Horizon, and inthe fame Level with the Point of the Gnomon: ) which being fix - ed in this manner, will very well supply the use of the Horizontal Line: or the Horizontal Line may be partly Thred, and partly drawn upon the Su. perficies, as occasion shall be. And upon it may any Point be transferred, and signed out by flip - ing knots of Thred tied upon it. . Upon the Superficies of the Dial, observe the Point of the Shadow of the Gnomon ( making a mark at it ) and the Sun ’ s Altitude, both of them at the fame instant of time. . By the Altitude observed, compute the Ai - much of the Sun from the Meridian. . The fame Azimuth must be transferred unto, or projected upon, the Horizontal Line by help of a Perpendicular Thred, covering to your fight ( as it hangeth down ) the Points of the Gnomon and Shadow both together; and at the fame view cut - ting through the Horizontal Line: observe then own & ually where it cuts through the fame Line, for that fame Section being signed thereon, shall be the Azimuth projected into the Horizontal Line. . Let any kind of Board or Past - board be now applied to the Point of the Gnomon; so, as that it may be staid, either upon the Horizontal Line ( where it may so be conveniently ) or at least so placed toward the Horizontal Line, that it may have a just respect unto it, and in that pofturemay have some stay for the edge of it to reft upon, that after it is furniftied with such necessary Lines as must be drawn upon it, it may be placed in its former just posture without any Impeachment. Upon this Plain so placed, let the Point of the Gno - mon be signed, which may be called the Center; and from this Center, to the Sign of the Azimuth, before prove & ed into the Horizontal Line, draw a right Line: this right Line so drawn, shall rere - fen t upon the Board or Past - board, the fame Ai - much which was before computed. . Then taking away the fame Plain, draw up - on it the Meridian or Line of iz; extending it from th Center before noted, at the true Angle that it hath from the Azimuth before computed and described, and also toward the true Ccaft of the World. And let it be extended on both sides the Center if need be. . To the Meridian so pitched upon the Past - board, draw ( from the Center ) the Lines of an Horizontal Dial made to the Latitude wherein you ate. . Then again, let the plain Board or Past - board be applied to its former situation, the Center of the Horizontal Dial resting upon the Point of the Gnomon, and every thing else answering to the fame just posture that it had at the first. Which done, let a Thred be fixed in the Center of the Horizontal Dial, by help whereof you may trans fer every Hour from the Past - board into the Hori - ontal Line. Let every Hour be therein noted ( by fixing marks upon the Horizontal Line where it is drawn, or by slapping Knots upon the Thred, where a Thred Horizontal Line is used ) especial - ly mark out the Hour of z: For which ( if it chance to run besides the Superficies ) some kind of Objecft ( whereon the Horizontal Line is alio to be ' drawn ) or an Horizontal Thred must be fastned, that may receive it, till such time as your Dial be finiflied. . After all this, take your Plain away ( f r there will now be no more need of it ) and cone - dure whereabouts the Axis of the World, would pals from the Point of the Gnomon to the Poles of the World, for into that place is the Meridian to be projected. Which that it may be done more commodiously, if no objeeft stand in the way that will receive it, you must place one there, it mat - ters not whether above or below the Gnomon, chuse that which is most convenient: Or, a Thred laid aslope in the Meridian justly as it ought, will serve as well as may be. If then you hold up a perpendicular Thred, so that by your Eye you may see the Point of the Gnomon, and also the Point of z in the Horizontal Line, both together, the fame Thred so hanging, shall shew where the Meridian is to be drawn. Or, you may extend a Thred from the Point of the Gnomon to the Point of z in the Horizontal Line, which Thred shall represent the Line of iz: And flaying your Thred there, close to it, hang up two perpendicular Threds at a good distance, so shall the fame two Threds, give you the track of the Meridian Line. ji. The next Work will be to project one of the Poles of the World ( that namely, which lies the fame way that this projected Meridian doth from the Point of the Gnomon ) into this Meridian. And this is done by elevating or depressing your Semi - circle, from the Point of the Gnomon towards the Meridian Line, according to the Latitude of your Place; for so will the Ruler of the Semicircle, or a Thred extended along by it, Sign out the very Pole Point. If now you extend a Thred from this Pole Point, to the Point of the Gnomon, the fame shall represent the Axis of the World. z. Last of all; by thele helps, all the Hours may easily be projected. For if the Eye do lay, or project, this Thred or Axis upon each Point of those Hours that were inferred before into the Horizontal y : rizontal Line, the Axis upon an Hour Point, of a Point upon the Axis, each one of those Projections hall represent upon your Dial, each of the Hours required, and will slew upon every Object that stands in the way, where the Hours are to be drawn. Or, where convenient room is wanting to place the Eye, so as it may make this Projecti - on there may two Threds be used for the fame purpose, one whereof must be fastned to the Point of the Gnomon, the other to the Pole designed in the Meridian Line. Then stretching one of the Threds to any of the Points noted in the Horizon - tal Line, and holding it there, you may take the other, and extend it to the Superficies, so as it may riofeiy pass by the first Thred, by which Work you may make as many Points upon your Superfi - cies as you please, thro ’ which each Hour is to be drawn. Having thus traced the way before hand, you may afterward draw the Hour without any difficulty, be the Superficies never so irregular. Among which Lines, the Shadow of the Point of the Gnomon, as it creepeth along, will shew the Time of the Day. If a Point be assigned upon any Superficies Flat or Curved, one, or more, wherein the Hour - Lines and Axis shall concur, how to project the Hours to that Point, and to fet up an Axis after the ord - nary manner to give Shadow to them without any knowledge how the Dial standeth, in respect ei - ther of the Declination or Inclination. . To the Point assigned ( upon any side of it ) by direction of your Semicircle or other Level, stretch out an Horizontal Thred, serving for the Horizontal Line: this Horizontal Line need not be one direct Lind, but may be turned at one or more Angles, provided that it lie totally in the Superfi - cies of the Horizon. . With a perpendicular Thred held up, project the Sun into the assigned Point, and into the Hori - ontal Thred, and tie a little mark of Thred upon the fame Horizontal, through which the Shadow cutteth. At the fame instant also, take the Sun ’ s Altitude. . By the Altitude taken, find out the Azimuth j This Azimuth, what - ever it be, is represented. by the knot. ' V . Apply a Past - board to the Assigned Point, and hold it fiat that it may answer to the Horizontal Thred also, and upon this Past - board, protract your Azimuth by a Thred extended from the Poi t assigned for the Center, to the mark upon the Horizontal Thred. This done, . By help of that Azimuth upon your Past - board, protract the Meridian Line, observing the true Coast, and quantity of the Angle from the A - azimuth. and to the Meridian describe an Horizon - tal Dial. . Applying the Past - board to its place again, all things standing right as before, project all the Hours in the Horizontal Thred from off the Past - board, and fet marks upon the fame for the Points of each several Hour, which marks may be little moveable Knots to flip to and fro upon the lame Thred. . Projedt the Meridian Point by a perpend - cular Thred upon some object into that place whereabouts you imagine the Axis of the World would pass, above or below from the Point assign - ed for the. Center, . With your Semicircle elevated or depressed ( as it shall be required ) from the Point assigned for the Center, according to your Latitude project the Pole of the World. . Extend a Thred from the Point assigned fob the Center to the Poles of the World, which shall represent the Axis. . By the Point upon the Horizontal Thred, and this Axis ( either by your Eye, laying the Axis to the Hour - points, or laying the Hour - knots to the Axis ) you may project all the Hours and draw them; Or else you may let the Axis alone, and content your self with the Pole, point projected in - to the Meridian, for if from the Point assigned to be the Center or meeting of the Hours and Axis, you extend a Thred to each Hour - point in the Horizontal Line, and do repose ( with your Eye ) the fame Thred upon the Pole - point, then shall the Shadow of the Thred give you that Hour - line, and do so in all the reft. . Tour Thred or Axis lying in its true fitua - tion, you may easily fit an Axis to the fame po - fture. If your Dial be described upon a plain Su - perficies, you may then ( by one side of a Nominal Square, applied to a Thred or Axis, and the o - ther side lying upon the Plain ) find out the fub - style, and measure from it the elevation of the Axis above the Plain: But if the Dial be described up - on a curved Superficies, you must be content to fet up your Axis by the direction of the Thred only. ; This Point assigned for the Center being a Point of the Axis, is as it were the Apex of the Gnomon, unto which all the Work is projected. But if it be required to fet up an Axis to such a Superficies, upon which the Axis and Hours will hot meet in any tolerable manner, because perhaps the Axis may be but of very small elevation above the Superficies, and yet an Axis is required: in this case, fet up any Point ( of Wire, or such like ) of such distance from the Superficies, as that the Axis and Hours may be distinct: And through that Point let it be required to make the Axis pass, you have no more to do but only to project to this Point, as before, by letting the Shadow of a per - pedicular Thred pass through that Point, and no - r ting the sam upon your Horizontal Thred, and counting that end of the Wire as your Center, pro - ceed as before, for the Thred that lies to project the Hours is a pattern for the Axis. This way is as general as the former, serving to project the Hours upon many Superficies, be they plain or curved, and however situate whether con - tiguous, or separate, and that without any labori - ous inquisition of any of their Situations, in respect of Inclination or Declination. If you will put in that Furniture which is usual, you must make some Mark ( Notch, or Button ) upon your Axis, unto Which ( as representing the Center of the World ) by help of your Semicircle you are to pro - jedt the Altitudes of such great or lesser Circles as you intend to insert as hereafter shall be taught., The Propositions in the first way were to pro jedt to an Apex. These Propositions answerable in the second way are to project to an Axis. And after this method it will be easie, and of - ten very useful and curious, to Projedt a Dial from a small Hole made in a Pane or Quarry of Glass ( the reft of the Glass being covered ) or which is better, a Plate of Tin with a round Hole of of an Inch in Diameter, being put in the room of a Pane of Glass for the Sun shining thro that Hole will east a bright Spot of Light into the Room. Suppose then Inch a Hole to be the Nodus, or Point of the Top of the Perpendicular Style of any Dial, you may draw one or more Dials, ( each side or part of the Room being a different Plane ) after this manner. ( r. ) Apply an Horizontal Dial in a true Hori - ontal Position, so that its Centre lie in that of the Hole in the Pane; and then by a Thred fixed at one end of the Centre of the Dial, and laid over successively, every Hour, Half Hour, Quarter, ( c. find corresponding Points in the Sides of the Room where those Hour - Lines intersect them: Then ( z. ) The Twelve a Clock Line being an Azimuth alio as well as an Hour Line, you may by a String and Plummet brought just to touch that Thred when strained over the a Clock Hour Line, transfer that Meridian Line up to the Ceiling or down on the Floor, as you shall find occasion. (. ) Next in this Meridian Line find another Point, ( by help of a Thred elevated to a proper Height ( in degrees ) by means of a Quadrant ) from which, a Line or Thred extended to the Hole in the Window may represent either the DireB ( or Eeverfed ) Axis of the Earth; and therefore if you fix a Thred in one or both of these Points ( or rather Poles ) and extend it or move it along by the side of the other Thred, as it is brought suc - ceifively over every Hour Line on the Horizontal Dial ( in whose Centre, as well as in that of the Hole it is fixed ) and as it is extended to the corse - spending Hour Points before found in the Room: I fay, that moveable String shall any where on the Ceiling or on the Floor, trace out any Hour Line which the Horizontal Thred shall successively re - present. And this Method of Projedtive Dialling, will dired us into this excellent Mechanick way of Dialling or drawing Hour Lines on any Plane how irregular soever as to Surface or Situation. Under the Plane where you intend to make a Dial, draw a true Level or Horizontal Line, and then to it fet horizontally, a Scaffold or Frame of Boards, great - er or lesser, according to the designed Bigness of the Dial. Next, by some good Dial, Clock, E - quinodtial Ring, ( c. get exactly the true Hour of the Day, and fet your Minute Watch to it. Then place a good Horizontal Dial for the Lati - tude of the Place and which hath a fine String fattened in its Centre, on your Level Plane or Scaffold, and the Sun shining, turn it about till it shew the true Hour of the Day there. Then fix it; and by the motion of your Thred over every Hour, Half, Quarter, ( c. you may easily proved them all into your Plane or Place designed for the Dial,

prolatespheroid.c: PROLATE Spheroid, is a Solid produced by the Revolution of a Semi - Ellipsis about its longer Diameter; but if a Solid be formed by the Re - volution of a Semi - Ellipsis about its shorter Dia - meter; ’ tis then called an Oblate Spheroid: And of this Figure is the Earth we inhabit, and perhaps all the Planets are so too, having their Equatorial Diameter longer than their Polar.

promontory.c: PROMONTORY, is an Hill or High Land running out into the Sea: The Extremity of which towards the Sea, is usually called a Cape or an Headland.

proportionalscales.c: PROPORTIONAL Scales, sometimes also cal - led Logarithmetkal; are only the Artificial Num - bers or Logarithms placed on Lines, for the ease and advantage of Multiplying, Dividing, Extrad - ing Roots, ( c. by the means of Compares, or by Sliding - I uies; and they are only so many Lines of Numbers, as they are called by Mr. Gunter, ( See Gunter Line ) But made Single, Double, Triple, or Quadruple - beyond which they seldom go.

prostyle.c: PROSTYLE, in the ancient Greek Architecture, was a Rank or Row of Columns only, and whose Station was in the Front of a Temple, - or other great Building.

province.c: PROVINCE, was used among the Homans for a Country without the Limits of Italy, and gained to their Subjedion by the Sword. But with us the word is most commonly used for the Circuit of an Archbishop ’ s Jurisdiction; and in some of our Statutes ’ tis used for a County.

provision.c: PROVISION, in the Canon Law, is u ( ed for the providing of a Bishop or any other Person, an Ecclefiafticai Living, by the Pope, before the In - cumbent be dead. ’ Tis called also Gratia ExpeBa - tiva, and Mandatum de Providendo.

provisions.c: PROV ISIONS: The Ads to restrain the exon - bitant abuse of Arbitrary Power, made in the Par - ligament at Oxford,, were called Provifityis; because they provided against the King ’ s Absolute Will and Plealure.

provisor.c: PROVISOR, is he that sues to some for a Pro - vision;. which fee.

provostmarjhal.c: PROVOST Marjhal, of an Army, is one ap - pointed to secure Diferters, and all other Crimi - nals: He is to go often abroad round the Army, to hinder the Soldiers from Pillaging: ’ Tis part of his Office to indite Offenders, and to execute the Sentence pass ’ d upon them. He likewise reg - lates the Weights and Measures, and the Price of all Provisions, ( c. in the Army. There is also a
PROVOST Marjhal in the Royal Navy, who hath charged the Prifoners taken at Sea, Car.. c..

prudence.c: PRUDENCE, is by the Writers of Ethicks d fined to be a Habit of the Mind, by which a ' Man judges and determines truly how he should a t and proceed, what he should do or avoid, in all things relating to his Temporal or Eternal Advan - take, so as to render himself happy here and here - after.

pryantin.c: PRY AN Tin, is a fort of Tin that is found mix ’ d with a Gravelly Earth, sometimes White, but usually Red; ' tis nor half so good as the other which is made out of Stone.

ptolemaicksyjlem.c: PTOLEMAICK Syjlem of the Heavens, was that invented by Ptolemy; in which he supposes the Earth immoveable any way in the Centre of the Univerle, round about which the Moon first moves in a Circle; next her Mercury, then Venus: above whom moves the Sun, then Mars; above him Jupiter, and last of all Saturn, all in the Zo - diack from Weft to East. Above Saturn he places the Sphere of the fix ’ d Stars, which he supposes to move slowly also from East to Weft, on the Poles of the Ecliptick. While the fix ’ d Stars themselves, and all the Planets, move from East to Weft on the Poles of the Equator, in the space of a Natu - ral Day or Hours. This Vulgar System of A - astronomy, ( in which I omit to mention the Epi - cycles and Deferents, &c, with which they en - devoured to solve the Phenomena which did al - most most all of them contradict this Scheme ) vyas plainly overturned and refuted as soon as ever the use of the Telescope acquainted us with the Pba - fes of Venus and Mercury; for from thence it was apparent, that their Orbits included the Sun, and therefore by degrees it came to be quite disused, and consequently I shall fay no more of it.

pullet.c: PULLET, in a Ship, is a little Room within her Hold, in which the Piggs of Lead, or luch like weighty things are put, that the Ship may be well ballasted in a little Room.

pulley.c: PULLEY, is a Compounded Mechanick Pow - er, confiding of one or more Shivers or Ppndles with proper Blocks, &c. to raise up any Weight, &c. and this Instrument lo fitted is called Trochlea or the Pulley and at Sea with Ropes, &c. fitted so to it, it is called a Tackle, Fig, i. In every Pulley, from the Position and Number of the Shivers, you may know how much the Weight TV is dimi - wished, by making the Vis Motrlx, or Power, to be to the Weight:: as i to the Number of the Parts of the Rope going up and down. Only this you must ob - serve, that it is the lower Put - leys, or Blocks with Shivers, that give any Force to the Motion; for if a Weight hang on any upper Pulley or Shiver, it will require a Power to sustain it that hall be fully equal to the Weight. Fig Thus if a Weight hang as in the Position a TV, it would certainly fall, if a Force or Power equal to it did aot hold the Rope h d. And all upper Shivers being eve - ry where of the fame Nature, none of them can conduce any thing to - wards easing the Power or lighten - ing the Weight; but they only serve for the Convenience of the Motion. But if you suppose the Weight TV ( as in Fig. i. ) to be sustained by the Hook h, above the Block a h, then ’ tis plain that the Hook h Will sustain just: half the Weight, and therefore the Power at P need be but equal to half the Weight TV; for ’ tis all one as if the Weight were hung to the middle of a Balance or Libra a h, whose equal Arms were upheld by two several Strings, as ha and P b. ’ Tis also apparent in Fig. i. That in order to raise the Weight TV, the Height of one Foot, each part of the Rope, viq. ha, and Pp; ( ' ac - counting downwards from the Hook h ) must be made a Foot shorter, i. e. the Power must move a Feet, in order to raise the Weight but one: Wherefore in this Engine, the way of the Power is double to that of the Weight; and therefore their Celerities will also be in the fame Ratio; wherefore if the Power be to the Weight as i: to a, its Moment will be equal to that of the Weight, and so will sustain the Weight. pullnat.c: PULL NAT, in Architecture, is the Term for a Freeze, which swells out like a Pillow.

pumps.c: PUMPS, in a Ship, are of several forts, as the, Chain Pumps which are used in great Ships j and j these go with more ease than others, yield more I Water, and are easily mended. Bare Pumps, are S small ones made of a Cane or a piece of Wood j bored thro ’, and are used to pump Beer or Wa - ' ter out of the Casks. Bur - Pumps, are used by the Dutch, who have them by their Ships tides. In these there is a long Staff with a Bur at the end like a Gunner ’ s Spunge, to pump up the - Bildge - water: These are also called Bildge Pumps.

Those that stand on each side of a Door are called Door Pun - chins.

punctatedhyperbola.c: PUNCTATED Hyperbola is, an Hyperbola whose Oval Conjugate is infinitely small, that is, a Point. See Curves.

punctumfermatum.c: PUNCTUM Ferma'tum let Generatum, in Co - nicks, is a Point determined by the Intersection of a Right - Line drawn thro ’ the Vertex of a Cone to a point in the Plane of the Base, with the Plane that constitutes the Conick Section. See De la Hire's Latin Conicks, p.,.

punctumexcomparatione.c: PUNCTUM ex Comparatione, is either Focus, in an Elliplis and Hyperbola; and it was so called by Apollonius, because the ReCtangles under the Segment of the Transverse Diameter in the Ellip - sis, and under that and the Distance between the Vertex and Focus in the Hyperbola, are equal to part of what he calls the Figure.

punctumlineans.c: PUNCTUM Lineans j is that Point of the ge - aerating Circle which in the Formation of either Simple Cycloids or Epicycloids, produces any part of a Cycloidal Line. See Epicycloid..

punitoryinteress.c: PUNITORY Interess, is a Term in the Civil Law, for such Interest of Money as is given for Delay, or Breach of Trust.

purehyperbola.c: PURE Hyperbola, is one which by the Impofft - ability of its Roots is without any Oval, Node, Spike, or Conjugate Point. See Curves.

purgativemedicines.c: PURGATIVE Medicines the manner of their Operation is very well accounted for by Dr. Cheyne in his Book of Fevers, thus: Purgative Medicines being receive ’ d into the Stomach by the Mouth, their Particles do there vellicate or stimulate the Fibres of the Stomach, and thereby encrease the Digestive Faculty i. e. bring the Muscular Fibres of the Stomach, and the Muscles of the Abdomen and Diaphragm into more frequent Contractions than ordinary, till they are admitted into the Inte - ftines; the Fibres and Glands of which being more sensible than those of the Stomach ( whose Parts, by the frequent rough Contacts of one again ! ! ano - ther, and of the gross Bodies which. are often thrown into it, are as it weredpadnedj they easily move and bring them into frequent forcible Con - tractions; whereby these Glands are squeezed, and so emit a Fluid which Lubricates the Passages: And this mixing with the Fxculent Matter cf the Intestines ( which is rendred fluid by the fame a tive and stimulating Quality of the Purgative, Medicine ) renders it more fluid; by which, and,; by p y T by the uncommon Contractions of the Intestines, it passes more easily and plentifully into the Re - Bum InteJlinum, and is thence ejected by Stool. Thus gentle and easie Purges act, and d only cleanse the Intestines, few of their Particles entring in by the Lacteal Veins and so affecting the Blood: But in violent Purgatives, the stimulating Particles are mixed with the Blood, and produce there ma - ny times very great effects by occasioning unnatu - ral Fermentations, by separating the natural Cohe - signs of the Liquors of the Body; and also by v l - locating the Spiral Fibres of the Veins and Arteries, bring thole into more forcible Contractions, and thereby accelerate the Motion of the Blood; all which may sometime. es have a good and sometimes a bad effect,
